of so much of actual devil worship, and of so much more of vague supernatural fear; all this insensibly melts from the mind as we study the evidence before us." "In that faintly open- ing world of spirit I can find nothing worse than living men." How forcibly th*Roman Catholic attitude on this question reminds us of the Scribes and Pharisees nearly -2,00571 years ago,. It was the self same cry that assailed b lesua. ," hath a devil," they said, because he did no adhere to the aimless mass of ritual of the Mosaic theology. Joan of Arc was one of the purest and noblest of women. Her record of, heroism and self-sacrifice has never been surpassed, yet the Church of Rome made the greatest efforts to damage her character. But they failed, and not a single charge was proved. They said she had a devil, because her mission was not ortho- dox, and it did not suit the priests. And so it has been from age to age. W. must, as a Consequence f such allegiance, accept, without question, his opinion upon a totally different matter? Also; is Mr. Ashworth quite sure that if Penningion were living to-day ho would, accept the proposals of the N.S.b. assuming him to be in favour of defending our shores against invasion?

Mr. A. Long's contribution carries one farther into the mire, fie. says: it is no use saying • • • . . that one discs not believe in. war." May I ask if by that he ineans that the N.S.L. does believe in war, and as a consequence is , advocating a nation in arms? If, however, one I says one does not "believe" in war, is that an indication that one is oblivious to the possi- bility of war breaking out at any moment? Per- haps Mr. Long will explain. Mr. Long is also of the opinion that because Jesus said, "When a strong man armed keepeth his palace, his goods are in peace," the N.S.L. is justified in advocating National Service. Now, sir, I maintain that this is not sound largument; rather is it likely to injure the cause Iso many Leaguers have at heart. As a matter of I fact, the above quotation has nothing whatever to do with a National Army, or its twin brother, Conscription. Mr. Long might refer to Farrar's Icommentary on St. Luke, p. 214, for a reliable

, explanation of his quotation. The fact of Jesus having thus, metaphorically spoken, by no means justifies the existence of the N.S.L. any more than it would he justified in disbandinq merely because Jesus said: "Seek ye first the Kingdom of God and,llis righteousness;" Matt. vi. 33.

One of the fundamentals of Christianity is peace and *brotherhood, and if Christianity is to be carried to its logical conclusion no Chris- tian can conscientiously advocate the taking up of arms. If it is necessary to be prepared for war—l do not say it is not—then the Christian nations of the world either have no confidence in the efficacy of Christ's Gospel, or have not yet imbibed the spirit of the teaching of Jesus.
JAS. iIAMPSON.
92, Oldham-street.

MR. CROSFIELD AND NATIONAL SERVICE. ,Sir,—There are two qualities we Liberals usually require and demand from the man who seeks to carry the Liberal flag when he-is cam- paigning for Liberalism; fairness in his argu- ment and lucidity in his statement of our case. Judged by his performance at Widnes, Mr. Cvosfleld is neither fair in his argument, nor lucid in his statement of the series of charges he levels at his opponents and his political friends who differ from him on one important issue.

Quite frankly, I propose to attack Mr. Cros- field on both these grounds, and I begin at the point where you report the gx-M.P. for War- rington as saying: " After the sound beating we have given them at three successive elections, the Tories see they have no chance of worsting us in a frontal attack, and it is the more necessary for us, gentlemen, therefore, to be on our guard against any attempt to defeat us by an attack on our flank. I propose to say a word or two about that, because this part of the country is an active centre for the efforts made by the mem- bers of the National Service League to intro- duce what they describe as universal military service, but what we have to, deal with more briefly as threatened conscription." As an example in the art of becoming in- volved, this would be difficult to beat, and I cannot imagine any prospective Liberal can- didate feeling specially urgent in claiming to be its author.

But the point to which I take special excep- tion, and make objection, is where Mr. Crosfield expressly declines to distinguish between Universal Military Service and Conscription. Some Liberals, at all events, have the satisfac- tion of knowing that there is a difference be- tween these two principles and that this differ- ence is recognised by• the Liberal Secretary of State for War, Colonel Seely Here is my proof:

The National Service .(Territorial Force) t ill was introduced in the House of Commons on the 11th Anril, 1913, by Mr. Sandys, the Conserva- tive Member for Wells, and seconded by the Liberal Member for Newmarket In the course of the debate, Colonel Seely said "I repeat that if anyone tries to attack the lion. gentleman (Mr. Sandys) in his constituency because he has supported.- Universal Service in this' Bill, I will go down and(Viipixirt him—not uptm any other grounds, Imit on this gcound— because we know he has supported it from purely patriotic motives." And the question I wish Mr. Crosfield to answer is: Would Colonel Seely have given such an undertaking and pledge if there is no differ- ence between Universal Military Service and Conscription? And again I must quote Mr. Crosfield :

There is another type of men with whom I am sure you are familiar—the type of men who are always telling us they hate party politics, and stand themselves only for the interests of the nation, and yet, strange to "say, seldom miss an opportunity for stabbing Liberalism and the Progressive party in the back." I do not undertake to explain what Mr. Cros- field may have had in his mind at this stage of his remarkable speech, but I do definitely ask him a second question: Does he suggest that we Liberals who desire a satisfactory and efficient home defence Army are stabbing Liberalism, in the back? If he will make this suggestion in writing, or eminciate it with .unmistakeable clearness in his next speech, it shaft be answered.

Again Mr. Crosfield "It seems to me a little bit fishy that this violent agitation for compulsory military ser- vice, and all the. lurid talk we have had about the imminent danger of overwhelming disaster with which this country is threatened, shuuld synchronise with the advent of a Liberal Gov- ernment to power." _

I leave Mr. Crosfield's elegant expression in the first line to the quiet contemplation of his friends, though I would remind him that the more or less descriptive language such as he elects to use is • no ordinary substitute for lucidity or .simple eloquence. I challenge him to prove the statement that the agitation for compulsory military service is violent, and that it did synchronise with the advent of a Liberal Government to power.

Meanwhile .permit ,me to add if Mr. Crosfield can prove that the propaganda organised and conducted by the National Service League deviates in the slightest degree from every, ac- cepted constitutional method, I will offer to him the loan of two motor cars for use on the next occasion he goes to poll at Warrington. Mr. Crosfield's airy statement that the National Service League propaganda did syn- chronise with the advent of the Liberal party to power is an imaginative episode not belong- ing to recent political history, but in case. Mx. Crosfield requires definite confirmation, I shall not hesitate to gratify him.

Then, and in the most vague and indefinite terms, Mr. Crosfield proceeded to charge " people" with exploiting Lord Roberts. With every respect I submit this sort of warfare is undignified, and it is not the usual Lancashire method of conducting an attack. If Mr. Cros- field will he good enough to Say who these dreadful people are, he may save his face in part, but I do suggest to him that Lord Roberts' is hardly the type of Man to lend himself to 'exploiting; and no Englishman, save the pros- pective Liberal candidate, would be guilty of attempting to besmirch Lord Roberts' reputa- tioni - with a stain so ignoble. Exploiting Lord Roberts is the miwning touch to a. speech unworthy of any public man, and, most of all, unworthy a place in the speech of a prospective Liberal candidate.

Finally, and in keeping with his utter want of lucidity, Mr. Crosfield proteeded to give What he was pleased to term a definitioü of the Lib- eral military policy; but, unfortunately for himself, he was contented merely to quote Mr. J. A. Spender and the Navy. There he ended, but it does not prevent me from asking Mr. .Crosfield if the defences of our Empire can be adequately Served alone, by the Navy? • From tiff report ~of the Widnes speech, Mr. Crosfield would infer that all, we do need for our defence is the Navy. If this does not accu. rately represent Mr. Crosfield's view, he has only himself to blame; but he will not, I ven- ture to think, have reason to complain of lack of opportunity to make himself clear on ,this point to the palic if he desires to take advan- tage of the hospitality of the columns of "The Warrington Examiner." DAVID ELDER ANDERSON„ ChairMati of. the County Committee, The National Service League.

NOTICE TO C TILE Enrron of "The Examiner" invites corrt sPondence on all subjects of public interest.
Lerma should be brief and pointed. Their object must be to impart or seek information, not. abuse.
POLLUTING WATER. Sir,--Complaints are frequently made of the Wilful pollution of water in wayside troughs. _ .

Children wash their dirty hands, dip their dirtier heads, and put mud and refuse, into , them. Muddy dogs are bathed, and, worse still, cyclists fill their lamps, and in doing so manage to taint the water so that the thirstiest animal refuse it. Motorists use bucketfuls to refill their tanks, and oil finds its way into the supply. Rushing through the country. at express speed it may be difficult to realise *hat the drought means in many localities. Water has to be carted or carried long distances to outlying homesteads, and every drop is precious. Farmers and others depend much on watering their horses when pa:Ming public troughs. May I appeal most earnestly to motorists, cyclists, and the public generally, to remember the dire thirst of tired animals? No one should pollute or take the water which is of inestim- able value for their relief, and is granted from public or private sources entirely for their use. E. L. DAUBENY. Cheltenham, October, 1913. (For the Animals' Friend Society.)

From my observations and conver. sations with the boys, I am convinced -that by the time they reach the age for being transferred to the Citizen Forces, all their objections will then have vanished. (I held these conversations with the Cadets, being dressed in plain clothes at the time.) In my conversations with parents and men of a mature age, I found no objections; they seemed to look at it as an excellent thing; one of the strongest points in, its favour I think is that there is no dislocation of a boy's work, as in the case of the Imperial Regular Army, wheile a man leaves his work and is sent then- sands of miles away, -and gets entirely out of touch with civil life. From my observations. I consider that in about four or five years' time, when we will have had- thousands of boys trained, the thing will be- accepted is quite natural, as it will then have entered the homes of all the people. In one street that I was in, there were about 25 or 30 boys all belonging to the Senior Cadets, meeting together for parade and going off to drill just the setae as if they were attending a football match. They did not look or speak as if there was any compulsion about it. The very strongest advocates for the scheme, I found, were amongst the people who had come out from England, although the native-born Australian is also a strong advo- cate."

Sir,—With regard to Mr. Brimelow's letter in your last issue, one can appreciate the desire to accommodate • the conscientious objector under a scheme of compulsory military service, by affording him the opportunity of joining the ambulance section. But what guarantee can Mr. Brimelow give that such an alternative would be carried out? Even if it were carried out, it would be of no value. Though not in- tended by Mr. Brimelow, the suggestion is obnoxious. He has failed to understand the nature of the spirit of the conscientious objec- tor. To take cover, by joining the ambulance section, would be to play the coward, but one cannot imagine a conscientious objector accept- ing such a mean and selfish position. Men (or rather youths- in this case) such as these are not generally cowards, so Mr. Brimelow can rest assured that such facilities as are proposed would be rejected. It so happens that .the Australian colonies are providing us with the kind of treatment meted out to the conscientious objector by military authorities. Hundreds of boys and lads under age, who have refused to serve in the cadet corps, have been imprisoned. The perse- cution has been going on for months. These "Defence Acts" allow the parents of these boys no voice in the matter. In addition to impris- onment;:there arti further penalties, such as disfranchisement, loss of Civil Service employ- ment, &c., &e. The whole of the civic life is being dominated and controlled by the military authorities. And what is happening in Austra- lia and New Zealand may be accepted as pre- cedents of what may take place here, should
the principles of the National Service League prevail. Fortunately, the old country is far from being converted to these reactionary pro- posals.
Tr. GRAY

div.head: SALE OF DRINK TO YOUNG PEOPLE.
div.p: SALE OF DRINK TO YOUNG PEOPLE.

Sir,—" Reformer's letter in your issue of the 25th inst. is surely late in the day, when it ad- vocates the adoption of the "Gothenburg System" of Disinterested Management. This System has long been exploded as a true tem- perance force; in fact, a prominent local teetotaler recently admitted that Gothenburg was "0110 of the most drunken towns in Europe." Further, I believe lam correct in saying that the system was denounced at the anti-alcohol congress held in Paris some weeks ago. A system that produces—as Mr. Charles Smith, the secretary of the British Temperance League, tells us—much drunkenness arid tending to municipal and social corruption, and where, making a comparison in proportion to the popu- lation, he finds, in Gothenburg, the home of Disinterested Management, the drunkenness convictions to be nine times as numerous as they are in, England and Wales, seven times as numerous as they are • in our county boroughs and twelve times as numerous as in such cities as Leeds and Shef- field, is certainly not 'one for adoption here. With regard to the proposal to prohibit the sale of drink to persons under 18 years of age, it is scarcely any wonder that the proposal was defeated by such a majority when the Scottish Temperance Bill was being considered in com- mittee. The time has not yet arrived when the ordinary individual is prepared to carry his birth certificate about with him and produce it at the request of any over-busy official. Surely such suggestions of petty interference and re- strictions, fit only for a nation of savages, are not in keeping with the old spirit of liberty that once animated most Englishmen. • October 28th, 1913.
G. E. 110LME.

div.head: IRISH DIFFICULTY.
div.p: THE IRISH DIFFICULTY.

Sir,—My scheme of devolution and federation for the United Kingdom in general, and Ireland in particular, propounded by me in your issue of September the 27th, remains unassailed and unassailable. My opponents are ?educed to all kinds of subterfuges to avoid acknowledging defeat. While " r.W.R." boldly admits and brings forward the fact that his section of the Irish nation intimidate, and while he glories in the men of '67, Mr. O'Brien palliates the mis- deeds of t4se same people. I wonder whatimay be, or what they, expected from men who go about with loaded pistols and concealed daggers? I do not know which of these to despise most, whether the man who approves of intimidation, or the man who palliates it. So far as regards Irish history, I have no reason to shirk its investigation, but I see no ground for going into the old and musty records of the past to prove the present. We have suffi- cient in the history of the past 50 years to demonstrate the .safety or otherwise of Home Rule. Byer since the passage of Catholic eman- cipation there has always been a desire by all British Statesmen to ameliorate and improve the condition of Ireland, to make it peaceful and prosperous, and one of the latest steps was the Land Purchase Scheme, piroted by the late George Wyndham, one of Ireland's sincerest friends.

The great factor against Home Rule is the, determination of the loyal and industrious North not to be put under the heel of the rest of Ireland. It is the duty of the rest of Ireland so to act that it shall become clear to the loyal North that it has no ground to fear unjust treatment. When that period arrives there will be no need to muzzle the House of Lords to pass the measure, but all will coalesce for their own mutual benefit. At present that time has not only not arrived, but is some distance in the future, I, need .not prolong my letter any fur- ther, for really there is nothing for me to answer.
Let me, in conclusion, invite the attention of my opponents to.a letter in a recent issue of "The Times" on this subject by Sir Edward Clarke.
PHIL SQUOD.

div.head: NATIONAL SERVICE IN AUSTRALIA
div.p: NATIONAL SERVICE IN AUSTRALIA

Sir,—An old friend of many in Warrington wrote to me this week, and I venture to send some extracts from his letter to your widely- read paper. My' correspondent, Setgeant Stam- ford, formerly - with, the local Territorial Bat- talion, now gymnastic instructdr to the National Service recruits in the Royal Military College, Duntroon, Anstralia, after expressing his plea- sure at hearing that on -the occasion of their Majesties' visit to Warrington last July the "good old corps were well to the 'front," dis- cussed the practical aspect of obligatory mili- tary training in Australia. HO wrote : "On attaining the age of 14 years, a' Junior -Cadet is posted to an area situated as close as ;possible to his Own home. If the distance is 'great he is provided with tram or train fare. He remains in the Senior Cadets until he is 18 'years old, and is then posted to the Citizen „Forces. During the year he must perform 24 night parades (11 hours), 12 half-day parades ' (three hours), four full-day parades (six hours). Ile is supplied with uniform. The greatest objection to universal training I found in the Senior Cadets is owing to so many of the parades taking place on Saturday afternoons, and there- by debarring the youngsters from taking part , _ bin games, &c. As they are only boys between 14 and 18 I think this is quite natural, but that • to a great extent has now .died away, and the 2; boys are taking to the Service very cheerfully. It is, -of course, quite in its infancy, and these 1)9Y5 now undergoing it being the first to be k trained, it is quite natural that they would kick TIP, just a little at first.. 'There have been a few cases where the Boys have been committed to a -"Detention Barracks for shirking, drill, but there are very few cases now. I think that, taken on ;the whole, there is no strongly rooted prejudice

div.head: SPIRITISM AND ROMAN CATHOLICISM.
div.p: SPIRITISM AND ROMAN CATHOLICISM.

Sir,—l am not surprised that the Rev. P. L. Buggins clings to the " sppntaneous" theory, because it is the only plausible excuse they have now for discrediting scientific discoveries. It is such a Convenient theory, becaxise it may be stretched to mean anything, or owing to its vagueness mean nothing, and to the ill-informed it may appear important. c But why does he not answer my questions about the collective testimony of the Passionist Fathers? !They repeatedly recognised the ghest as a former member of the community who had died, and to whom Father Hubert admitted he had made a promise. There were, under the circumstances, no excuses whatever for sus- pecting fraud, eollusion, of hallucination. Now will the Rev. P. L. Buggins face these facts with some controversial honesty? Does he be- lieve the Passionist Fathers or not? If he does, are the facts more conSistent with the doctrine of Purgatory than with Spiritualism? As these questions about the Ardoyne case are both relevant and reasonable, I shall continue to ask them until they are answered. With regard to the Scriptural quotAtions, I hold that the Bible in a general way supports Spiritualism more than any other form of religion, simply because all kinds of phenomena and manifestations are therein recorded, and correspond with modern records, but I do not regard any part of it as evidential, or to be com- pared in value with scientific conclusions, based apon living testimony, and . a long impartial observation cf facts. If, however, it seems de- sirable to give quotations, it is much more con- sistent to choose them from the New Testament, simply because they are more in accord with the present laws and moral code. The quota- tion, or it would be more correct to say, the misquotation, which the Rev. P. L. Buggins has given us from Deuteronomy, is quite out of place in a modern controversy. How many things do the Roman Catholics neglect to do which are commanded in Deuteronomy? I can give a long list if necessary, but perhaps one will suffice to show the absurdity , of quoting from such a source. Tt is there commanded that when a son is rebellious and stubborn, his .parents should take him out to the gate of the city and have him stoned to death. Will-the Rev. P.' L. Buggins suggest that remedy at the 'present time? But there is, perhaps, a little excuse for him, as the priests have always been fond of quoting Deuteronomy, because it exalts their office and apportions their dues and tithes. After I pointed out in my last letter that men of high character Sand scientific eminence had cenducted seances for Over 20 years without tfinding anything demoralising, I hoped that the Rev. P. L. Buggins would not again use the word "immoral," but he has done so without the smallest justification. T must therefore tell him that if be continues to let his imagination carry him any further in that direction, I shall be compelled to refer to some historical records of the Confessional, which are infinitely worse than anything which can be charged. against Spiritualism. I have not had an opportunity of referring to Flammarion's books, but I do not believe the quotation given at the end of the Rev. P. L. Buggins' letter fully or faithfully reflects Flainmarion's conclusions at the present time. No one has published better 'or more definite testimony than he has, and most of it from Roman Catholics, who have in many eases seen and recognised their friends and relatives. But, fortunately, we are not dependent upon one or two scientists, as we have abundant evidence from all quarters. The late F. W. H. Myers, after 30 years of investigation, says in his book entitled "Human Personality," vol. 2, p. 78 : "All that world 'old conception of evil spirits, of malevolent powers, which has been the basis

div.head: "THE ARBITRARY POWERS OF BAD LANDLORDS."
div.p: "THE ARBITRARY POWERS OF BAD LANDLORDS."

Sir,—lt is rather a remarkable coincidence that Mr. Lloyd George's attack upon the arbi- trary powers of bad landlords should receive such striking confirmation in our own town. I allude, of course, to the generally successful attempt to raise in wholesale fashion the rents of working-clasaliouses Within the borough. Your 'readers may, or may not, have been prepared for this by a resolution passed at a recent property owners' meeting, to the effect that all rents should be raised to -tenants who were not paying their fair, proportion of rates. On the face of it, whatever' it meant, it seemed a perfectly harmless sort of procedure, and one felt perfectly assured that whoever were pay- ing their fair share would not be affeded. But the contrary has happened, and those wha probably felt the safest have been the first,- to be affected. ' Now, sir, I want to know what equity or justice there is, oirtaidek the resolu- tion, which thus gives the members of the Pro- perty Owners' _Association the legal, let alone the moral, right, to penalise 'certain 'respect- able, law-abiding citizens of the , borough?. I am well aware that the prevailing opinion is that landlords, good or bad, have the legal right to charge what rent they think proper, but it is not generally recognised that there is both an economical and a legal limit to such right, the economical being represented by vacant tenancy, and the legal by assessments. My reason for bringing this important matter before yOur readers 'is because' I believe very strongly that a very deliberate and unscrupu- lous violation of the property owners' resolu- tion..is taking place, making it absolutely neces- sary to prove that a very large number of ten- ants are paying much more than their fair share of rates under their present assessments. I need only state my own case, which is typical of many others to prove this. I have been paying for a number of years £l5 12s. for a house assessed at xll los. gross .value, and rated at .R 9 10s. Taking ss. per ,week as fair rent for .tla'innotbloe assessment, nlypayingmy fair pro- portion value, on he rata contributing is. per week toward my landlord's share. On the top, of this I am forced to pay another 3d. per week on the strength' of the famous 7es. ornesaoll9tioione,. abereienegeinienc nginyi'wonder what rent up to the members Of the Property Owners' Associa- tion have to say to this kind of interpretation y ever do, raise of it, and I also wonder how long the assess. movem e n t iauthorities t ea rii e Surely,goj.ng to t.: be ye, h. before power' otNi,h majorityyeyr: to compel landlords to report all raising of rents, or how do they, if the assessments'? If my own case is • typical ..f the Corporation 'coffers? . how much money has been going into the land- -book in lord's pocket, of which a fair proportion should have gone' into t In conclusion, is it impossible for. a liylaw to be passed compelling every landlord to state gross, and ratable value on every rent use? . FAIR RENT. Warrington, 6th Nov., 1913.

div.head: QUAKERISM AND NATIONAL SERVICE.
div.p: QUAKERISM AND NATIONAL SERVICE.

Sir,—Your issue of Saturday last contained three letters criticising 'the attack upon com- pulsory soldiering now being vigorbusly made by the Society of -Friends. • One writer quoted . Isaac Pennington's approval of defence against foreign invasion. I o'ingeorfoluvsm foreign Burrough advis- ing Policy to the Pro- t Edward could add a quotation from George Fox recom- . the Pro- tector, e nodtr nega and s dronsides to march to Rome The essential idea of Quakerism—that of individual enlightenment and personal conviction—is well illustrated by the discrepancy between our liv- ing convictions and these utterances, all of which come from the very earliest period, the. first decade, of the Society's history, "Peace" was no part of the original testimony of George Fox. He preached the indwelling God as the great fact of human life, and it took the early Quakers a little time, but not a very long time, to find out that all war was the enemy of the indwelling God. It was a practical deduction they soon made. To begin with, many of them were Cromwell's soldiers—and to the Common- wealth Army they looked to maintain liberty. But, at the very beginning of his organisation, in 1653, George Fox, then, as' ever, a natural leader of men, declined an offered commission, because he came "to lead men out of the spirit that caused all wars." About 1660 the testi- mony of the Society became fixed in its well- known form, and it was never held so firmly as it is to-day. The second correspondent says that conscien- tious objectors will be set to ambulance work. How does he know? It is not being done in Australia and New Zealand under the scheme of National Service there. There is relief only to the "religious" objector; and that is worked so as to apPlir to Friends alone. It would suit the Government Well to get rid of this troublesome body, who are too few to be missed as soldiers. But Friends scorn to receive a special privilege for themselves; they perform their national service in fighting conscription for their fellow-citizens, and so should we here. National Service League promises are worthless. The League will not ever be our responsible government. And I think but little of a body ' which, if it agrees with Lord Roberts, believes that it really takes three years to make a ' soldier, -but is so false to its native country as to advoaate, first 12 months, then six months, and now, for Infantry, four months' training, afterwards kept up in annual fortnights. That is all they think they can get at present. Beware of the insertion of the wedge, and of a political organisation so slippery! Your third correspondent has as little know- ledge of the nature of Christian teaching as the first has of Quaker teaching. Neither teaching lays down detailed laws of conduct. Both en- shrine a spirit—whose , fruits /are "love, ,joy, long-suffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meek- flees, self-control ",--and war denies all these. But there is no such definite text as "All War is Wrong "—and no attack upon the "Army, as your correspondent points out. Neither is there any word against drink, but, on the con- trary, Timothy is advised' to take a little Wine; or slavery—indeed, Paul returned the runaway slave, Onesimus. to his master, Phi-lemon; or the' position of Eastern women—yet the Chris- tian spirit made us, abandon slavery, and will yet make us abandon war. The New Testa- ment provides no ready-reckoner advice on speculation, light literature, aial plays, luxuries, Socialism, Women's Suffrage, or half the questions we have to face. We test them by its spirit, and 'that is how we test war.' National Service is an ill-considered, unneces- sary and reactionary scheme, launched at the Very time when civilised man is learning to look away from war. JOHN W. GRAHAM. Dalton Hall. Manchester.

Sir,—Being one of those individuals who still retain an open mind with reference to the pro- posals of the National Service League, and ever on the alert for arguments either for or against such proposals, may I respectfully ask Messrs, A.. Long and T. R. Ashworth just what they mean, and in what relation the N.S.L. stands in regard to the utterances of the two individuals quoted, viz., -Pennington and Jesus? • Does Mr. Ashworth wish to infer that, because Isaac .Pennington had no personal objections tc anyone taking up arms in defence of theii country, the proposals of the N.S.L. are neces sarily right, and that those who subscribe to the religious fonftula propagated by Pennington

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.
A DISEASE OF CEREALS AM) ROOTS.

Mr. Walter E. Coiling° has submitted a paper on "A Peculiar Disease of Cereals and Roots and the Action of Sulphur and Lime upon thG Same." On, a largo farm in Warwickshire in the' early. part 01,1,906 his.. attention Was directed to some- 40 or 50 •acr-es of wheat attacked by a disease locally known as " Maysick." Since then the disease had been observed in other localities in Warwickshire and at one in Cheshlre.':7

In various parts of the field, either in large circular patches, or in straggling lines, the wheat plants were turning yellow in the leaf and had attained a height only about half of that of the non-diseased plants. Later in the season such plants had a scorched appearance; very little growth took place, they never devel- oped ears, and were of' little use for straw. Oats and rye had much the same apdcareulce, whilst Mange's and potatoes turned yellow In the leaf, growth was arrested to a large extent, with the result that the ,roots or tubers were. undersized.

Experiments with varying quantities, of sul- phur and lime and sulphur showed that Sulphur sown in' the autumn for spring sowings•or in the spring for autumn sowings.' at.. the rate ,01 about'6 cwt. per act'e' afforiledc a complete cure. In other cases ground unslaked lime, applied before the sulphur was put on, gave even better results. As to the cause of the disease, the view formed was that it was due to bacteria that inter Wed with themutrition of the plant.

div.head: FOOD AND THE FLAVOUR OF MILK.
div.p: FOOD AND THE FLAVOUR OF MILK.

The influetlcr.: of food upon the flavour and keeping capacity of milk is not quite so fully rec9j;nised as it should be. In this country lyre is an almost universal admission of grains and turnips which .in Copenhagen are strictly forbidden. Time and :experience hive proved that without regulations of this kind the high character of the butteriwould be impaired, that the butter wbuld be affected. through the milk. The 'Use of grains, however; implies only half the truth: In summer; when this food is cheap, sweet, and appetising, it is purchased and pitted for use in winter,, when it becomes acid and foul, and although it is consumed by the cows in a mixed ration, it cannot be regarded as whole- some. %Turnip leaves', like the crowns of the swede, convey flavour to milk, while turnips themselves are quite impossible in the produc- tion of good butter.; indeed, mangels, which are of quite a different character, are unsuitable for cows in a butter dairy, allthough beet, like car- rots, are permissible in a limited sense. In this country both ,linseed and cotton cake are used by farmers -producing milk, but in Den- mark the farmer, is, in producing milk for sale, practically confined to rape cake, which, if less palatable, is one of the cheapest or foods. Rich in albuminoids and containing a good quantity of oil, it is at once nourishing and good for the enrichment of the manure, a fact which should not be ignored.

div.head: USE IN MODERATION.
div.p: USE IN MODERATION.

Even. this food, however, should be used only to a modest extent, and not exceed 21b. a day. The best dry foods of all tile large number used. are crushed oats and bran. Both are sweet, sound, and good for milk production, and abso- lutely safe for the cows. It is quite true -that less attention is paid to the food supplied' to cows whose milk is sold than where it is used for making butter; but this is chiefly because the milk consumer has not educated his palate to the same extent as the butter-maker. Milk is often a little disagreeable in flavour, and this is genc+ally attributed to the presence of some one of those wild' plants in the herbage, which are known to taint the milk,•but I believe'that more often than not it is due to the food which has been supplied. Vetches are an objection- able food in a butter dairy, and this fact is marked where the cows are .kept on the Soiling; system. Although that system has its advan- tages, it does. not contribute to .the health of the cows. It cannot be supposed that a cow kept entirely in a stall, however well she .may be fed, can retain health and vigour to the same extefit as a -coW at liberty on a good 'pasture, living entirely in the air. In-. Lheir practice, therefore,. English farnierS are right, and many of the farmers of the Continent Wrong.. -Where cows are supplied witri'grtien forage in auturrin it should be laid upon the pasture grass, and not taken to the stalls. •

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.

For worms in ti lawn put one pound of lime in a bucket of water and let it stand for 24 hours. Water the lawn with the clear water, when the \\*OrMS will come to the surface and can be swept off. Docks, plantains, and Other weeds in a lawn should now be got rid of by piercing the heart of the weed with .a sharp pointed piece of wood, clipped in some burning substance like creosote, paraffin oil, vitriol, weed-killer., or 'sulphate of iron solution. Decay soon sets in, preventing Ihe plants from producing side shoots. A most suitable plant for edgings. under -trees is ivy, which gives little trouble after it is planted, apart from one or two 'cuttings if it runs too much. Pieces put in now, and pegged down, will -soon root. - The common honeysuckle will grow in any aspect, but it llOwers best where it can get' some hours' sunshine each day.

A new French Marigold was recently shown, which is the exact counterpart of the Scotch marigold Meteor, which is golden yellow, with orange edges to the ray florets, instead of the usual brown Characterklic.of the French mari- gold. The flowers are double.
American celery blanches without being c;Lrthed up, and is said to, be equal in flavour to the ordinary kinds: It will not, however, stand frost.

The gooseberry is usually grown as a bush, but there are other shapes of cultivating this popular berry. There are advantages in 'grow- ing -trees on a "leg," or extra long stems, the fruit being kept well off the ground. Extra long cuttings should be utilised for this purpose, i)lanting ,them. shallow. Another form of g,roWth is on the cordon principle, all-owing three stems to branch off a rather long "leg."

TTING DOWN HERBACEOUS PLANTS. \ (any gardeners, on the score of tidiness, cut down their herbaCeous plants almost as soon as they have -given their last blooms. The old foliage protects the roots by keeping out mois- ture, which does more mischief than frost. Those who leave the foliage to die down .natur- ;llly have much better 'Mauls during the sum- mer months. -
The same remarks apply equally to ferns, the fronds acting as a proter•lion to the crowns.
I'On A SPRING DISPLAY.
As soon as dahlias are blackened it is time to take up the tubers, and, 'after drying by hanging them upside down in an airy place for a time, store them away for next season.

The autumn has been remarkably open, (nd !here has been a welcome display of bloom in the summer beds, longer than usual. •It will, however, be necessary to- clear away the tender subjects, and prepare for planting fOr az;(riqg display by ultilising bulbs, wallflowers, pansies, violas, double daisies, primroses, polyanthuses, auriculas, .aubrietias, arabis, silenes, thrifts, yellow alyssum', and forget-me-nots:- Among; these, bulbs may be planted with effect,. Work- ing but colour schemes to suit the individual taste.

div.head: MAI MN ROUGH DIGGING.
div.p: MAI MN ROUGH DIGGING.

All vacant soil will be greatly benefited by being turned over and left in a rough state through the winter. Heavy soils should be thrown up in ridges, without breaking the clods of soil. By the time spring planting arrives the soil will be in b. more friable state for cropping. The atmospheric agencies freshens the grounth wonderfully, allowing the bad gases from the fermentation of Organic Matter to escape, ,and reducing the numbers of soil pests. By the loosening of heavy soils rain water can more freely penetrate and drain away, and it will not be in nearly zo heavy a state when planting operations commence again.

div.head: WINTER LAYING.
div.p: WINTER LAYING.
Encouraging Ducks to Produce Cold Weather Eggs. WARM FCOD NECESSARY.

Unless stock ducks are supplied lineralfy with suitable foods in winter, eggs are likely to be somewhat scarce. It pays to supply good food to stock birds, particularly early in the season, for unless the materials for the formation of eggs are put into the duck's body, it cannot be expected to lay satisfabtorloly. If breeding ducks are permitted to become thin and in poor con- dition, their laying powers are seriously affected. When they have a free range and are able to wander _about arable and pasture land, they can usually obtain a large proportion of their own food, since they are; generally speak- ing, excellent 'foragers. Natural foods, sUch as NVOITIIS, grubs, seeds, &c., are excellent for them and, apart from their good feeding properties, they reduce the food bill very considerably:

WARM FOOD REQI.II{FD. When ducks are confined in a run—the other method is by far the better, both for the birds' themselves and for One's pocket—they require to be fed more liberally, and in this case they should receive at least two good meals a day. If the weather is very severe, or if there is an entire absence .of natural food in the soil, three meals 'must be provided. With ducks at liberty, save during very cold. Weather, one meal a day is usually ample. Warm food should be supplied during the -winter months, and a ration I have used with success is four- parts barley meal, three-parts middlings, two- parts maize Meal, and One-part bean. or pea t Heal. During mild weather the addition of two- parts brewers' grains .is recommended, as they are 'cheap and help to reduce the cost of feeding.

div.head: BARLEY AS A FOOD.
div.p: BARLEY AS A FOOD.

- WhilSt barley may be used as-a change wilD wheat ind oats, for adult stock, it is generallY found that, hens do not do well on it. In fact-, it r.iumot be claimed a good • egg-producer, and the fat formed is not of a "kind" nature. Bar- ley is low in flesh-forming, and its best state for all purposes is when it is malted, it being then an excellent aid to digestion. Pure malt is, of COUPSO, expensive,. but it is possible in most towns to purchase malt culms or combings, which are the sprouts Unit are brushed off the malt. These are comparatively cheap, and havti a higher iceding value for poultry than even malt itself, not only being easy of digestion, but also an aid to the digestion of other foods. Large quantities of barley meal are used for soft food, but Sussex ground oats mixed with sharps are preferable. The analysis of barley shows flesh-forming elements 9.0, fat 2.0, heat- producing 68.0, fibre 5.0.

div.head: DOG I'ELDS HENS.
div.p: DOG I'ELDS HENS.

.lit Indiana former named Sitka claims that his dog takes the .prize for intelligence, and points to an inci(lent showing this and an ,un- usual friendship between the dog and his prize poultry., .Sitka's grain is kept in a small Shed behind The, house, and Sitka found that when he left The door of this shed open the chickens would enter and feed themselves. This led him to place a. spring on the-floor, so that it would close of its own accord when open, and would only need a push to open it. Much to his sur- prise Sitka,found that his grain disappeared at an alarming rate despite all his precautions, and this led him to investigate. Seated at his window and watching the door of the shed, his attention was drawn to the dog, which sneaked up to the door, followed by several hens. Then the mystery was explained' when the dog pushed against the door with its nose and held it open while the berth entered, gorged them; selves and retired to roost.

div.head: " The Following of Christ."
div.p: " The Following of Christ."

"The following of Christ" was the theme, of the Rev. T. T. James at the Wycliffe P.S.A. on Sunday afternoon. What did that moan, asked the speaker, a marking of time? Ile did not think so. The first disciples left the boats and nets, .and, at the expense of their occupation, followed Jesus.. People to-day could not follow that example, as times and customs had changed, but if they could not follow the example literally they still could follow Christ. George Bowen was quoted by the speaker as affording an example of what could be done to- day. Bowen, as a young man, was an atheist. "If there was such a person as Christ," said Bowen, "let Him show me what I can do?" Jesus showed Bowen, and in India, where he was misunderstoOd by the people, Bowen realised what it meant to follow Christ. _ _

That was not the way all of them could follow Jesus. Life must go on, work must be 'done, employer and employed must exist, yet they could not follow Christ without rendering faith. ful service to God and man, faithful in their daily occupation, and doing always their best and giving of their best. That might seem diffi- cult in the common round of life under poor circumstances, but their mission kvas not to die for Christ, but to live for Him by assisting the poor, by being honourable and straightforward, and by seeking to become what Christ was, a blessing to the world. The Chairman, Mr. J. W. Travis, spoke about charity and Christian unity. The atheists sar- castically said, "See how these Christians love one another." What Christians 'should be was lovable and charitable to all. Mr. A spinall, of Orrel, led the prayer, "Mr. Yearsley read the lesson, and seven new mem- bers were heartily welcomed. Miss Morley ren- dered the hymn very sweetly, and "The lost chord" was admirably played as a cornet solo by Mr. W. Rutter. •

div.head: HALF-TIME MENACE.
div.p: THE HALF-TIME MENACE.

- Forty per cent. of the half-timers, said Mr. Morgan, the new president of the Half-time Council of Lancashire, Yorkshire, Cheshire and Derbyshire, at their meeting at Manchester on Saturday, were physically defective. The sys- tem was a serious national menace. The cut- look, he thought, was rather cloudy, but the new developments affecting children which had taken place in national and municipal life gave some ground for hope.

div.head: Now Number 30 Million, Says a Speaker at Bold-Street Anniversary.
div.p: Now Number 30 Million, Says a Speaker at Bold-Street Anniversary.
MAYOR-ELECT AS CHAIRMAN.

John Wesley started out with the world as the parish he intended to convert, and the denomin- ation he founded has since done so well that the speaker at the afternoon gathering in connec- tion with the Bold-street Wesleyan Church anniversary on Sunday was able to announce that the disciples of Wesley now numbered over 30,000,000. The gathering was enthusiastic and interesting, and it undoubtedly gave a great fillip to the cause of the Wesleyan Church in Warrington. The chairman was Councillor P. Peacock, the Mayor-elect of Warrington, and gathered around him on the platform were the 'Res, H. William- son and the trustees of the church, Messrs. J. Taylor, J. Weaver, F. Pendlebury, W. Gleave, and W. Isaac.
Councillor Peacock and Our Amusement Expenditure. - -

Councillor PEACOCK said that when he • was asked to preside at that gathering he imme- diately consented on various grounds. One reason he was there was due to the recoliection of his very early days, when he used to attend Buttermarket-street Schools, under Mr. Benson, and as he looked on the platform he was pleased to see present Mr. Taylor, who was one of the teachers at the Buttermarket-street Schools. He remembered that time because they used to walk to Bold-street every Sunday. He consented also on the ground that when men and women took up public work it was their bounden duty to help to further every good cause in the town in which they lived, and he was also present for other various reasons. Turning to the expenditure and income, the Chairman said that they were apt to forget their responsibilities for the upkeep of the fabric, the lighting, the warming, and every expenditure which the church had to meet. They could not compare what people gave in -church to what they gave for their amusements, and he felt quite sure that the deficiencies which the trustees had to meet year by year would be wiped off if the congregation would only give in proportion to what they spent in amusements. That chapel Was in the centre of the town, and he had no doubt that as the members of their congregation became better off they would go into the suburbs, where they would support the chapels there. Some Old members, however, did divide their attention between their old and new churches. In conclusion, he impressed upon them the necessity of wiping off the deficiency this year.

Tribute to Councilior Peacock. The Rev. H. WILLIAMSON, in opening his ad- dress, turned to the Chairman and said: ' it is only fitting that one should begin one's remarks this afternoon with a word of con- gratulation to you on the honour which you will shortly assume. And yet it is not only the honour on which I would congratulate you, hut rather on the wide sphere for service upon which you are now privileged to enter, and the number of opportunities awaiting you now, sir, such as you have never had before, and we, all of us, join together heartily in wishing you "God speed" in the task you will soon be tak- ing up." , ,(. The preacher further stated -that he might congratulate. Councillor Peacock on taking the chair at any gathering at their Methodist Church. It was always for one thing an honour to do anything that could in any way further the Kingdom of God, and if they liked to take a lower view it was still, an honour to have any connection, in one way or another, with the Methodist. Church. For one thing, the Metho- dist Church was the largest Church in the world.

Numbered Thirty Million. They were young, it was true; they had not lived very long, but the followers of John Wesley throughout the world to-day numbered 30,000,000 ,souls, and that was a' thing that no • other Church could claim. So if they could not ,go back through the centuries to endorse their authority and give weight to their words, they could still point to the great work they had done, and the number 9f men and women who owed all that was best in life to the work of the Methodist Church. Then, again, Methodism had something like .190,000,000 invested in eccle- siastical property, and when they put those things together - they learned, contrary to the view of some, that Metltdism was not an insig- nificant Church, a thing to be despised and trampled upon. It was not only a question of numbers, and it was not 'simply a question of wealth, but as a /Church they could claim to be a national Church because of the immense national, ser- vices that they had rendered, and to illustrate his point Mr. Williamson quoted from various authovities, Anglican and Methodist; to show the great work of the Methodist Church. and remarked: "We do not want to boast of these things, but as Methodists we do deprecate, and deprecate strongly, the spirit that would rele- gate us to the background, and that would treat us as a thing of yesterday." That day was their afiniversary, their birth- day, and what was their feelings as they tle- brated their birthday? He supposed that when one was at sweet seventeen they thought of what

div.head: FISH MARKET! WORKERS IN ULSTER.
div.p: THE FISH MARKET! WORKERS IN ULSTER.
Wooden Stalls to Give Way to the More Sanitary Marble Slabs.

div.head: QUESTION OF STALL RENT.
div.p: A QUESTION OF STALL RENT.

At the Warrington Fish Market several valu= able bnproxements are in progress. When fin- ished, Warrington will , have a fish market equal to the best in Lancashire. The stalls are in course of re-building, and the old wooden benches will give place to more suitable, as well as more sanitary accommoda- tion. The new stalls will consist of marble slabs resting on iron legs, and, while this will keep the fish fresh and, cool, the stalls will be Practically rat proof, and thus remove a .nuis- ance which is. a fault. of Hip' old stall system. Hats share with cats a passioh for fish, and they have been a plague at the market in the past. In fact, in one rat hunt recently an animal nearly the size of a half-grown cat was killed. Master Bat, in the renovated market, will find it less easy to gel a fish diet, and this denied him, he may be tempted to migrate elsewhere. Any way, if he does not, the means of exter- mination which the new arrangement offers will make ratty's " life less happy than it has been.
To Cost Over £3OO.

Along both sides .of the hall a , seven-foot screen is to be erected, to afford much-needed shelter to those engaged in work at the market. To afford better accommodation for customers the entrance is beingTwidened; storage space, which will be vermin proof, is to be provided, and the whole scheme will bring the market thoroughly up to date. The cost to the Cor- poration will be somewhere between £3OO and £400: 1

So far as the alterations go, the stallholders are fully satisfied'. There is a fly in the oint- ment, however,' and this is the threat to in- crease the rentals of the stalls, a new scale of rent being about to mine into operation. "Under the new scale," said one stallholder o representative, "1 shall have -v'e"fthoepaEyxagsim.6dv" .for the same frontage as at present I have for 4s. per week. I simply- ' cannot afford to pay such a rent. All of us; I think, are prepared to Pay something to recoup tile Corporation for the very desirable altera- tions, but. extortionate charges ought not to be made. In order to meet the extra rents some people are taking half 'stalls, but this method is not likely to prove a success."
Competition from Hawkers.

The stallholders, "The Examiner" represen- tative discovered, have other 'grievances. One is the competition from hawkers.. '"These hawkers,"_ said a StallhOlder. "pay only is." per week, .and go to the doors of customers, but we, on the other hand, have to pay stall Tents, and do our best to attract catotn, which we often find filched from us by the hawkers." There is the question, of the stalls on which ,cheese, sweets and cakes are displayed, and the dealers who trade solely in fish object to the "foreign" trade being introduced into the market, but, so far, their objections have been futile.

div.head: Convinced of the Future.
div.p: Convinced of the Future.

There had been changes; of course, there would be more changes as time went by, but as one who had laboured in that church for more than two years be could say that he was more than ever convinced Of the future which 'lay before the church, which they had met together to honour that day. . "We- are not dead, we are still living, and we are growing in life, and if God wills it we shall' grow more and more, and we will do more than we have yet done for the bettering of the men and women Who worship with us day by day," said the speaker, He concluded: ".Let me say, in conclusion, / appreciate your presence this afternoon. I. hope you will be amply re- warded for coming, and will always keep .a warm place in your heart for the old church which is celebrating its birthday to-day." , . The music was excellently rendered and in- cluded a couple of Selections by the Orpheus Quartette Party, Messrs. L. Aukland, E. Walker, W. Critchley and IL Cook. These were "Far from my heavenly home" and "Rock of ages." Solos were rendered by. Miss Hilda Cragg-James, a Birkenhead lady, "hear my prayer," "I. wig sing new soneof gladness" (Dvorak), and "Rest of the weary" (Wilfred Shaw). 16,. Frank Hickman's renderilig of "Concert Toccata ". (Mansfield) was particularly fine. "Lovely appear," a selection from Gounod's "Redemp- tion," was excellently given by the choir. Mrs. Booth was the soloist. Mr. F. Hickman presided at the organ throughout.
In conclusion, Mr. Williamson thanked Coun- cillor Peacock for presiding, and the Mayor- elect briefly replied.

div.head: Conditions that Prevail in Loyal Prosperous, Enlightened Belfast.
div.p: Conditions that Prevail in Loyal Prosperous, Enlightened Belfast.
REFINEMENT OF SWEATING.

Mr. Harold Smith, during, his open-air Orange campaign, stated that he had never seen such placards as "Hell roast the Pope" in prosperous Ulster. Now since I have it from a past Lord Mayor of Dublin that such was the case at Killykeen on the occasion of Sir Edward Carson's visit to Newbliss, I presume Mr. Smith will not say again that the same is un- true. However, I do not desire to dwell upon that again, but would direct the attention of the Catholics and workers of Warrington to ,a couple of letters which appeared last week in an Ulster Nationalist paper—having been for- warded by remarkably tolerant and educated gentlemen.

• , I. "Sir,—lf you don't believe we are in earnest come here (Belfast) and We will show, you and your, Papist crew that we are. 'No Popery,' no priests will interfere with Belfast's Progress. The city is progressing, while Dublin of the slums is starving; and bigoted Cork always in poverty. Are we going to swap for that? We are not slaves. We belong to a religion which allows us to think for ourselves; we do not lie under the tyranny of the Pope, and never We opened Churchill's eyes when he crept into Belfast and ran away as fast as he could. No Rome Rule.—Yours, &c., No SURRENDEL"
The second one shows how educated this Ulster loyalist is

"Sir,—What do you think of Winston Churchill? Home Rulers are running about Belfast the dsy with •their tails between their legs, like whipped curs. Yous may start the new. Home Rule is dead and damned. Your ould Papish sheet can —. Hell rip and ropt the Pope, you know.—SANDY Row."

There are quite a number of priests to ad- minister the spiritual wants of 80,000 Catholics living in Belfast—not an inconsiderable " frac- tion " to reckon with in the future happenings in that centre' of righteousness. —_ _ _

"The Lady Next boor," a book written last year by a Protestant, Harold Begbie, says of the, loudly-vaunted prosperity and piety.- of "No Surrender's" city: I would rather see my own children dead than working in the very best of the Belfast linen mills" and "A man would have to travel far before he found city where the foundational 'principles of Christianity are more ignored." The vast number of people in the city of Carson's Covenant . are, lie writes, 'horribly, wickedly, and disastrously poor." Think of it trade unionist! Ponder on it Worker!

Then Mr. Begbie gives the details of the wages earned by the ordinary workers in the linen mills, and states that when there is an agitation for an increase the usual remedy is a threat to put the workers on half-time. The home workers are in even worse case, and the sweat- ing of them is so atrocious that one wonders with Mr: Begbie how civilised men—men, more- over, who are enormously rich ,and ostenta- tiously yious—can bear to reap the profits of it all. A tablecloth, 45 inches square, takes a borne worker three days to embroider, working eight hours a day. "The remuneration is eight shillings for a dozen cloths"; in other words, eightpence a cloth, less than threepence a day. Divide threepence by eight, and you get the rate of pay per hour. Another firm gives out an immense amount of work called top-sewing, that is tucking in the tiny ragged corners of the fine cambric handkerchiefs and stitching them neatly down. It is work that puts an enormous strain upon the eyes, and demands the very best care with the needle. The cleverest worker can top-sew two dozen handkerchiefs in an hour, and the wage is a halfpenny per dozen. Therefore in an hour a woman earns id. A day's 'incessant work of eight hours brings .eight coppers into her purse. But she must go to and from the warehouse, :wait her turn. with a crowd of other iniserables; and buy her own needles and thread. Wesaw the wage-book of a poor young widow who does this work, with the help of her three little boys, who separate the handkerchiefs and thread the fine needles. These were the weekly earnings, varying with the amount of work she could obtain: 3s. 2d., Cs. Old., 6s. 14d., 4s. sid. The wage-book, of another cambric worker showed that between the 4th and the 16th of March she had earned us. 2cl. These books would not look well either in an employer's library, .or on the table of a directors' boardroom. They are documents fitted for the Congo. Another hymn, please, to glorious Belfast! What hypocrites! _ Cannot be Worse than Id. an hour. _

But that is not all. Mr. Begbie further tells us that in this city of Carson's. in which "Pro- visional Government" is to sit, the pay for stitching lace on handkerchiefs, one handker- chief taking threequarters of an hour to finish, i§ 9d. a dozen. Women stitch print shirts, find- ing their own thread, for is. 6d. a dozen. "Ladies'" blouses, Is. ,;(1. per dozen, one ,hour to a blouse, cost of thread 11d. a dozen blebses. Men's heavy. cotton • shirts, double sewing, is. 4d. per dozen, less 20. for thread, thirteen hours for one dozen, rate of pay a penny per hour." .4.nd there is nothing like this in Cork. We wonder if such men as "No Surrender "- 1 a sample of whom we recently had at Cornhill —ever 'read the report of the Medical Officer of Health, Dr. Baile, who • gives the case of a woman who was paid a penny for embroidering by ,hand 300 dots on a cushion cover; for a day's work of that kind she would have difficulty in making sixpence. He also mentions other workers who had to sew 384 dots on a handker- chief for a penny! 'Among the out workers in loyal, prosperous, enlightened ,Belfast, says .Dr. Bail°, "one, penny per hour is the ordinary rate, and in many cases it falls below this." Mr. Begble's caustic, comment is that even if everything foretold came to pass, after the Irish Parliament meets' in. Dublin, wages can hardly go below a penny per hour, and find your own thread and sewing machine; nor is it likely that even Mr. ,Redmond will 'be able to make some poor wretched woman sew more than 384 dots on a handkerchief for a penny. Now, is it to be wondered it that in the last year for which we have figures (1911), no fewer than 1,.21 in- fants under one year old died in this " pros- perous ".city of Belfast? It is not Nationalists 'or Romanists who have imposed on Belfast the awful conditions of which Mr.' Begbie. writes. " No Surrender" and Mr. Harold Sinlth must admit this, for their contention is that "Loyal- ists" rule the city. And this is. the result— women worked. to death, and no hope of ever bettering their condition. Does Mr. Harold Smith or any other "Loyalist" imagine that under Home Rule such a state of affairs would be allowed to continue, or that the "sweater"
would still have his own way of evil?
A trial

of native Government will convince to th& con- trary, and it is because of the fear of this that some of the linen lords and their friends, whose wealth has been amassed out of the blood and sweat of the toilers, have engineered the oppo- sition to Home Rule. But Bonin Rale will come whether they like it or not. The day of emancipation for Catholic and " Protestant worker is at hand, ..and tyranny .• will go down, never to raise its foul bead again. • • What is the . remedy you. ask? A Labour leader, .Mr. Henderson, has given the answer: "Home Rule." Worker, look yo a to it
F.W.R

THE REAL WISH OF THE FARMER.

. *lWe do not know what the land policy of the Unionists will he exactly. But we must assume that it will not be of a more purely vote-catch- ing character in the bad sense than that of Mr. George. If it is, then we deserve to be beaten. But, in the meantime, what of agri- culture itself? Most farmers, landowners, agents, auctioneers, and valuers, if asked what would be the best thing to do with agriculture, would say, Let it alone. .The doctrinaire May, of course, know better than the practical man, but it is doubtful. Of all the good and true things the late Lord Salisbury said, one of the best and the most true was that the two things that most affected agriculture were the weather and the prices, and that the Government could not alter the weather even if they would, 'and would not alter the prices even if ;they could. The condition precedent to all agricultural im- provement that human agencies can affect is the price of products and the amount produced by the soil. To manipulate the prices by means of a tariff is Protection, and seems further off than ever."—Lord Willoughby de Broke, "National Review," October.

div.head: PERIL OF THE SEA.
div.p: THE PERIL OF THE SEA.
Splendid Acts of Devotion to Duty
and Self-Sacridce.

To speak of this subject without reference, however slight, to the "Birkenhead," is to be guilty almost of an irreverence to brav- ery; for of all acts of human splendour, the deliberate intention of the men to drown, ra- ther than attempt to swim to the boats, in which were the women and children, is one that rises' so near to the sublime as to com- mand of us a never-failing memory. An in- cident regarding this world-famous deed has never, to my knowledge, appeared before in print. One. of the men swam to the nearest boat, caught at the gunwhale, and, raising himself somewhat from the water, handed in a small packet, saying, "Give this to ray wife, she lives at" (naming the address, which I regret to have forgotten), "tell her how it was. Tell her I thought of her to the last." Then he loosed from the boat, which was hideously 'overloaded, and swam away a little, to drown. This was told to me by an old sailor-man whose wife's friend was in the boat, and received the package and the mes- sage. •

div.head: DOCTOR'S HEROISM.
div.p: A DOCTOR'S HEROISM.

Of a more modern date was the tra- gedy of the "Francesca," which bred so marvellous an act of heroism in M. Artois, the young French doctor. He was outward - bound for the East on a "voyage of health." They had rounded the Cape of Good Hope, and were running up into fine weather when, early one day, the look-out reported a full- rigged ship right ahead. As they came up on her, it was remarked that something was wrong; for she was backing and filling all round the compass. With their glasses they soon discovered that there was no one at the wheel, and presently, having come up with herl they put the ship in irons and lowered the gig, intending to go aboard, to see what was out of gear, and whether help was need- ed. The second mate was put in charge of the boat, and M. Artois asked permission to go, which was granted. As they came along- side the strange vessel, it wae observed that a peculiarly- revolting stench. hung in the air around her. The second mate laid one of the oars up against the side of the ship, meaning to shin up it and so get aboard; but suddenly the doctor who had been sniffing at the air, caught at his arm and begged him to let him go first, • as he believed there was illness aboard. On hearing this the officer, know- ing that he was a doctor and with a natural deference to the man's own special knowledge on such a subject, stepped back and allowed him to go first to take a preliminary medical survey. As the doctor's head rose above the vessel's rail, he gave a cry, and then, look- ing down to the boat, shouted to them to shove out from the ship's side immediately, that there was plague aboard; yet he himself made no move to escape, but climbed over the rail and disappeared. They heard him running about the decks, and stopping here and there ass though he went from one thing to another. Then they heard him go aft. They saw him go up on to the poop, and down the companionway. Once or twice they heard his voice, calling, as though to find out whether anyone aboard was alive. A little later, they heard him returning along the main-deck, having evidently come out by the door under the break of the poop. He went into the fo'cas'le, but ran out • again quickly and came to the aide. The second mate; a young Swede, described him later as looking very white but determined. He called down to them a terrible tale. There were six dead men on the main-deck and many of the bunks in the fo'cas'le contained dead. Down aft there were two more dead, the captain, so he thought, and the steward. The first and second mates were in their bunks, still alive, and two of the 'prentices still alive, but all down with the plague. When he had finished this brief tale, he sent them back to their own vessel for a cer- tain case of medicines. They went, hurried- ly and awed, and came back swiftly; but now the captain was in charge of the boat. He would have coma aboard the plague ship, but the doctor warned him back with such earn- estness and FO many proofs that did he come, he not only risked his own life but those of all his crew, that at last he contented himself with staying in the boat. After a little fur- ther talk in which the doctor made it clear to the captain that he intended to stay in the ifiague ship. and nurse the two mates and the two apprentices, and that the captain had better leave him, and continue his voyage, the young medical man disappeared from sight, and they beard him go aft; then they heard nothing more and so went back to their own vessel, to plan what was best to be .one.

div.head: ON THE PLAGUE SHIP.
div.p: ON THE PLAGUE SHIP.

In the end, it was resolved to cruise for a day or two in the neighbourhood, keeping the plague ship in sight and to send a boat night and morning; also, one of the men of- fered to go to assist the doctor. During the the night, however, it fell calm, whilst the vessel was on a tack that had taken her some six or seven miles eastward of the plague ship; so that, when day-break came, and the boat was sent off, it took some considerable time to reach her. When they did, however, they had to hail her many times before they heard anyone stirring aboard. Indeed the captain had been on the point of allowing William Yeatson the man who had yolun- teered ,to assist Artois—to go aboard to search for the doctor. But hearing something moving they waited, and so heard a slurring, I dragging sound, which presently stopped somewhere about amidships. They all looked towards that portion of the rail, and then suddenly a bluish, puffy face rose into sight. No one recognised it for a few moments, un- til Yeatson cried out, "The doctor! It's the -doctor." It was. They pushed the boat aft, alongside of the vessel, and the doctor called out to them in a weak voice that the four men were dead, and be was dying and they had best put back to their own ship, au, leave him, but Teatson shouted that he WOll 0 aboard and nurse the doctor. At t: M. Artois cried out that he would shoot lii self, if any of them came aboard for it ;a, sure death to come near him, or any of t: corpses that were already putrefying. Yea sou, :not *lnking he meant it, began to mal his way up the oar which he had .alread., leaned against the vessel's side. At that the young French doctor cried out rapidly, "Go back! It is too late! Sink the ship, cap- tain." And with that he raised his right hand above the rail, and they saw he had a revolver. He put if to his forehead, and with a final cry of "Go back!" shot himself through the head and fell out of 'sight:Thus was achieved one of the most splendid acts of heroic determination of .which the mind could conceive. It may interest ,the reader to know that Yeatson, when he saw the doc- tor die, climbed back 'into the boat, and that they returned to their own vessel or the car- penter, who scuttled the stranger—she being of wood—by boring holes through her sides a little below the water line. And so she sank, csarrylinit. her daitaaem.. :111111__ •

div.p: HENRY SMART.
An Organist and Composer who did
much for Church Music.

div.head: PLACED BEFORE BRIDGE IN 1844.
div.p: PLACED BEFORE BRIDGE IN 1844.

Sunday, October 26th; was the centenary of the birth of Henry Smart, an excellent organist and a composer, the amount and beauty of whose music for the service of the church entitles him to our utmost reverence:

Henry Smart was born in Foley-place (now Langham-street), London, on October 26th, 1813, and declining a commission in the Indian Army, was articled to a solicitor but gave up the law. He was a nephew of the celebrated Sir George Smart, who was such a prominent figure in the musical World in the early years of. the reign oT Queen Victoria, and most likely in- herited his great natural gift in music. He was to a large extent self-taught. He was organist of the Parish Church, Blackburn, Lancashire, from 1831 to 1836, afterwards going -to London as organist of St. Philip's Church, Regent. street.

In 1844 he was appointed to St. Luke's, Old- street, and in 1864 to the Parish Church of St. Pancras, which appointment he held faithfully till his death. When the post of St. Luke's Church became vacant four well-known organ- ists—Scotson Clark, organist and composer; Mr. Caddock, Mr. Thelluson, a clever organ- ist, hailing from Norwich, and the Royal Aca- demy of Music, and Sir Frederick Bridge, C.V.O.—were selected to go before the Vestry to be interviewed, the appointment being in their hands.

Henry Smart was an organist of no mean ability. He was exceedingly great -in extem- poraneous playing and a prolific and admirable composer, and this not only as regards organ pieces. His best secular work, I understand, was an opera, "The Bride of Dunkerron," pro- duced with success at the Haymarket Theatre on 26th May, 1855. He also composed other various music including part songs, service set- tings and organ works. One can hardly doubt that his name will be long rezhembered in connection With Church music as the composer of two very 'fine an- thems. These were "Sing to the Lord" and "Lord, Thou hast been our refuge." These splendid anthems, I am sorry to say, are not as well known as they deserve to be, although his equally fine services in F and B flat find a place in nearly all our cathedrals and parish churches. His organ music is well known to every organist. Any of his Andantes are suit- able for in-going voluntaries, and either his March in G or his Festival-March is quite appro- priate as an out-going voluntary. For many years his sight had been failing him, and soon after the year 1864 he became blind, and his compositions had to be com- mitted to paper by the weary process of dicta- tion. In June, 1879, in acknowledgment of his services in the cause of music, he was granted a Government pension of £lOO a year, but unfor- tunately he did not live to enjoy it, for he died of cancer on the liver, after-much suffering, in the year, 1879, and was buried in Hampstead Cemetery. His last composition was a Post- Jude in E flat for organ, finished shortly before •his death.

div.head: CANADIAN FARMERS AND FREER TRADE.
div.p: CANADIAN FARMERS AND FREER TRADE.

"At a meeting at Regina of the Canadian Coinicil of Agriculture, composed of representa- tives of the grain-growers of Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and of the United Farmers of Alberta, it was unanimously decided to send a deputation to Ottawa to urge the Government and Parliament to increase the British pnefer- ence to 50 per cent., and to provide for a gradual increase from year to year so as to secure Free Trade with Great Britain in five years. It was also decided to ask the -Government to accept the offer of the United States for free inter- change of agricultural and animal products; to put all foodstuffs, and also agricultural imple- ments, lumber, and cement on the free list; to provide that any tariff or trade concession granted to any other country be immediately extended to Greit Britain; and to place cp- operative societies under the jutisdiction of the Board of Grain Commissioners."—The "Times," October 28th.

div.head: WOMEN WITH VOTES—Continued.
div.p: WOMEN WITH VOTES—Continued.

on many other things pertaining to the welfare of the race: The rational treatment' of the in- sane, mosquito districts, bastardy, and child labour have been attended to, and this record shows in a most concrete form why women need the ballot and bow they use it for the conserva- tion of humanity and the preservation of the home.

This granting of the vote to women. .has h'ad a stirring and quickening influence on the public life, and it has reacted upon the men, and re- sulted in a wider discussion and study of political questions. Truly we in this country ought to "get rid of our old pedestal for the sake of stepping on to the finer, broader pedestal, on which enfranchised women rest." E.W. "
