WOMEN WITH VOTES.
How Granting the Suffrage in California has Worked.

div.head: LIGHTNING LEGISLATION.
div.p: LIGHTNING LEGISLATION.
BY A LADY CONTRIBUTOR.

One of the most interesting meetings at the Buda Pesth Congress was that which was given up to the speeches of the Govern,ment delegates from women-enfranchised countries and States, and among these Miss Younger's about Cali- fornia was the most striking. She said that the women of the State had accomplished more in 20 months of their full citizenship thrtn they had in 20 years before, when they had no vote. The official statistics for the whole of Cali- fornia were not forthcoming, but in Los Angelos there were 70,000 registered women voters, and 99 per cent. of all the women in the city, and later 98 per cent. of these women went to the polls and recorded their votes.

div.head: PRINCIPLES NOT PARTY.
div.p: PRINCIPLES NOT PARTY.

The anti-suffragists were among the first to record their votes "for the salvation of the coun- try," they said, but now there are no "Anti's." Miss Younger also said that there were only 59 women voters in the old Red Light district of San Francisco at the time of the nomination of the President, these being about 5 per cent. of the women in the whole town. Of the remaining voters, 80 per cent. gave their occupation as "housewives and home - makers." (The anti-suffragists had been in the habit of placarding the town with notices that ." the woman who loves her home does not desire the vote." In California there is no special political party for women. They divide politically, just as men do, but when some great question of principle arises, moral or humanitarian, they rise above party, and all unite for the principle at stake, quite apart from any question of poli- tical party. The women voters had brought about the re- call of a corrupt judge. The men recognise the importance of their vote and all public ques- tions are submitted to them. In Los Angelos there was a woman's club, known as "Friday Morning"; 1,309 women voters belonged to it, and the opinions of these women were taken on all questions, and the candidates for election appeared before the club to ask for the support of its members at the polls. One of the things the women's vote did was the reservation of a large building for civic purposes, which had been put aside to be sold in lots,

div.head: "SOME" OF THE BILLS PASSED. .
div.p: "SOME" OF THE BILLS PASSED. .

Recently the first State Legislative Assembly to meet since women were enfranchised, was ad- journed, but its record was as fine one. News has been cabled from America of the Bills which have gone through since this Congress in Buda Pesth. The following are some of them : A mother's pension law, granting aid to needy parents, in order to keep the children at home, rather than have them committed to institu- tions.

A minimum wage law, creating a commission to investigate the conditions of industry of women and children, with power to invoke a minimum wage in industries paying less than a living wage. A health certificate law, requiring a certificate of freedom from venereal diseases of all men before obtaining marriage licences. A red light abatement and injunction law, placing the responsibility of disorderly houses upon the owners and lessees rather than upon the inmates, and forbidding such houses. A joint guardianship law, giving mothers equal rights over their minor children. A juvenile court law, separating dependent from delinquent children. An extension of the eight-hour law for women, to include workers in apartment houses and nurses in training.
An age of consent law, raising the age from 16 to 21. ,
A State training school for girls, providing a separate institution for girls, with the most ap- proved correctional methods and thorough voca- tional training. _ _
A teachers' -pension law, granting pensions of 500 dollars a year to all teachers who have been in service 30 years.
A net container law, specifying that packages shall show the amount of net contents.

A weights and measures law, providing for a complete standard of weights and measures, and regular inspection of dealers. A Roberts Bill, forbidding the destruction of any foodstuff fit for human consumption. (All New York housekeepers groaned when they read of cargoes of .fish being deliberately destroyed in order to keep the price up.) A creation of a State Housing and Immigra- tion Commission to prepare for the coming of immigrants with the opening or the Panama Canal.

A State Civil Service law, bringing practically all State employee under the merit service. Prison reform; all sentences, except for mur- der, are made indeterminate; straight jackets and cold showers are prohibited, and arrange- ments are made for the payment of wages to State's prison 'convicts and for assistance to dis- charged prisoners. A milk inspection law, providing for strict regulation of dairies. A white slave law, prohibiting traffic in women between countries.

A tuberculosis law, providing for tlie report- ing of all such cases. A workman's compensation law, regiring compulsory compensation for injurielr and establishing a system of State industrial insur- ance.
In addition to the above there have been laws

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY,NOVEMBER 8, 1913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY,NOVEMBER 8, 1913.
COMMIE EXAMINER STOOL
THE VICAR'S SECRET.
BY GEORGE A. WADE • • Author of "Lady Muriel's Lovers," "Eighty Miles an Ho,— " " A IsTifrrow Escape," " The ChoiiLur," " The Roses of Towton,"

"As a matter of fact, Ida darling," whis- pered the curate, "I believe I've laved you ever since I first saw you come to the speech. day festivities at the school, when Vernon and I were chums there together. Do you re- member, darling, how you used to wear a pretty dark-blue dress, with yellow favours in it, as a tribute to the school's colours, in those days? How lovely I used to think you looked, strolling round the fine quadrangle at Christ's Hospital on a glorious summer after- noohnAnd how little I ever thought at that time, Ida dear, that the day would come when you would promise to be my wife, as you have just done!" She smiled gaily, and gazed into his eyes with such a love-glance, as must have told him how much her heart was his. They were walviim together op the charming little beach at Babbacombe, with the big red sandstone c„ oevopshire as the background, and the delicious Blue sea in front, lapping the apple-green coloured stones with its gentle waves. 1 "it was delightful at Horsham that first year or two," said the young lady, softly, holding the curate's hand in her own as he bent to kiss her when they reached the pro- jecting cliff that hid them from prying eyes. "Yet even then I used to be struck by your superiority ,to the other boys in father's house," she went on. "I seemed to take to you from first meeting you there, and I think I've loved you ever since, though, like all true and modest, girls, I had to keep my own secret till you yourself broke the bonds that held it, and set me free to confess my love by telling me how much you wanted me for your wife. "I do' I certainly do, darling Ida!" he re- plied, full of ardour and eagerness. "Yes, I've loved you from that first sight of you. I'm sure of it! Of course, then I thought that the good old house-master, Mr. Dailey, was really your father. I had no idea that you were his adopted daughter only, his niece, in fact, brought up by him and Mrs. Dalley when your own mother was dead, and after your own father had disappeared. But it was you I loved, you, Ida darling; so what does it matter whether Mr. Dailey was your father or your uncle? It won't make a pin's differ- ence to our love and marriage, will it?" "I don't see why it should," answered the girl, tooking proudly at her lover as they turned their steps back again towards the white road which leads to the top of the cliffs and to Babbacombe parade. "I don't see why it should. And yet, dearest Roland, I often wish I knew where' father had died, and more about him and mother. One seems to have only half a history when one knows so little about one's parents! Even my uncle and aunt r never appeared to know more about father than that he went away to seek his fortune abroad, and died somewhere in Australia, as takethey me earodn ltartuesrt., suSloelyyofuo what I am on my, dear, will have to own merits, small though they he. I've no fortune or influence to 'bring you, Roland, and you know well how important and useful such things are to a young curate who has great talents and much ability, who has many gifts, and is absorbed in hieipeplendid work for God, but who has not family connections or high iefiw3nce behind him to give him assist- tance when necessary." _ _ . _

The Rev. Rolan4 -Watson burst out laugh- ing heartily, and took advantage of the bend in the white road to kiss the fair and beauti- ful maiden again. She blushed and laughed in return, but her warm kiss in answer to his made him intensely happy, and told him how thoroughly he had won her heart. "Never mind either about wealth or influ- ence, darling Ida," he said. "We can live comfortably, at all events, for I'm not alto- gether dependent on the one hundred and eighty pounds a year that I get as a curate, as you may know. I won that scholarship at Christ's Hospital, and I had a rare time at the fine old school to which I owe so much to-day—including you. Then from it I got the scholarship at Queen's, Cambridge, and with that and the money the school gave me too I did well until I was ordained. And now, since I've obtained my heart's greatest de- sire in winning you, Ida, what does it matter that you've no fortune, or that your people are not of aristocratie influence? I've got you; and I'd rather have you than all the money or influence in the world." Her cheeks reddened at his eager declara- tion of passionate affection, but her smiling face showed how much she was pleased. "It's so good of you to say so, Roland," she answered. " I'll try to make you happy, at any rate, clearest; I'll promise you that. Oh! you foolish boy, don't you know we're nearly at the top of the cliff, and that there are a, dozen people who can see us," The last remark was made in response to the clergyman's attempt to steal another kiss astlriend they came Bn troundwiththtehelansht characteristic of daring wind- ing of an old Bluecoat boy, he took it, nevertheless.

Mrs. Dailey, widow of the former House- master of Roland Watson when at school, sat in the little front room at her residence by the side of Wandsworth Common. And it was on the third evening after the betrothal of Roland and Ida at Babbacombe that her son Vernon, who had been let into the girl's secret, broke the interesting news to her. "Mother," said he, "whom do you think Ida and myself met at Torquay? Why, good old Watson! You remember Roland Watson, who was in father's house at school? He was a close chum of mine—one of the best of fellows, as you may recollect." "Yes, I certainly remember Watson," re- plied Mrs. Dailey, with a slight appearance oi interest. "Let me see, he became a clergy- man after leaving Cambridge, didn't he?" "Exactly! He is curate in a village not fat from Torquay, and is very populsr. We met him several times while there, and we'd many jaunts together. It was quite like old days! " "I suppose he'd hardly remember Ida, even though he and you were such friends," said the lady, with a curious glance at her sailor son, for Vernon was now a young naval officer. "Not remember Ida? Of course he did! Why, were not Ida and I just like brother and sister, instead of cousins, at that time?" Mrs. Dailey smiled, wanly as it seemed to the enthusiastic youth. "I used to wonder in those days, Vernon," she said, quizzingly, "whether Ida and your- self would ever fall in love with each other? And so did your poor father!" Vernon laughed till the tears came into his eyes. " Not a bit of it!" he said. "Ida and I never thought of such a thing, I'm certain! We are as fond of one another as possible, but not in that way. Ida'A not my style of gir) for a wife, and I'm quite sure I'm not Ida's ideal of a husband. But tfiere, now, as you have' mentioned it, I have a piece of news for you, mother. Roland has proposed to Ida, and she's accepted him, fer they two really do love each other. Of course she'll ask your consent • but they know they'll have that, eh?" ' But consent; Dalley's face grew white and her form trembled. Her sewing fell to the ground, and the muscles of her features twitched. The careless, genial Vernon stared at her in amazement i.for he saw that something had occurred for which none of them had bargained: "Whatever is the matter, mother?" he said. "Aren't you well?" "Roland Watson has asked Ida to be his wife' and she has consented? And he is com- ing here to get my sanction? Do I under- stand you aright, Vernon?" "Exactly," answered the young man. mystified. "What is wrong in that? Hasn't he known and loved Ida ever since he first saw her at school? And isn't he a man to be proud of—a real. true clergyman of the very best sort.? 1 think Ida extremely
and I should say you do also, to have won the love of suen a man

But Mrs. Dalley only sat staring, dry-lipped and haggard. So Vernon, rose to call Ida from the room above to bring some restora- tive, for his mother seemed ready to faint. But she motioned him to sit still, and then she spoke almost in a whisper. "Vernon. this must not be! Ida's marriage* vnth uoittA,d vvatt is .npk.sibte ! 'lacy two could never be man and wife ! "
"But why?" asked the young man, utterly nonplussed and astounded at this unexpected turn of affairs. " Why, mother? What is wrong with Roland? Isn't he a most desirable husband for our Ida?" .

"It can't be!" was the frightened reply. "Whatever Mr. Watson is or isn't, Ida must never marry him. of all men! It is simply out of the question!" "But don't ,you see you must give a better reason than that, clear?" he said. " For,lda's whole life's happiness is at stake, and Rol's, too!"

Mrs. Dailey groaned aloud. She let her head sink on her hands and sobbed. But to her son, sitting there in wonder, all her behaviour was so utterly mysterious that he felt quite lost. "You must give us a better reason, or neither Roland nor Ida will ever draw back," he said.

"I had hoped it would never need to be spoken of again ! " she murmured. "I used to think long ago that Roland liked the girl, but I hoped nothing would come of it further when he got away from the school. And now-"

She quite broke down in her distress. Her son put his arm round her neck gently. "Tell me what is the trouble, mother," he whispered, softly, as he stroked her hair. And in broken accents, with falling tears, she told him the hidden story. When she had finished it was Vernon Dailey who sat with a face deathly white and with quivering lips. "Gracious Heaven!" he muttered. "And I must tell them both that?"

Vernon had gone down to that pretty little lvillage just outside Torquay where his friend was so popular and well-beloved as a curate. The two old chums were Walking along one of the sweetest country lanes in all Devonshire, that leading to Cockington, and young Dailey had been trying to tell his comrade how much his mother objected to the engagement. Roland stared in surprise at him, but luckily the two soon arrived at the curate's lodgings, and there, in an attractive and pleasant sitting-room, they thrashed the affair out. The clergyman's dark eyes were resting full on the face of Vernon as he spoke. "Mrs. Dailey forbids our marriage! " ex- claimed the curate. "And she has a serious secret reason for doing so! You have been told it, and you also declare that our engage- ment is quite impossible? Is that what you wish me to understand, Vernon?"

The other man's eyes looked troubled, and his gaze sought the floor. He scarcely glanced up at his friend as he said: "That's it, Rol! I assure you, old boy, it's made me feel worse than you can dream Of at all! And I do trust that/ you'll not require me to give you mother's reason, for I'd much rather not do so."

"Oh, but you must see that's perfectly absurd, Vernon," exclaimed the clergyman, .impatiently. "There's my darling Ida, who has 4ove me• for t years, •and there's myself, who has been loving and waiting and working and hoping ever since I left Christ's Hospital, eagerly wanting to win her affection and .to take her to be my wife. And now that we're both. so happy you and Mrs. Dailey can't for a minute ,suppose we are going to break our engagement without some extraordinary reason for so doing. Why, it would break Ida's heart for me to leave her like that, and without her knowing why!" "Oh, I feel that; and I told mother ;it would be necessary for you to know the secret, if you insisted," said Vernon. "I do insist!" was the curate's reply. "Well, then, I'll speak. But you must keep it from Ida's knowledge somehow or other. This is mother's story: "Your father was, as vo are aware, a Leeds woollen merchant who made a fortune.: His head manager was a man named Pilsen, a most capable fellow, who always expected to receive a partnership, .however small, for what he had done in the business. He, under that expectancy, lived far beyond his means and got deeply into debt. When he found later that your father would not listen for a moment to any such proposal as his having a share in the business he became half-mad. He hardly knew what he did, for he was in such financial straits. "Pilson then owed at least three thousand pounds to various folk, and naturally his creditors began to demand their money. But he hadn't the least idea where to find even half of it. So he forged your father's name to many cheques, and swindled hita out of some two thousand pounds. Of course a warrant was issued against him, but he had fled abroad and IN as never caught—never seen again. No doubt he changed his name as well as his ways and work." "But what has all that to do with me and Ida?" asked Roland, staring and impatient. "Wait a moment and you'll see. His wife died heartbroken a few months afterwards. She was a sweet woman indeed; but this terrible business, of which she had known nothing till her husband was gone, killed her. And--she left behind her when she died—a little gift! And—this Mrs. Pilson was the sister of my mother! Don't you understand now, Roland? Is it necessary for me to con- fess the shameful thing further?" The curate hastily rose and put his hands to his head. He understood indeed! His darling Ida was the little girl, the daughter of that man who had robbed his father, who had killed a loving wife by his dreadful crime. Ida's father—lovely, dear, sweet Ida's father—was a criminal of the deepest dye! No wonder :Roland reeled as he stood there. But after a slight pause his lips whis- pered hoarsely: 'Yes, I understand, old fellow—I under- stand. And—is—he—dead—now?"

"Nobody knows," answered the other man. "But you see how impossible it is for you ever to marry Ida, Roland, he said. "You and I have been friends—close chums—for years. I shall never forget your kindness, nor, I am sure, will Ida; but as to your marrying her, of course you see it'6 quite out of the question!" The curate smiled as he laid his hana ten- derly on Vernon's shoulder. His voice was soft, and the love-light in his 'eyes was worth going miles to see. "Is it?" he said, quietly. "What do you take me for? Should I be worthy of the grand school where you and I were chums together, where darling Ida used to wear the dark blue dress with the deep yellow flowers as our colours, if I deserted you and her when you need me most? Not a bit of it, my boy. Let bygones be bygones, and let the dead past bury its dead. Ida shall never know more than she does now, if I can help it. But Ida shall be my wife; whilst Vernon Dailey shall be my best friend, as ever. And Heaven bless YO u both!" "You're a fellow to be proud of, old 'chap!" exclaimed the naval lieutenant in his enthusiasm, as he grasped the other's hand warmly.

When his old Cambridge college presented the Rev. Roland Watson, M.A., with the vacant living of All Souls, Richmond, there was no happier or more delighted couple in England than the curate and his beautiful and charming wife, who was just as popular in the village outside Torquay as her dear husband was. . .

And when the new Vicar and Mrs. Watson were fully installed in their, parish by the Thames they soon made as 'many friends and admirers as they had left behind ethem in South Devon: For Ida went about the parish daily like a regular ministering angel, and it would hardly be exaggerating to say that there were many old folli in Richmond who literally worshipped her. Her presence was like a gleam of sunshine brightening each poor home she entered, whikt her gifts and smiles and encouraging word's were dispensed with a graciousness that drew all hearts to her shrine. Whether her protégé was a little cripple like Laura Dawne, or an old man like Thomas Back- house, Ida Watson, the Vicar's wife, St as to that protégé a goddess•indeed! Old Thomas Backhouse was simply enthusi- astic in his praise of Mrs. Watson. He had lived for the past five years in the parish on a very small private income, and his hold or life was now fast ebbing away. He had, in-

weed, been under the doctor's hands tor some months, and the doctor had hinted to the Vicar that it, would be well for him to call on the old man regularly, as he would not live much longer. Hence it came that Roland and his wife were such frequent visitors at the little cottage not far from the banks of the river; and Thomas Backhouse's face always brightened when it saw them there. "Is there anything more I can do for you, Mr. Backhouse? " asked the Vicar one after noon when the old man seemed weaker than ever. "Yes, sir, there is one thing you can do; ii you will. But I'm afraid to mention it. Still, I must tell you, if you're to grant my one deep desire ere I die." "It shall be don" if at all possible," answered the Vicar. "Well, sir, I've no relations, as I've said before to you. Leastways, only one, who is lost to me. But I'd be glad if you'd bring your dear wife to-morrow and let her kiss me, for I'd like to have one kiss nom some good woman—from her—before the end." The Vicar smiled indulgently. "I 'don't think she'd object!" said he, musingly- "But why do you specially wish it to be from her?" "Because," said the old man, with a strange look in his face, as his eyes rested on the clergyman, "because--she's—she's—my —daughter! Ay, I thought that'd make you stare, sir!" The Vicar jumped up suddenly, as if struck unexpectedly. Ile stood dumbfounded as he looked eagerly at the dying man. "And who are you ? " lie asked, not un- tenderly, after that tense, silent minute or so. "I:ra he murmured. "Yes, was, Mr. Wat- son!". I went to Aus- tralia, made a.bit of money after some years, and came back here to live my life out. Yet I did not wish to kill my girl, as I had killed my sweet wife by the awful crime. But as soon as you and, she came here to this parish I knew you both at once! I'm sorry, sir, and I beg your forgiveness for it all now, Mr. Watson!" , "I forgave you long ago," was the quiet reply. " For if ye forgive not 'men their trespasses, how shall your Heavenly Father forgive you? So says the good old Book, and I believe it! Yes Mr. Pilson, she shall come; Ida shall come and kiss you. But she must re- main ignorant about your identity!" It was as they sat together in his study, at the Vicarage that evening that Roland said, as casually as he could: "Oh! Ida, I saw old Backhouse to-day; the doctor thinks he's nearly done for, poor chap. And the old man made a curious request of me. He says, he's no relations living except one daughter, whose name is like yours, Ida, and who is far away somewhere. And he says he'd like you to give him a kiss for her before he dies, since he's taken such It fancy to you. What do you think," dear? Can you humour the old man's whim?"

Her face was lit with love for that manly form whose hands took it in them and kissed it most affectionately as he spoke. "You don't mind losing one, Rol?" she said, shyly, as she smiled. "Not in this case, dearest," he said, softly. "I think it would satisfy the poor fellow ere he passes away, for, from what he told me, he loved his daughter dearly:" "I'll do it, darling," she replied. "I'll do it, as though I were his own daughter, if that'll make him happy." And so next day The youthful and beautiful wife of the Vicar of All Souls, Richmond, leant over the bed of a man who was dying in a cottage near the banks of the Thames. His half-closed eyes opened and smiled at her most tenderly as she kissed his face thrice affectionately. His life was almost gone; but he managed with an effort to kiss her in return.

"Yes, I'm glad I kissed him," she said to her husband that evening. "Yet it was a curious request, wasn't it, love?" And Roland looked at her with his sweetest smile as he nodded. But his eyes appeared te- be fixed on vacancy, as if he were seeing something far beyond that room.
ITEM END.)

div.head: HUNTED OVER THE WORLD.
div.p: HUNTED OVER THE WORLD.

A remarkable instance of a son's fidelity to his murdered father's memory .has just b,een revealed before the Drome Assizes, France. Five years ago a young Corsican named Emmanuelli, shot dead a policeman named Guglilmf, who remonstrated with him on his dissolute conduct. Guglilmi did this in a kindly manlier, for he was a friend of Emmanuelli's family. Inspector Ristori, who had rushed to his comrade's help, was also shot dead.

The murderer fled the country and was sup- posed to have gone to America. Ristori's son vowed that he would avenge his father. He started for, America, and atter' travelling over the .greater part of the New World at last dis- covered Emmanuel in the City of Panama, where he had become a cafe concert proprietor. Ristori handed the murderer over to the police. Emmanuelli was extradited to Corsica, and the venue being changed in order to avoid family influences being brought into play, he was ,tried at Drome Assizes and sentenced to penal servitude for life.

div.head: SAVAGE WIFE ASSAULT.
div.p: SAVAGE WIFE ASSAULT.
Albert Edward Smith (47), labourer, Was .charged before Mr. Justice AVory, at the Liver- pool Assizes, on Saturday, with - feloniously wounding his wife, at St. Helens, on September 25th.

It was said that prisoner, who pleaded guilty. was practically blind, almost stone-deaf, and was of weak 'intellect. For some time he had suffered from delusions, and believed his wife to be unfaithful to him. Early-in the morning on the date named he got up, wakened his wife, and questioned her as to •whose company she had been in the previous Sunday. When she stated that she was not with anyone, he stabbed hel: in the stomach, in the forehead and throat, and severed the muscles of her hand when she tried to take the knife from him.—Smith denied that he had any intention of, doing his wife aaY grievous bodily harm. His Lordship .said :'prisoner must try to. bear his afflictions more patiently. He must be pun- ished for the assault upon his wife; but, having regard to his physical condition, he would be sent to prison for six months only.

div.head: as a Seat of Honour.
div.p: as a Seat of Honour.
WOMEN'S CLUBS.

Clubs are almost as old as .history. China had theiij in the days of Noah, but Women's Clubs are quite a modern development. When, however, once fairly started; the movement grew rapidly, and there are now • nearly forty such organisations in the Metropolis alone. ,Women of this country seem to have the club instinct very strongly developed. They were the first - to make it a part of thei life of the nation. AMericans are doing their best .to copy British ideals, but Frenchwomen have not so far adopted the movement with any great enthu- siasm, two or three clubs being the highest number they possess. Class restrictions would seem to have passed away, at ,feast where women congregate in clubs, for many types meet. together as equals, and. enjoy the same interests.

THE UNIVERSALITY OP CLUBS. • The movement began with social, political, and residential organisations, and undoubtedly the club has been an important factor in the education and progress of women, and in altering the outlook of \hundreds individually. Some 41 the London groups are splendidly housed, and the social clubs are, without excep- tion, admirably managed.;. thus a woman • can now find in her club the same interest and pleasure than men have found in theirs for generations. The mOst interesting clubs are those where workers congregate, where novel- ists, dramatists, journalists, painters and artists meet together to discuss ideas, hopes and theories. • All kinds of interests are united now- adays; recreation, suffrage, travel, &c. A visit to a Women's Travellers' Club is a revela- tion in the records of mountain climbing and exploration accomplished by the modern woman. But the East End has quite as many of these organisations as the West, and their influence is everyvThere for the good or toe race, and the benefit • of the community.

div.head: SOFA ON THE CONTINENT.
div.p: THE SOFA ON THE CONTINENT.

For a young girl to seat herself on the canopd or sofa, when at a social gathering in Ger- many, is regarded as a solecism of the worst kind. In Italy respect for the sofa becomes almost reverence, arid to be asked to take a seat on it is one of the highest compliments an Italian hostess can pay a favoured guest. Only extreme age or distinction in the higher cal- lings of life convey the privilege of sitting un- invited on this comfortable piece of furniture. Chairs do well enough for the undistinguished middle-aged, and the youthful men and women. Nor is the etiquette of the sofa confined to the secular world alone. It is in Italy, and in Southern Germany quite as strictly observed in the Church. For instance, at a reception given 133 i a high Roman dignitary, no member of the priesthood below a bishop—and an aged one— would be invited by the host, perhaps a cardinal, to sit on this scat of honour. Visitors from this wuntry, quite unaware of the breach of good manners, thus committed, ofteh inad- vertently seat themselves uninvited on the canop6, but the surprise and consternation such a proceeding calls forth is as productive of equal astonishment and not a little awkwardness and malaise. - • COLOURED FURS.

Furs dyed in unnatdral colours will,probably have a vogue when employed for coats and sets, although when the experiment was first tried in Paris it was intended that pelts so manipulated should be used for millinery pur- poses only. Coats and sets in various colours are being shown in the big houses in London, and the effect when one has got over the novelty is in some cases rather pleasing. In dark 'shades of green and purple, the pelts of the mole and fox are very successful. As the fur tippet of early Victorian days has been revived, it is probable that these dyed skins will be used for this quaint 'little garment, which can be made to match' the colour of the dress with which it is worn. For the trimming of dresses, narrow fur bands are also used. In fact, hats, tailor- mades, evening and day gowns, all have a touch of fur, and the touch is not without a certain fascination. FUR HATS. .

There are signs that the tiny hat, pressed low down on the brows, is losing- something of its popularity, and .some of the latest modeis have a soup-plate brim, ridsed at one side. The hat often matches the muff and necklet, and the idea is decidedly. pretty. The -shoulder scarves for autumn evening wear are so lovely that (hey will be sure to find wearers. Many are ruched at the edges, some arelined with filmy lace, and weighted at the ends with tassels; and others are made to accompany the Persian tunic, which is suitable only for evening dresses. A new and very sensible sports hat is made of cash- mere. Fur hats have now made their appear- ance, and are evidently to be very much favoured. They are seen in all the new shapes, carried out in squirrel, Seal, coney, and mole- dyed Coney, also in the more expensive furs. They are trimmed with a contrasting fur, or their decoration consists of tiny sprays of flowers, or berries, in silk or velvet. THE FABRIC GLOVE.

The fabric gloves of this season are marvels of imitation, and take a quite. important place in this department of dress, whiCh is not sur- prising .when the perfection to which manu- facturers have brought them is considered. >Tho imitation silk-lined suede fabric gloves are so smart in appearance, and as well cut and shaped 'to the real thing. Moreover, they are to be had in all the newest shades, and .the Colouring is as good as the glove. The fur- lined duplex glove is a novelty, which,. as itis warm, and yet not clumsy, Will be sure of popu- larity when the cold weather sets in,. The newest ringwoods are a:great improvement on former makes of this useful glove; for they are lined with imitation suede, and with— silk. Poverty is no excuse in these days of cheap fabric gloves, for wearing old and shabby kid, which, when even of the. best .make, look the quintessence of shabbiness after much constant use. VARIETY OF SLEEVES.

, Sleeves play an important part in the, scheme of dress just now, and as there is a great variety in shape and trimming; every woman may find a type to suit her. individually. The Raglan, baggy under the arm, with-seams carried as far as the shoulder, is a favourite for dressy blouses. It ,may be short or long; in the latter instance it is trimmed with little runes of tulle or mousseline, very finely pleated. The bell (Continued in next column.)

div.p: Farmer's Cattle ?
A SECRET CONCLAVE.

What seems 'a remarkable action for the Warrington Guardians to take happened at the close Of the fortnightly meeting on Wednesday. They decided to discuss a matter in private, and thus made the subject one of myste;ry. _

_ Towards the close of the meeting Mr. BROOKES asked if it-was a 'hitt that. the Master of the institution had given orders or instructions for inmates to take and drive .home cattle belong- ing to a farmer? Was it also a fact that the men so employed were out of the institution during the greater part of the day, and that one of them returned in a state of intoxication? , When the matter was raised it-was decided to exclude the Press, and in the absence of the reporters the matter was considered.

div.head: NEW OFFICES.
div.p: THE NEW OFFICES.
WORKHOUSE ADMINISTRATION.
The House Committee minutes stated that negotiations were being entered into•at the Post Office for a wire to be Connected to Dr. Hodg- kinson's residence.

It was decided at the meeting of The House Committee, that the Chairman, Vice-chairman and the Clerk inquire into the general adminis- tration of the Workhouse, and report as early as possible. The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: AN ANONYMOUS POSTCARD
div.p: AN ANONYMOUS POSTCARD

The anonymous postcard which the Rev.. A. M. Mitchell mentioned at the last meeting, which stated that there were children in the Padgate Homes Who should not be there,- was again discussed., Xiarcum, asked if there was anything to be said in regard to it. He had had another postcard from the same source. , The CLERK: I do hope the;Guardians will not take notice of anonymous letters or postcards' of this kind. The postcard makes a serious charge against one of the officers, but if the writer gives no name, you ought not to take any notice of it. (Hear, hear.) Inquiries have been made, and I find out that we are aware of the whole circumstances of the case. The woman is married, and •is •living in a lodging-house in Warrington, and as there is no proper house, it would be cruelty to send these children out under such circumstances. ' Mr. MITCHELL made a remark as to where the woman was now living, and The CLERK replied: Let. that gentleman 'come forward, whoever hp is, and show himself. I don't like to deal with cowards. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: LOAN.
div.p: A LOAN.
THE CHILDREN'S ACT.
The regulation in the Chi Wren's Act that anyone taking over the care of a child under the age of seven should report at once to the Board of Guardians, • was: fully discussed.

_ Several members were of the opinion that the regulations of the Act should be advertised, and that prosecution should not be taken at present. On the other hand, it was stated that the fact had been advertised, and several mem- bers urged for prosecution. It was decided that in the next case that came before the Guardians, there should be a prose- cution. • •

div.head: MOTOR CAR SHED.
div.p: A MOTOR CAR SHED.
Discussion at the Meeting of Runcorn

SMOKE AND FUMES FROM WIDNES.

Mr. C. E. Linaker presided at the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorniitural District Council at Dutton on Tuesday. f Mr. P. H. The matter was referred to the Highways Executive ComMittee. That Motor Shed.

The Clerk read several letters from Arr. Gray Brandreth in regard to ;the motor shed which the Council had instructed :Mr. 'Brandreth to remove. The letters stated that the people in Oakwood-avenue did not object to the shed. It • was moved .and seconded that the original resolution of the Council be adhered to, and that Mr. Brandreth remove the shed. .Councillor Basnett proposed an amendment that the request of Mr:'Brandreth for the shed to remain be granted, Councillor Booth seconded. Councillor Mclntyre: I suppose you all know that his action is in direct contravention to our by-laws. Cguncillor Lister-Kaye: He is evidently work- ing on his solicitor's advice.
On a vote being taken, the resolution was adhered to.
Moore Water.
On the recommendation of Dr. Adams. if was decided. that a sample of the L. and N.-W. Rail- way Company's supply of water from wells at Moore be analysed. Smoke and Fumes.

Councillor Milwdesley complained that hedges in the district were being destroyed by smoke and fumes. They had an inspector, but they -heard nothing about the matter. It would be better if they 'had a man residing in the dis. trict.
Councillor Spruce said considerable damage had been done during the Year .to the. hedge- rows. Some of them -appeared as if they had been Scorched: _
Councillor Wright: The trees in 'a garden were half killed at the time when the King visited Widnes.

The Chairman: You don't hold the King re- sponsible, do you? (Laughter.) Mr. Woodward suggested that the complaint be sent to the Local Government Board. The Chairman said that farmers should make complaints when the vegetation was green. On one occasion the hedges,facing Widnes had been green, and, those facing the river had been as black as- his hat. Councillor Lister Kaye: The stuff must drop over the hedge. (Laughter.) It was decided that the matter be mentioned in the proper quarter.

div.head: AN INTERESTING FIND.
div.p: AN INTERESTING FIND.

A very fine specimen of a fossil of a dinosaur, which was received at the Victoria Memorial Museum; ,Ottawa, from Alberta some time ago, has now been mounted in the original clay in which it was found and displayed to .excellent advantage against a wall. The work of raising the enormous frame containing the skeleton, weighing in all'about five tons, was carried out without mishap, and the exhibit;-,yvhich is the finest of its kind on the Continent, is a,.centre of a very great interest.

div.head: SOMEMIVG TO ADMIRE.
div.p: SOMEMIVG TO ADMIRE.
THE CULT OF "SELF"
Men Content to be "Led by the Nose

div.head: Like Asses."
div.p: Like Asses."
STIRRING ADULT SCHOOL ADDRESS

At Sankey Bridges Men's School on Sunday morning, Mr. George Shaw gave a most instnic- tive lecturette upon "Self-respect." The speaker said the phrase was much, used, but very little understood. For self-respect implied that one understood the object respected. Yet how many ever study seriously that wonderful and mysteriouti thing. called " self "? When one considers, for instance, industrial life, with the. many horrors attending it, one is driven to the conclusion that man, as the highest type of animal, endowed with so many -fine attributes, is lacking in the respect due to himself. Men hold themselves too cheap; if they hail a gent- ine pride in themselves many of the things which are taken as a matter of course, would not be tolerated, Speaking of self-respect as applied to citizenship, Mr. Shaw said it was painful to see how little interest was, taken in civic life by the workers in such questions as sanitation, clean streets, drains, smoke, &c. He deplored the fact that in the using of the vote, many men were woefully indifferent to, and ignorant of, real, live issues, and were con- tent, like Othello, to be "led .by the nose as asses are." The speaker finished by saying that the respect in which men held themselves was reflected in their surroundings. An animated and interesting discussion followed. The Bible lesson on " Man : His Leisure," was introduced by Mr. David Ridyard, who said that under a well-regulated and thoroughly organ- ised system man would have considerably more leisure than at present. But the value of leisure depended upon the use made of it. Life was much more than eating,.drinking, working and sleeping. The world was full of , objects of interest; there need not be a dull hour. Sports of all kinds ought to be enjoyed, but they shoula not be allowed to occupy a man's whole mind. Spare time could often be profitably spent in reading, but a very important thing was to foster one's observation, and to train an alert mind.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH MEN'S.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH MEN'S.

Mr. Harry Wardman gave a lecture on Sun- day morning on "Armaments." The speaker said the topic was a most appropriate one for an Adult School, which had for one of its objects the ',brotherhood of man. To si)l3nd money on armaments was antagonistic to the teachings of Christ. The speaker p9inted out how many nations, which had tried to live -by the sword, had ceased to exist. It was not in the sound of battle, but -rather in its moral laws that a country's greatness depended. Mr. Y. A. Jenkins ably opened the Bible les- son on "Man and His Leisure." He said that leisure well spent would re-create men.. The

speaker mentioned that a visit-to a popular sea- side place. on a general holiday was a very in- structive 'example how .leisure should not be spent, and drew attention to the contrast in the delightful picture given in the lesson from the second chapter of -Mark's Gospel, where the little band of comrades were seen taking a holi- day stroll through golden cornfields, and rowing across the lake to revel in the rest and quiet of the hills. He advised all present to spend part of, their leisure by strolling round the country, and let God speak through Nature.

div.head: BEWSEY MEN'S.
div.p: BEWSEY MEN'S.

On Sunday morning .A 1 r. C. R. Muir gave a delightful talk on ",Music, and its Effects on Life and Character." The lecturer said Darwin wrote that "music is the basis of all language." It was more expressive of feeling, moods, im- pulses\ and emotions, for mere words would not cover what it meant. It was the interpreter-in- chief Of man's inner soul. It spoke to hearts and spirits, to the very core of their being. The speaker related an interesting story of Dr. Moffat, the missionary, who had found much difficulty in teachinig the English alphabet to the African natives, until he began to sing the A, B, Cto the tune of "Auld lang syne." The natives were charmed, and the Doctor soon dis- covered how easy they learned the alphabet to the tune. Mr. Muir referred to the important place occupied by music in military expeditions, how martial music filled the hearts of soldiers with buoyancy and hope. Among the. common things of life, when weary and depressed after a hard day's work, many men found the burden to be lifted when some familiar melody wafted through the air.

div.head: ACADEMY-STREET WOMEN'S.
div.p: ACADEMY-STREET WOMEN'S.

On Wlldnesday evening Mrs. Hill spoke on the Bible lesson for the week, "Man and His Work.:: Afterwards there was a discussion as to what women could do towards improving the industrial conditions of to-day. There was a unanimous opinion expressed that a good home life did nuich to ease the burdens borne by the workers. Also that a junior 'club for girls of working age, where physical exercises, probably in the form of country dances, would help much to train girls for the duties of life. Afterwards Mrs. Nurse gave an enjoyable recitation called "Courting Time." . ,

div.head: ACADEMY-STREET MEN'S.
div.p: ACADEMY-STREET MEN'S.

Mr. Joseph Elwell, of Sankey Bridges, in his lecturette on Sunday morning, lucidly traced the "History and Growth of Trade Unionism." In 1740 they saw great' improvements in the manufacture of iron, and this expedited the use of machinery. Small workshops prevailed until the latter part of the 18th century, when capi- talists combined' to maintain the existing op- pression, tinct even Parliament sanctioned the employment of children for 16 hours a day. Weavers' wages in 1817 were ss. or 6s. per week. So acute did poverty become that the House of Commons instituted inquiry, but. the Members of Parliament were themselves capitalists, ,and it was the persistent demands of Labour that brought 'about a maximum of 10 hours per day for children up to nine years of age. The next move on the part of the employer was to in-

crease the size of his shop, and to lodge the workers on the premises; and heartless and in- human, were the conditions under which the factory hands worked. Acts of Parliament pro- hibited meetings or any conclave of the work- ing classes, and the lecturer pointed out the difficulty the workers had to contend with to get these laws repealed. The year 1868, how-, ever, saw the commencement of the Trades Union Congrev, which followed a Royal Com- mission held the previous year, when, R. Apple- garth, replying to 633 questions, and subjected to severe cross-examination, proved that most of the charges levelled against trade unionists were unsupported by evidence; that the few cases of violence committed against the capi- talist class were the direct result of forcing men to meet in secret to counteract, as they thought, unjust laws made against the com- ibination of workers. Mr. Elwell appropriately responded to the few questions afterwards submitted.

WISHED "A MERRY CHRISTMAS."—George Pos- tlethwaite, 8, Morris's-court, was charged on remand with sleeping out in Connor's yard, and also with stealing workmen's tools, value 205., from the yard of the Cooper's- Arms.,—The Chief Constable said that men engaged by. Messrs. Robert Collins and Sons were pointing the Cooper's Arms. On Wednesday the men left their tools in the yard. About 7.30, Mr. Loy, the landlord of the house, saw prisoner in the yard and coming from the shed where the tools had been placed. Prisoner feigned sick- ness, but Mr. Loy' sent for the police, and then prisoner departed. In reply. to the charge he said "Yes; I was drunk when I did it."—He had been before the Court 21 times previously, and that was his 15th appearance for larceny.— Prisoner was sent to prison for six months.—On going out of the dock he turned to the magis- trates and said, "I wish you a merry Christ- mas and a happy New Year."

- THEFT OF CLOTHING.—Edwin Blake wa-§—cliarged with stealing clothing, value £3, from the shop of Mr. Ashton, 4, Golborne-street, on October 15.—The Chief Constable said Mr. Ashton. left his premises safe at night, but the next morn- ing the property had been stolen. Prisoner had surrendered to the Liverpool police. He, had pledged some of the clothing at St. Helens and some at Liverpool.—Blake was committed for three months.

THE OTHER WOMAN AGAIN.—John Thomas War- burton. 5. Beaufort-street, Liverpool, was charged with leaving his wife and two children chargeable to the Union. Mr. Shearer said prisoner had deserted his wife and went to live with another woman. Be had pawned all his elothing.—Trisoner: I will not go back to her.— Ile was sent to prison for three months.

div.head: IN THE COURTS.
div.p: IN THE COURTS.
GOLD IN A PIGSTY.
A Curious Police Court Story.

Mr. Robert Smith, off-licensee, Manchester- road, Warrington, left over £4O in a bag in his trap, whilst he made a call of a few minutes' duration on Friday evening last. On his r turn the bag containing the money had bee. stolen.
A •-,eeqUel was. heard ..at Police, Court

Monday morning, when, before ,Mr. S. Wrigi (in the chair), and other magistrates, Day, Algie (18), 18, Barnard-street, and Harry Walmsley (16), 5, Hepherd-street, were charged with stealing £42 145., the money of Mr. Robert Smith, Manchester-road, Warrington, and Alexander Algie, sen., and Alexander Algie jun., were charged with receiving £37 of th( money.

The Chief Constable said that on Frida night, 31st October, Mr. Smith was making calf in a trap. He called at a place which was, no far from where a municipal election meetin, was proceeding. He left the money in the trap, and on his return the bag had been stolen. In- quiries were made, and the younger prisoners were arrested. Young Algie admitted having taken the money, and said he -had handed handful of gold to his father. The father ha, been indignant when taxed with receiving th money.

The police learned that £2O had been en trusted with Alexander Algie, jun., and also that £l7 had been entrusted to the manager of a public-house by Algie, sen., who had said that he had had some money left him and he did not want his wife to knoW. A bar, containing papers was still missing. When Algie, sen., got the money it was alleged that he. had buried it in a pigsty or in a garden. Many of the sover- eigns were covered with dirt.
Algie, sen., said be caught the young boy David digging money up in a pigsty. He had taken it off him awaiting information.
The Chief Constable: Ile stoutly denied any knowledge of the affair at all.
Prisoners were remanded for seven days.

div.head: BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
div.p: BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SATURDAY.
Before Messrs. R. T. Fairclough (in the chair), '

1. Pemberton and A. J. Jolley. A SCENE IN THE COURT.—Charles Barlow, 21, King-street West, Manchester, was charged with obstructing and impeding an officer of the L. and N.-W. Railway. It took four police officers to drag Barlow to the front of the dock. —The Chief Constable said that at 6.20 that morning prisoner had come off the high level platform and Shad refused to give up his ticket. tie was somewhat erratic, and whether he was sane or not they were unable to say. He had acted in a most peculiar mann,er whilst in cus- tody, although they could not say whether he was putting it on or not. He had been causing them trouble in the town for the last day or two, and it was desirable that he should be committed to the Workhouse in order that his sanity might be tested. The business he was carrying on was of a most shady character—can- vassing for subscriptions for key labels.—Pris- oner was committed to the Workhouse on a 14 days' order.—As he went " below " he struggled and shouted loudly.

div.head: MONDAY.
div.p: MONDAY.
Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Bolton,, Smethurst and James Evans, Messrs. S. Wright, W. Roberts, G. Pilling and T. Locker.

SUPERINTENDENT ASSAULTED.-JOhll Robinson, 71, Dallam-lane, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly, and also with assaulting Supt. Williamson and John P. McCabe. Mr. McCabe said prisoner was with one of his female lodgers, and when stopped from enter- ing a lodging-house he became abusive, and struck witness in the eye and on the head.— Supt. Williamson said that, when he tried to quieten prisoner, he said, "I will have a 'stack up' with you." He struck witness in the face, and a cab had to be procured to get prisoner to the Police Sthtion.—A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed, with an alternative of 14 days' im- prisonment.

FIST THROUGH THE WINDOW.-7Thos. Cafferty Or Delaney,- Barbauld-street, was charged with being drpnk and disorderly in Barbauld-street, with assaulting Frederick Mullins in the Old House at Home, and with breaking a glass panel value ,X 2 10s. in the public-house door.—lt would appear that prisoner was being turned out of the house, and IT was alleged flat he struck the sons of the licensee, Frederick and Thomas Mullins. When he was put outside it Iva); alleged that 'he had put his fist through the window, and Mr. Charles Wright, 39, Winwiek- road, prevented him doing further damage, and assisted in his arrest—Prisoner was fined 10s. and costs (..e3 in all), or one mortal's imprison- ment.—. Mr. Wright was thanked for his services by the Chief 'Constable and the Bench, and it was stated that any damage he had sustained would be met.

A PLACE TO SLEEP.—John Bell, no fixed abode, was sent to prison for fourteen days for being found on the Warrington Cricket Ground for an unlawful purpose.—P.C. Skelton said pris- oner was acting in a suspicious manner at 11.15 on Saturday night, and made for tii cricket pavilion. When taxed he said he wanted to go to sleep.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.
Before Councillor H. Roberts (in the chair) Colonel Edelsten and Mr. C. Jackson Holmes.

A MAN OF WEALTII.—TWO strangers to the town, Thomas Gray, alias Johnson, and Alicia Buck- ley, alias. Johnson, were summoned for obtain- ing food' and lodgings by false pretences from Mrs. Twist, 20, Parker-street.—The Chief Con- stable stated on Monday of the previous week: the prisoners went to the house of the prosecu- trix, intimated that they were seeking lodgings, and were in search of a tobacconist's shop. The male prisoner, prosecutrix said, informed her that he received .22 10s. a week from his father, in addition to .215 from other sources, and Mrs. Twist, believing their tale, took them into her house, and the following morning they made further statements. On Monday this week, it is alleged, the prisoners left the house, having smuggled all their paraphernalia 'out, and in- tended going to Liverpool. Mrs. Twist became suspicious, and called for the assistance of. the police, when the male prisoner is alleged to have said that they would have sent the money from Liverpool. The Chief Constable said he believed, although they had been living to- gether, the prisoners were not man and wife.— The case was adjourned for a week.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.

Before Mr. J. W. Hayward (in the chair), Alder- man Smethurst, and Messrs. C. Jackson Holmes -andW. T. Williams. A " SALTY " TALE.—James Varey, a hawker, giving an address at a lodging-house in Stanley-

street; was charged with obtaining 7d. by false pretences from Mrs. Alfred Wright, of 727, • linutsford-rokul,--The evidence of the police showed that prisoner visited the grocer's shop, 727, Knutsford-road, occupied by Mr. and Mrs. Alfred Wright, and after asking whether the "boss" was in, told Mrs. Wright that her hus- band had sent him with a piece of salt-rock, weighing 7ilb., for which he wanted 7d. It was later discovered that the husband had not sent the man to the shop at all, Mr. Wright stating. that Varey was becoming a nuisance.—lie was. fined ss. and costs, or seven days..

div.head: THURSDAY.
div.p: THURSDAY.
Before Mr. J. F.airclough (in the chair), Alder- man James Evans, and Messrs. A. J. Jolley, W. Richardson and W. .Roberts.

• DANC.E in THE SEQUEL.—In spite of many protestations of innocence from four prisoners, the Bench agreed to accept the story of an aged Irishman named Michael Keaveny, who' alleged that he had been robbed of 11s, by a party of fellow boarders at a lodging-house in Stanley- street. The prisoners were Thomas Evans, John Griffiths, Mary Evans and Lydia Brick- ley.—The Chief Constable said that on Wednes- day week last the four prisoners arrived in the town from Altrincham, and commenced crink- ing together in a public-house, and later at the lodging-house. On the following night the prosecutor went .to the lodging-house, and after objecting to dance with them, the two women got hold of his arms as if to dance, and the male prisoner Evans placed his hand into Keaveny's left-hand trousers pocket. Prosecu- tor immediately afterwards discovered that his money was gone. He reported the matter to Mrs. McCabe, who in turn called in the ponce, and prisoners ,were taken into custody. Grif- fiths made the prosecutor an offer of money if he would promise na,to say anything. When 4 being taken to the Police Station the female pris'oner Evans laid upon the table us., made up of coins similar to those alleged to have been Stolen. The prosecutor, Acting-Sergeant Whitby, and Mrs. McCabe gave evideace.— Prisoners protested their innocence, but the Bench sentenced Brickley to 14 days, and the other three defendants to three months' hard labour.'

MARGARINE FOR Brrrea.—George Starkey, a shopkeeper, of Chorley-street, was summoned under the Food and Drugs' Act with selling margarine for butter, and, in prosecuting, Mr. Hallaway, the deputy town clerk, stated that Inspector Flood visited the shop on September 24, and was served by defendant's wife. There were only two blocks of stuff in the shop, and on these no labels were displayed to indicate that the blocks consisted of margarine. In ad- dition the sample was supplied to Mr. Flood in a ,plain wrapper. Mr. Steel defended and pleaded guilty. He explained there was a' serious illness in the family, and it had upset Mrs. Starkey. Mr. Starkey was out at the time, and ,whilst out he purchased the proper paper for wrappers.—A fine of £5 and costs was imposed.

BEGGED PARDON.—A man of no settled abode. named George Naylor, was charged with doing wilful damage to a window at the Raven Hotel, and doing damage to the extent of £7. When asked if he had anything to say, he replied ", I only beg pardon if I have done anything wrong."—He was remanded for seven days. LOYAL: TO HIS FRIENDS.—James Miller, a youth of Winwick-street, was charged with playing a game of chance with cards called "brag," at Six Arches.—The police evidence showed that defendant refused to give the names of those playing with him by saying that he did not know them, and later he supplied four names, which proved to be false.—The Chief Constablo stated that these people arranged that if one was caught he should not give, the others away, and they would all pay towards the fine.—Mil- ler was fined 20s. and costs.

SHOT IN THE STREET.—William DUEL)°bill, Lower House Farm, Lower Walton, and Thomas Arnold, of 92, Greenall's-avenue, were sum- moned respectively for causing a horse to be worked and for working a horse in an unfit state. —Evidence for the prosecution sho`wed that the horse was in a very poor condition, and was so weak that when it fell down in Winmarleigh- street, it was unable to regain its feet. after attempted efforts, and had to be shot on the spot.—For the defence it was contended that the animal hurt itself in falling, which accounted for it being unable to get up.—On this defence the case was dismissed.

div.head: UNIONIST INDECISION.• The Unionist party appear to be in a state of
div.p: UNIONIST INDECISION.• The Unionist party appear to be in a state of
great indecision, and we know what fate is said to await the man who hesitates.
Last
week Mr. 80N.A13, LAW professed one day to be- lieve that a .General Election would end 'Home Rule. and the wicked ,Government that is pro- moting that measure of justice for Ireland,
while. within a few hours he was lamenting the fact that his party might be in the wilderness for
forty years. A couple of months ago a 'group of Unionists who had been working upon the

subject of labourers' wages on the initiative of Mr. BALFOURi for ,two years, recommended that District .Wages. Boards should be called up to regulate those wages.. All looked well for an -opposition land reform scheme ; but this has been side-tracked. The ,"Times.", tells us that Unionist members and candidates have
just received a communication from head-

quarters, as to the urgent need of concentrating the attention of the country on the grave posi- tion in Ulster. "Much attention," therefore, was not likely to be paid on the Unionist side to the Liberal land campaign. Possibly an inquiry into the subject of labourers' wages might be ,undertaken, as "an earnest of
Unionist intentions, while the public mind would not thereby be diverted from the crisis in Ireland." But it is the crisis in Ireland

upon which Unionists are most involved. The great sin of the Government, according to all Unionist speakers, is that they are giving 'Home Rule to Ireland without the authority of . a General Election.' They forget what they them- selves said when the Government last appealed to the, conntry—that a Liberal victory meant Home Rule. It is strange that they should invite people not to believe what they said a short' three years,ago, but there it is. Carrying out the "no mandate" idea, they ask for an election. Ali-. HAROLD SMITH, M.P., when he entered upon the late Anti-Home Rule campaign which had so inglorious an end, joined in the chorus, "Consult the . people!" and then, 'pre- sumably, the fraction of Ulster for which he spoke would be satisfied. But What say CARSON and BALFOUR? The " coATnanters " "will not have Home Rule," and Mr. BALFOUR, who, like all the rest, calls for a General Elec- tion, kindly confesses that whatever the verdict may, be, we shall be no nearer a settlement of the ilome Rule issue. We know that to save the Lords' Veto .the Unionists were anxious to col promise on Home Rule, and that in a moment of frankness they admitted that Ire- land needed redress. Tht, "Times" points out that the Unionist policy has changed, and states that Unionists who are blind to the change are not those who inflnence the counsels of the party. The "Daily Telegraph" goes further and. says: "He is a very short-sighted Unionist who thinks that no change is neces- sary in the government of Ireland. It is quite clear that change there' niust be, to whichever side the -victory in the present contest. may fall." Yet it is now full steam ahead in oppo- sition to Irish reconciliation and Unionist land reform, like food taxes, has gone overboard. It is difficult to understand these entrances and exits, these flounderings and desperate devices, these asSertions and contradictions, .except by one method'of reasoning. That is, that when a party deliberately sets out to prevent nine tenths of a country from having that which it requires, because the remaining one-tenth 'wishes to retain an arrogant domination, that Party must inevitably be reduced to desperate devices, which lead to devious and strangely contradictory conclusions.

div.head: ARE OUR SCHOLARS DETERIORATING?
div.p: ARE OUR SCHOLARS DETERIORATING?

There is a decided division of opinion. as to whether the schoolboys and schoolgirls of the present generation are equal to those of a past generation in real .efficiency. The present gen- eration are handicapped by , the fact that it is the past generation that act as judges, which is scarcely fair. The natural result is adverse to the outcome of modern methods, and the handwriting of the new office boy is held up as a something at which all the world may mar- vel. "The Schoolmaster" i'ecently' had some- thing to say on this matter, the following being a summary :

Complaints that reading, writing and arith- metic are not so well taught as they used to be are frequently heard in America concerning American 'schools, as well as in England. Here in England it is very much a matter of opinion, but in Springfield, U.S.A., it has been brought to a test. In 1890 there were discovered in the attic of the High School building in Springfield, Mass., U.S.A., several old sets of examination questions that had been, written in the fall of 1816. They consisted of printed questions in geography and arithmetic, with answers written on the printed sheets, and written tests in spel- ling and penmanship. Two of these tests were later (1905) given to 245 ninth-grade pupils in the Springfield Schools, and the results were carefully compared with the results of the tests of 1846. The following is the comparison :
SPELLING. In 1846. In 1905. Number of pupils who took tests... 85 245 Average per cent. correct
ARITHMETIC. Number of pupils who took teits 79 215 Average per cent. correct 29.5 65.5

Of the class in 1846, only 16 of the 85 pupils stood as high, in spelling as 70 per cent., the present " passing " mark in most schools. Three pupils had no words spelled correctly; nine had only one right; while 24, or more than one- fourth of the entire class, mis-spelled 17 or more words. Comparisons of the geography and .penmanship were even more conclusive evidence of the superiority of the pupils of 1905 over those of 1846.

• Have oui• local schools any old papers which could be classified and compared Vith modern, work? If we had some of the actual papers of our old-world critics it would be more con- vincing than their memory of their own work. The writer has a few copy books, exercise books, and drawing books that haVe stood the ravages of time, and run the gauntlet of an untold number of spring cleanings. Others may have similar relics which could be pressed into the service of the Education Department if they wish to' apply eugenic methods to our school system:

It will be seen from our report of the annual meeting of the association that last season was very successful, and that in addition to.linding themselves nearly, a hundred prizes, the asso- ciation handed over £6 each to; the Children's Summer It amp and the Nursing Association. They have an example in what may be done by proper organisation and the "nimble penny" at Messrs. Rylands' Recreation Ground, where a body of working men are running grounds, buildings and games on an elaborate scale. ,

div.head: PASSING – Ei&
div.p: THE PASSING - Ei&
THE MAYOR!

Mayor-making should take place to-morrow, the ninth of November, but to-morrow is Sunday, and while some towns will have the pleasurable experience to-day, some will post- pone the event until ,Monday. Monday will be. the great day locally, and as soon after twelve noon as possible the following resolution will be submitted for the approval of the Council:— . That Mr. Peter Peacock be and is hereby elected Mayor for the ensuing year, and until the acceptance of office by his suc- cessor. •

The Friendly Societies ha;*e taken steps to make Mayor's Sunday a red-letter day in their history. , They will accompany ;Councillor Peacock, who is one of their most respected members,' to church, and so add much to the dignity and importance of the occasion.

div.head: SOME BIG MAJORITIES.
div.p: SOME BIG MAJORITIES.

It was one of the Welters who expressed a doubt as to whether it was worth so much trouble to' gain so little as was got by learning the alphabet. Was it, we may ask, worth our while 'to have three contested elections in the wards last Saturday, at the cost of, say, £lOO, in order to re-elect the same gentlemen who had retired, by majorities ranging from 202 to 335? The former majority was obtained in Latchford by Councillor Henshall, who, as .an Independent, resisted the • Conservative on- ,._ slaught and incidentally increased his majority of 86 three 3',.ears ag,o to 202. We expressed our doubts as to whether the shrewd people of Latchford N);'1)111(1 S War) their. very good horse for . another when they have schemes half throUgh of which the old horse has the,complete measure. The only out-and-out political fight was in Whitecross, where the largest majority of the day was obtained. :Need we say it was obtained by the Liberal candidate? Here, as in Latch- ford, there was in possession, in the person of Mr. Hawthorn, a live representative, who is always in, the thick, of good work for his ward, and the town generally. Could Whitecross forsake its Liberalism, and, if it could, would it cast Councillor Hawthorn? Those questions were answered with an emphasis which has much meaning, when it polled 808 for Mr. Haw- thorn, against 471 for Mr, ni•ookes, the Conser- vative nominee. Three years ago Hawthorn's majority, was 356. 'Perhaps his opponents will learn to look upon his position as invulnerable, and save themselves some trouble in future. Mr. Brookes professes to be satisfied with his "trial trip." Councillor Hawthorn has no need to be dissatisfied. Councillor Broadhurst, the Conservative'can- didate in st. Austin's, succeeded in retaining the seat by a majority' of 316 over Mr. Arthur, Browne, Independent. Three years ago he succeeded against a Liberal by 14:,?.. • In the remaining wards four Liberals and two Conservatives were returned unopposed.
