This leaves us five short. The deficiency is. accounted for by the fact . that five . aldermen retire, and will not be re-elected until after the Mayor has been chosen. These aldermen are three Conservatives (Aldermen Bolton, Forshaw and Smethurst); one Liberal (Alderman James Evans), and one Independent (Alderman John Evans). Their election will bring the Council up to full strength, 36, and assuming the same gentlemen are again chosen as aldermen, the Council will b composed as follows Liberals, 16; Conservatives, 15; Independents, 5; total, 36.

Several Councillors have refused' to agree ttl the re-election Of retiring Aldermen. They have decided to keep themselves free for action on Monday ; but we believe it is the law that speeches cannot be made on the. election of aldermen.

div.head: PROGRESS OF NVESLEYANISM.
div.p: PROGRESS OF NVESLEYANISM.

As Byron says, a thousand years scarce serve to form a State. A religious body, fired with a peculiar type of "enthusiasm, knows less of the trammels that encounter the progress of a State, and so it comes about, in part, that the Bev. H. Williamson, at . the anniversary :services held in Bold-street Wesleyan Church on Sunday, was able to say that the followers of John Wesley, whose life is only' separated from our day by a little over a century, now number something like 30,000,009. The Methodist Church has about £90,000,006 invested in ecclesiastical property, and has all the other indications of a prosper-

ous, progressive, and progressing, Church. Locally, the cause has reason to approach the future in optimistic vein. The Mayor-elect pre- sided over these very interesting proceedings, and, as is usual with him, he had something of a practical 'nature to say. The best of churches have their deficiencies, and Councillor Peacock asked his atatience to have a care as to the amount they, spept _on amusement, a class of expenditure which IA 'growing rapidly among all ranks. The troubles of church trustees would be wiped off, said Councillor Peacock, if the congregation would 'only -give ,in the same proportion as they spend, upon amusements.

div.head: WORKS BOWLING GREENS.
div.p: WORKS BOWLING GREENS.

Those who are at the. head of the Works Bowling Association are to be commended for the high ideals they entertain. They wish to have a club-house and .a ground of their own for several reasons. In the first place they are compelled to, use existing greens belonging to others, which means that games are crushed into a linlited period which does not give the players a fair, chance. In the next place, the Works Competition is the Works Competition, and though the association may be indebted for the accommodation that has been placed at their disposal,. there is no valid reason why all members should be forced to attend public- house greens if they are to follow their favourite pastime. Time was when bowlers were exclu- sively middle-aged and old men—" the old man's game" it was called by the young and perky 'cricketer and footballer. But now bowling is universally followed, and the best of .conditions and the most healthy surroundings should be associated with the game. We there- fore hope that the appeal that is to be made ter

div.head: "OLD GENTLEMAN."
div.p: THE "OLD GENTLEMAN."

On our fifth page we have an illustration showing how a certain gentleman once men- tioned by the Mayor may be made to appear not so black as he is painted. The application of the-Whitewash brush is a means that comes ready to hand, at all events according to our artist's imagination. There is another saying relative to the same old gentleman with the 'repulsive traditions. To "Give the devil his due" is supposed to be the acme of fair play, and we wish to be quite fair in dealing with the chimneys of Warrington. We have 'observed a distinct improvement this week. Frequent observations of our friends that belch forth black smoke on . the least provocation show that they have this week been content to send forth smoke that has been suggestive more of reasonable manufacturing methods . than of reckless stoking that cares little whether or not it poisons the populatic,n and desolates a countryside. We hope that if the secret of the improvement is that stokers have received instructions how to do their work, they will be kept up to their duty, and assisted as soon as may bd by the introductionuf smoke- preventing and fuel economising apparatus.

div.head: WORKHOUSE SMOKE.
div.p: WORKHOUSE SMOKE.

. At the Workhouse on Wednesday the Bev. A. M. Mitchell called attention to their chimney, which was smoking as bad as ever, notNifith- standing the notice of the Corporation to abate the nuisance. The reverend gentleman was asked to be patient, and was informed that steps had been taken to change the boilers and raise the chimney. We are clearly making progress.

div.head: BLUE EYES.
div.p: BLUE EYES.

Warrington has had a lucky escape. Mr. Harold Sinn, M.P., was among his acting friends in London on Tuesday, and, as chair- man at a luncheon given to bid farewell to "Happy Fanny Fields," the famous music hall comedienne, who is returning to America to marry Dr. Rongy, discharged his duties. wit- tily. Miss Fields, returning thanks, made the following remarkable conclusion : I have never met Mr. Smith before, and woe" is, me. I don't know what would have hap- pened if I had not met the _doctor first, for
there is something in _those kindly blue 'e-Yea

which would have- said "Come over here!' That, We may say, is A lucky 'escape for War- rington. But escapes, like rigors and sneezes and inflammations, are sent as warnings, and they are useless unless they are heeded. In the one thousand, more or less, women, who are to come from Ulster to Warrington—some day - -there will, presumably, be many who are not on their way ,to marry a doctor in New York. And Irish girls, wh6 themselves are noted for their grace and beauty, are connoisseurs in blue eyes!

div.head: POPULAR APPOINTMENT.
div.p: A POPULAR APPOINTMENT.

We desire to associate ourselves as, closely as we can with the congratulations that have showered upon Mr. Sydney W. Jeffery upon his suCcession to the post held so long, and with so much distinction, by his life-long chief, Mr. Alfred COrney, headmaster of the Wycliffe Day School. Mr. Jeffery has every qualification for the post, and everyone will be glad it has come his way unquestioned and uncontested. We are strong advocates, in the main, for "free trade" in public appointments as in most things in public life. Building walls round a place and crying "Warrington schools for Warring- ton teachers," "Warrington jobs for Warring- ton architects," and the like, is a process that has no attractions for us. What is best should be the only test', and if Warrington best cannot hold its own, Warrington best must give way to somebody else's better. But it would be im- possible to improve upon Mr. Jeffery• for the post for which he has been in training for a quarter of a century, and the Managers and Committee have acted wisely in deciding not to wake the pretence of trying to do so.'

div.head: DISAPPEARING HALF-TIMER.
div.p: THE DISAPPEARING HALF-TIMER.

Noiselessly and 'imperceptibly the half-timer in our schools is becoming a thing of the past. Mr. 'Jeffery remembers the time when there were eighty of these unfortunates in Wycliffe School alone, a drag upon their classmates, the despair of their teachers, a misery to themselves and a disgrace to our civilisation, to say noth- ing of our Christianity. Now, says Mr. Jeffei•y, you can scarcely find one, in the whole town, thanks to the administrative ability of the Education Authority. This is an illustration of the truth of the saying that in many direc- tions our laws are sufficient for all practical Purposes if properly, carried out, without wast- ing time calling for, fresh legislation. While others have been calling for powers to . abolish half-time in school and factory, the Warrington Education Committee have abolished the .half- timer.

According to Mr. Morgan, the new President of the Lancashire, Yorkshire, • dheshire and Derbyshire Half-time Council, 40 per cent. of half-timers are physically defective. It was, he said, a national menace, though/new develop- ments affecting children in national and muni- cipal life gave " some ground for hope." Developments at Warrington are decidedly hopeful.
"THE PRAYER OF A HORSE." "To thee, my master, I offer my prayer:

" Feed me, water and care for me, and when the day's work is done provide me with shelter, a clean, dry bed, and a stall wide enough for me to lie down in comfort. Talk to me. Your voice often means as much to me as the reins. Pet me sometimes, that I may serve you the more gladly and learn to love you. Do not jerk the reins, and do not whip me when going uphill. Never strike, beat, or kick me when I do not understand what you mean, but give me a chance to understand you. Watch me, and if I fail to do your bidding see if something is not wrong with my harness or feet.

"Examine my teeth when I do not eat. I may have an ulcerated tooth, and that, you know, is very painful. Do not tie my head in an unnatural position or take away my best defence against Hies and mosquitoes by cutting off my tail.

"And, finally, oh my master, when my use- ful strength is gone do not turn me out to starve or freeze or sell me to some cruel owner, to be slowly tortured and starved to death. But do thou, my master, take my life in the kindest way and your God will reward you here and hereafter.
" You may not consider me irreverent if I ask this in the name of Him who Was born in a stable. Amen."
"The Prayer of a Horse" is posted in many, American stables. It might be seriously studied in this country, too.

div.head: From Everywhere.
div.p: From Everywhere.
The very polished are often very dull Just the same.

Even the fastest women find it very difficult to leave their peas behind them. I would rather lose my character than my powder puff on a hot day.—Louise Heilgers. Women should, not be brought up to believe that all men are possible husbands. Most men are impossible ones.—Arthur Pendennis, in "Books of To-day and To-morrow." Half the world is trying to be with someone it should not be with, and the other half is try- ing to get away from someone it should be with.
The people who always want to attract atten- tion often do it in the least attractive way.
Some people talk so much they haven't time to say anything. _
If you treat a man like a dog you can't blame him for acting like one.
- Beauty is only skin deep and yet the average woman is taken at her face value.
Where Is It?
Who can say where Castle-street, Warring- ton, is? Is it one of our thoroughfares that re- quires widening badly?
Lady speaker in the Warrington district, dis- coursing upon the Japanese : "The men dress like we dot" 3
Probably. When a pretty woman and a clever man put their heads together it always leads to some- thing--probably a kiss.
Of Course. Teacher.: What is the highest form of animal life? Johnnie, frantically, waving to attract her attention: I know, teacher! It's a giraffe.

"Bottles and Rags !" "Bottles and rags !" called the 'ragman. "Why do you always put these words together?" asked a - passer-by. "Because, madam," said the ragman, touching his hat, "wherever you find bottles yOU .find rags.",
Note for Christmas. Customer (with a grievance): ," And recollect, I don't want any of your aeroplane turkeys !''
_ Shopman I don't understand, sir." Customer: " I inean the species that is al wings and machinery, and no meat !"
Humour of the Country.

If 27in. of snow give 3in. of water, how much milk will a Ow give when fed upon turnips?,— Multiply the flakes by the hair of the coW's tail, then divide the product by a turnip, add a pound of chalk, and the sum will be the answer.
NVisdom and Folly.

Most people -make the mistake of trying to talk interestingly, whereas the only thing that really interests people is silence. A fool says the things that need not be said, while a clever man leaves .unsaid the things that might be said.—" The Tatler."

Nionotony. A little boy at a village school on being asked what was "monotony," replied promptly that it was "living with one wife." A similar Mor- monic confusion between monogamy and monotony is often made by much Older,boys.— Annesley Kenealy.
An Anxious Father.

There is at least One advantage in a school where two languages are taught. A London paper tells of a Welsh father who wrote a note to the school teacher, ,saying: "Please do not let ray son John learn Welsh to-day; his throat is so had he can hardly speak English."
A Woman's " Aim."

• A Kansas farmer purchased a revolver for his wife, and insisted on target practice, so that she might be able to defend the house in his absence. After the bullet was dug out of his leg, and the cow buried, he said he guessed she'd better shoot with an axe. A Room for Criticism.

• Speatiing of the model houses in the Ideal Hoine Exhibition a writer in the "Daily Mail" says of the Russian house, "There is no room for criticism." We had never thought of that, says "The Tatler." What an excellent idea; in future we shall always set apart a. room with a baize door in which to shut people who want to criticise and complain. •
Insult to Injury.

A motoring gentleman smashed, through a fence at right angles into a farmyard, and then went crashing into the pigsty. In the yard was a man sawing wood, who had a great dislike of motoring. He watched the scene with cool irri- tation, and then cried out: " hi! ye blind fool. Come out of that. Don't ye see the pigsty is full already."

The Resourceful Milkman. The milkman stood before her, nervously twisting his hat in his hands. "So," she said sternly, "you have come at last?" " Yes, madam. You sent for me, I -believe," he replied. "I wished to tell you that I found a minnow in the milk yesterday morning.". "I am sorry; madam; but if the COWS will drink water ,from tha.brook instead of from the trough, I cannot help it."
On the Run.

A correspondent writes charging us with hav- ing missed an important piece of news in cOn- nection with laSt week's great thunderstorm. "Pity must be extended to the Tariff Re- formers of Warrington," he reminds us., "Mr. A. 11. Crosfield recently said they were on the run and must be kept on the run. Even the ele- ments are conspiring to do that, for a big de- monstration was arranged for Monday night, and the Reformers had to flee from speech- making. A lightning flash, a thunder crash, and a deluge of rain set the Tariffites scamper- ing for shelter, which they showed a very Free Trade spirit in securing."
We plead guilty, but we cannot keep an eye on everything.

div.head: "THE CONQUEROR."
div.p: "THE CONQUEROR."

It's easy to laugh when the skies are blue, And the sun is shining bright; Yes, easy to laugh when your friends are. true And there's happiness in sight; Rut when hope has fled and the skies are grey And the friends of the past have turned away, th, then, indeed, it's a hero's feat To conjure a smile in the face of defeat.

It's easy to. laugh when the storm is o'er And your ship is safe in port; Yes, easy to laugh when you're on the shore Secure from the tempest's sport; But when wild waves wash o'er the stormswept deck And your gallant ship is a battered wreck, Ath ! that is the time when it's well worth while To look in the face of defeat with a smile.

It's easy to laugh when the battle's ,fought And you know that the victory's won; Yes, easy to laugh when the prize you sought Is yours when the race is run; But here's to the man who can laugh when the blast Of adversity blows, he will conquer at last, For the hardest man in the world to beat Is the man who can laugh in the face of defeat.

div.head: GAMBLING AMONGST WOMEN,
div.p: GAMBLING AMONGST WOMEN,
A Social Plague which is Wrecking Homes in

div.head: Warrington.
div.p: Warrington.
INNOCENT FEMALES TRAPPED INTO EVIL.
SPECIAL.

he goes next day to the bookmaker, draws cash, and is a fresh victim dragged within tlt.t gambling vortex. Such Mrs. Newcomers al.` continually being dragged in." The above 'gives a fairly good idea of 11° women in, poorer class districts are tempted tc/j become, and do become in the end,,confiriee_ gamblers. Many cases could be discovered Lu. prove that such does happen, and it does 111 need imagination 'to trace the after fate women of .the type of Mrs. Newcomer, there al" to hand scores of examples.

div.head: " EXAMINER!"
div.p: " EXAMINER!"

"The most subtle, pernicious evil, which is spreading cancer-like roots amongst the women and girls in working-class homes to- day, is the gambling evil. It is astounding the amount which does exist, and (lit hal-,it is alarmingly on the increase." So said a prominent woman trade unionist, Whose work brings her into close touch with women and girls in this part of Lancashire,, to "The Examiner" repre§entative. Inquiries went to show that the eVil is on the increase in Warrington, and this opinion is confirmed by social. workers, Who meantime are nonplussed to find a remedy whereby to check the spread Of the mischief. The' police would take actions but they are confronted with almost insur- mountable difficulties,, the chief of which is finding the proof required Lo bring about a conviction.

Women gamblers, unlike men who "put a bit on," carry through their .transactions more secretly. Perhaps this is due to ,the female love of secrets. The usual street bookmakers are not dealt, with openly, although the money may in the end reach them by various channels it is apt possible .to tap. The men go openly to the bookmakers at some appointed place, but the women have a more elaborate system.. Much of the betting is transacted in the homes or at gossips in the, backyards, and in such cases it is rare .the police can get evidence of what gces on to support a prosecution:

div.head: GIRLS AS GAMBLERS.
div.p: GIRLS AS GAMBLERS.

Girls of twelve years and upwards are often dragged into the mesh of the gambling craze. They, perchance, learn what their mothers and elder sisters are doing, and find how to do it through acting the part of messengers. The rest is easy. That girls of tender years do bet the police are aware, and only a few weeks ago. in a betting prosecution in the Warrington County Police -Sessions, it was stated that the polk.e saw a lrookmaker take bets from a num- ber of young girls. This showed that even female gamblers practise :openly, but they are few in mlinber to those who do so under the cover of secrecy.

It is a cOmmon thing, " The Examiner " representative was informed, for women to meet daily z-it one or Other 4:4 their houses, 011101' in a supply Of beer, and, while they imbibe, discuss the tips for the raees of the day. Sport- ing papers, whieh give So-called tips as to " dead certs" or "snips," or other things fffiiiiltar to turfites, have a considerable sale amongst the xvomen m sonic. parts of Warring- tdn. The tissues, or single sheets, containing practically nothing but racing information, which conic out 'about mid-day, find, we Are told, a ready sale amongst the women of the town. They are studied carefully for "good things."

div.head: WOMEN BOOKMAKERS,
div.p: WOMEN BOOKMAKERS,

The betting habit seems to have got a terrible grip upon some sections of women, and a con- siderable .amount of money changes hands weekly on aecount of this, money from people who can ill-afford to throw it away in this fashion. Women bookmakers, or women who act as agents for male bookmakers, are fairly numerous, and work a lot of mischief by entic- ing other women to bet. In some of the poorer districts nearly every woman in a street bets with. one of those women harpies, and, what is more, she gets into debt through the gambling transactions, borrows money from the "bookies," and then she is at the complete. mercy of th lender-bookmaker. "A young woman may go to reside in one of these districts," said one familiar with the methods pursued, "and she is not long there until she strikes up a, friendship with a neigh- bour. The neighbour is affable and invites the newcomer into her home. There she 'meets other women and has drink. The talk turns upon racing—in fact, the whole discourse is upon betting.

div.head: BAIT AT WORK.
div.p: THE BAIT AT WORK.

• "The newcomer learns how Mrs. .' has just won a • sovereign on a horse called Gee-gee H. Nothing is easier, she is told, than to win money on a* horse race, proihded she can get good information. Eve-like, Mrs. New- comer becomes a bit envious of the luck her neighbour has experienced. She .iS not asked there and then to make a 'bet, but she is allowed to go home and ponder over what she has heard. One daSi, she sees Mrs. a fine ,dress, or a new hat, the envy becomes more pronounced. Doubtless Mrs. the money for that 'hat or dress out of her earnings from bets. Mrs. -ha S a husband who does not make as much as her husband, Mrs. Newcomer thinks. Surely, the latter argues, if she can afford to have a bit on and win so much, she, Mrs. Newcomer, can. Fem- inine envy does the rest.

div.head: SO EASY TO BEGIN.
div.p: SO EASY TO BEGIN.

, "Later, Mrs. Newcomer has a long chat with Mrs. Neighbour over the matter. 'Just you try your luck with a sixpence,' suggests Mrs. Neighbour, you have a sixpenny bit on "Never Wins," it's a fine thing and is sure to win.' Mrs. Newcomer thinks she will, and then she discovers Mrs. Neighbour ready to make all the arrangements for putting on the bet. If Mrs. Neighbour does not bet herself as a book- maker, as a bookmaker's agent, She ias. a friend who does.

"The money is laid on this particular horse prior to Mr. Newcomer arriving home for dinner. Ile never hears of the transaction, the usual advice of one gambling woman to another being to keep such 'good things to themselves, otherwise the husbands might

capture the profits, and they, their wives, would get nothing out of the 'plunge.' All afternoon Mrs. Newcomer is in a fever of excitement until the evening paper gives the result of the race. 'Never Win ' has finished first .and she has made a pile.

div.head: CONGRATULATED ON HER LUCK.
div.p: CONGRATULATED ON HER LUCK.

"Mrs. Neighbour comes in and congratulates her upon her good luck. How much have I won?' innocently queries Mrs. Newcomer. The friend scans the starting, prices given for the race. "The price,' says Mrs. Neighbour, is thirty to one.' 'Yes, but what does that mean?' Mean, lass, mean? Why, you've got to draw 15s. and your sixpence back.' Mrs. New- comer is amazed at her good fortune. She

div.head: TO FIGHT PENURY AND ILLNESS. Mr. Lloyd George's Message to the Reading
div.p: TO FIGHT PENURY AND ILLNESS. Mr. Lloyd George's Message to the Reading
Electors.
Mr. Gooch, the Liberal candidate in the Read- ing by-election, has received the following mes- sage :

"Good luck to you! I see your opponents are as usual abusing the Insurance Act. No amount of misrepresentation can get rid of the fact that the Liberal Government have raised thirteen millions a year to protect the aged against penury and seven millions this year to provide workmen with free doctoring during illness, and to save them and their families from privation by giving them sick and un- employment pay. When Toryism has achieved a tenth part of this service it will have some claim, to criticise our efforts. "LLOYD GEORGE."

div.head: BECOME INVETERATE GAMBLERS.
div.p: BECOME INVETERATE GAMBLERS.

It is a well-known fact to social refornicros that once women become addicted to the ertlir; of betting they become more inveterate ganlble„, than the men, and this weakness is made TC of by the women who act as bookmakers. plungtrs are encouraged to plunge still 111°12;4 Drinking parties are held, and at these the conversation is betting tips, horses and meetings. Some women can be found "d Carry in their memories almost all the nanles,lc racehorses to be found within the pages of 'fis racing calendar, and they are looked up t°,„"e oracles by the less informed. , Next tO female bookmakers these women do the greaft; amount of harm, for their non-useful knowlell' is utilised to incite lhe others to plunge 5" further into the mire.

div.head: Licensing Transfers.
div.p: Licensing Transfers.

Tile following licensing transfers were granted ftt the Warrington Police Court on Monday: 'Or-licence, 2, Melville-street, to A. G. Renwick, -from Lawrence Whitfield; off-licence, 64, Knuts- -ford-road, from Sarah Ann Buckley to George Buckley.

div.head: Illness of Mrs. W. Peter fly lands.
div.p: Illness of Mrs. W. Peter fly lands.
Mrs, Rylands is at present indisposed, and on 'Wednesday was unable to open the Arts and -Crafts Exhibition at the Old Academy ,as arranged. Her condition, however, dues not give ..cause for alarm.

div.head: Famous 111.P.'s Visit.
div.p: Famous 111.P.'s Visit.

Mr. W. A. Barton, M.P. for Oldham, is to address a mass meeting, organised by the War- rington Junior Liberal Association, in the Co- operative Hall on Monday, 17th November. Mr. J., Davies, Liberal candidate for Crewe, will be .the other speaker.

div.head: Freemason Feslival.
div.p: A Freemason Feslival.

The "Lodge of Friendship" held the annual -festival on,Monday evening. Bro. James Edward Warren was installed W.M. bY W. Bro. H. H. 'Evans, assisted by W. Bro. W. Greenhouse, P.M., in the presence of a 'representative gathering. 'The installation banquet followed.

div.head: Illness of Lord Acton.
div.p: Illness of Lord Acton.

The illness of Lord Acton proved more serious than was at first thought. He has suffered from an attack of acute rheumatic fever and will still be confined to bed for some time at his residence at Appleton Hall. The latest ,report is that he is progressing as well as could be expected.

div.head: Cinderella Doll-dressing Club.
div.p: Cinderella Doll-dressing Club.

In connection with the. above, -250 dolls, the gift of Messrs. Hulton and Co., Manchester, are being dressed by Warrington ladies, under the supervision of the Mayoress (Mrs. Arnold Nield). An exhibition of the dolls will be held towards the end of the month,. after which they will be distributed amongst the poor Warring- ton children as Christmas gifts.

div.head: Auctioneers Win Their Case.
div.p: Auctioneers Win Their Case.

In Warrington County- Court on Thursday, Judge Stanger awarded £4O 19s. sd. and costs to Messrs. J. Mainwaring and Co., auctioneers, Warrington, in the action they brought against Mr. W. Rowlands, farmer, Sutton, St. Helens, due over the purchase of a quantity, of hay Sand straw at an auction conducted by the -Pain- tiffs. Defendant did not appear to defend the ease.

div.head: Chtb for the C.L.B.
div.p: A Chtb for the C.L.B.
The committee of the St. Paul's Church House have very generously given the members of the C.L.B. in their parish the use of the club, and the boys are taking full advantage of the offer.

:The Si. Paul's 'Company now have over 100 en- rolled, on their books, which constitutes a record for the town. Captain L. S. Henshall and Lieu- tenant L. Henshall are receiving' the apprecia- tion of the lads for their hard work.

div.head: Mother's Furniture.
div.p: A Mother's Furniture.

Before Judge Stanger, at Warriirgton County *Court on Thursday, Jane Houghton, -Lincoln, rand formerly of Warrington, sued Mr. and Mrs. J. Collin, 16, Ashwood-avenue,- Padgate-lane, for the return of furniture left by her mother to be divided amongst the female relatives, includ- ing Mrs. Collin. The 'value was 01:13. The de- fence was that the mother had gifted the furni- ture to Mrs. Collin, and in that circumstance she did not think it necessary to make a will. The case. was adjourned until 4th December.
X 272 Realised by Parish Church Bazaar.

The conclusion of the Parish Church Bazaar was reached on Saturday, when Mrs. Whitley, of Hatton, performed the opening ceremony. The Rector spoke. at some length of the history -of the two Missions at Crossley-street and Bank- street.. Mrs. Whitley said that it was unneces- sary to point out the worthiness of the objects to be assisted by the proceeds of the sale. Charity, she said, began at home, and it was for their own charities that she was present, and was pleased to declare the bazaar open. (Applause.) Entertainments were provided by the children from St. (gorge's Sunday School and the pupils from the Training College. The total proceeds realised about Y-272.

div.head: Band of Hope Entertainment.
div.p: Band of Hope Entertainment.

A Band of Hope entertainment was given in the Ebenezer Church, Buttermarket-street, on Monday. The chair was taken by Mr. 'H. Thorn- ton. Recitations were given by theibMisses Lily Hibbert, Beatrice Houghton; and Mister George Hasler. A cornet solo was rendered by Mr. Walter Ward, a duet was also rendered by the Misses Margaret Le Roy and Beatrice Houghton; a song, entitled "Buy a broom," was given by the Misses . Daisy Boughey, Alice Gough and Emily Higham. Action-songs, entitled " HoN.v'd You like to be a baby girl?" and " The- singlng lesson," were rendered by the children. A dia- logue, "The contest of flowers," was also given, Miss Lily Hibbert taking the part of Fairy.

div.head: Mayor Assists the Poor.
div.p: Mayor Assists the Poor.

At the distribution ,of the "Shaw Thewlis" Vharity on the anniversary of the deatli of that Alderman on Tuesday, it was found there were Iflare applicants for relief than the funds of A:l2 9s. id. would permit relieving. The Mayor, br, Joseph, rather than allow the old people to 1)8 disappointed, undertook to pay the, extra looney required. The fund was started under the will of the late Alderman Shaw Thewlis, who left £513 9s. 7d. of- Consolidated Stock,

, bearing interest at the rate of 21 per cent. per ' annum. The distribution took place at the . Charity Investigation *Society Rooms, and the total interest received this year was ,tl2 17s. lid., but expenses swallowed up Bs. 10d.

div.head: St. John's Presbyterian Guild.
div.p: St. John's Presbyterian Guild.

The members met on Monday evening, Mr. R. lqungall presiding. A paper was read on " Calamities; why God permits them" by Mr. eca• The speaker pointed out bow this great Problem had exercised the minds of men throughout all the ages, and more especially in ;Ps present time of questioning and inquiry. nere were many kinds of calamities. Public Pinion usually associated the word with a death-roll through some disaster at sea, 'll the mines, on the railways; but, in the aPeaker's opinion, the loss of a single soul was a ealemity. Many calamities could be directly traced to human defects, ignorance, inexperi- ence or folly, and others were attributed to a visitation of God. These were hard to under- stand, but one thing was certain, that all the inquiries into these matters resulted in a great inaPetus to human progress, knowledge and 4ehiovement.

div.head: Tribute to the Insurance Ad.
div.p: Tribute to the Insurance Ad.

At a well-attended meeting of the Wairington liraricli of the National Union of Life Assurance Agents on Friday, under the presidency of Mr. P.d‘vard -Plinston, Royal Liver Society, Mr. Edwin Plinston, Victoria Legal, was presented with a Swan fountain pen for services rendered for many years past. The Chairman gave a brief outline of the various changes made dur- ing the past 40 years for the betterment of 4gents generally. Referring to the latest addi- tion to the agent's lot, namely, State Insurance; its said there were certainly differences of opin- ion as to the wisdom or otherwise of this Act, but, after a practical twelve ohs' working, he sincerely believed it"was a blessing for the masses of the country, although a burden and loss to tlie agents at the nominaL payment received 'from their offices. Bro. J. Crusham made the Presentation, and, in doing so, congratulated Mr. Plinston upon his new appointment. Messrs. nird (secretary), Sixsmith and Heywood bore • -testimony to Mr. Plinston's past services. Mr. Plinston,• in reply, thanked them sincerely fer The Present, and as it would be daily in use in the discharge of his duties, it would remind him of the happy years spent with others in endeav-• "ring to do something to better the lot of his fellow-agents.
liITCREN RANGES, FIRE GRATES, TlLES.—Large atoek, reasonable .prices.--J. S. GARLAND, Iron- Inonger, 51 to 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.
Scarlet Fever Cases.
Scarlet fever is still prevalent in WarrtnS—n, and seven new cases were reported last week, while 44 were in hospital.
New Territorial Adjutant.
Lieut. K. W. Izod has taken over the duties of adjutant of the 4th Battalion South Lanca- shire Regiment, the local Territorial corps.
Stockton heath Liberals.
Mr. P. M. Oliver and Mr. T. H. Garside are to address a Liberal mass meeting in the Hall Cafe, Stockton Heath, on Thursday. Councillor H. Roberts is to preside.

div.head: 'Warrington Market.
div.p: 'Warrington Market.

The prices on Wednesday were: Wheat, 4s. 2d. to 4s. 41d. per 701 b.; oats, 2s. 6d. to 2s. Bd. per 451 b.; straw oats, 275. 6d. per ton; straw wheat, 275. 6d. per ton; XX sour, 235. 3d. per 2401 b.; bran, lid. per 201 b.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A.
An open temperance meeting is to be held to-morrow in connection with temperance Sun- day. The meeting starts at 2.45. Mrs. Dodds will preside, and Mr. G. Boyle will be the speaker.

div.head: Mavor-eleet as Fireman.
div.p: Mavor-eleet as Fireman.

Members of the Warrington Fire Brigade gave a demonstration with the new motor engine on -Wednesday afternoon before a deputation from the Sale Council on the river hear the Electricity Works. Several councillors, inehld- ing the Mayor-elect, rade on the engine to the scene.

div.head: Victim of the Line.
div.p: Victim of the Line.

, Yesterday Thomas'llannah (43), labourer, n, Kerfoot-street; employed by Messrs. Pearson and Knowles at Dallam Forge, had occasion to cross the L. and N.-W. line to the siding in Dallam-lane. He slipped in front of an engine, which ran over both his legs, and inflicted severe injuries. Hannah was conveyed to the Infirmary, where he died last evening.

div.head: Pen Wesleyan Band of Hope.
div.p: Pen Wesleyan Band of Hope.

A public mee,ting and Band of Hope rally was held in the Wesleyan Sunday Schools, .Penketh, when Mr. T. D. Leslie, of Wigan, the represen- tative of the -United Kingdom Alliance, was the deputation. Mr. J. G. W,ithinshaw presided. Forty temperance pledges were signed, and Mrs. Dodds presented the members with souvenir cards, in memory .of the jubilee year of the Lancashire, Cheshire and North Derbyshire Band of Hope Union. Mr. Leslie preached in the Wesleyan Church on Sunday.

div.head: Ministers' Need of Humour.
div.p: Ministers' Need of Humour.

The Rev. G. T. Lovat, of Aintree, delivered a lecture on: Thursday night, at the Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church, on Scotch wit and humour, and his many stories were responsible for much merriment. Mr. J. T. Ambler pre- sided, in the a:bsence of Mr. C. E. Parker. Mr. Lovat remarked that it had been said that a sense of hiimour was a very necessary trait for 'everybody, and, further, that it was a necessary trait, most of all, to ministers, who must have a sense of humour to carry them through what were sometimes very difficult and trying circum- stances. "A little nonsense now and again," said the speaker, "is relished by the wisest men."

div.head: Warrington Philomathic Society.
div.p: Warrington Philomathic Society.

Mr. Charles Madeley, on Wednesday evening, at the Old Academy, gave an instructive lec- ture on "Warrington Bridge," to the members and friends. The lecture, which was illus- trated with an interesting series of lantern slides, dealt with the history. and the structure of the various bridges which from time tci time have spanned the Mersey. In his characteristic style, Mr. Madeley recalled many delightful features of Old Warrington, hardly credible to present-day inhabitants, and brought home to the audience something of the romantic past of the ,town.. On the proposition of Alderman Bennett, who supplemented the lecture with an amusing account of his own experiences in con- nection with the building of the new bridge, a vote of thanks was accorded Mr. Madeley. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. Walsh, president of the society, and Mr. Hedley H. Taylor oper- ated the lantern.

div.head: Photographers Indulge in Whist.
div.p: Photographers Indulge in Whist.

The weekly Meeting of the Warrington Photo- graphic Society on Tuesday was devoted to the exhibition .of the box lantern slides selected by the judges for the Lancashire and Cheshire Photographic Union. Three of those present had the .satisfaction of 'seeing their own work thrown on the screen, namely; Mr. E. Wilkes, Mr. W. B. Jackson and Mr. C. Wilcockson. The judges' criticisms were read by the Treasurer. The most successful whist drive and dance in the spciety's history was held at the Winmar- leigh Cafe on Thursday. Over 80 sat down to supper in the interval between whist and danc- ing. The prizes for play :were chiefly framed photographs by the .society's members or lec- turers, the first gentleman's prize being a beau- tiful picture of cactus dahlias by Mr. E. Sey- mour, of London; and won by Mr. Poster. The scoring cards were also photographic, being printed on picture post-cards, views taken by the three Vollendammers last year, during the Holland Convention week.

div.head: Baptist Missionary Week.
div.p: Baptist Missionary Week.

The Baptist denomination in Warrington have been celebrating the missionary week during the past few .days. The missionary deputation was the Rev: A. T. Roberts, of Monghyr, Special services were held on Sunday in all the Baptist Churches, Mr. Roberts addressing ser- vices at Hill Cliffe, Golbornerstreet, and Latch- ford. The Rev., G. Curtis, the Rev. 11. Ogden, and the Rev. J. S. Chedburn also preached special sermons. 'During the week the Mission- ary has addressed meetings at Little Leigh, Acton Bridge, and Widnes, and a widely pre- vailinc, interest has been stimulated. On Thursday, at Golborne-street, a joint missionary tea and meeting was held. Tea was served by Golborne-street, Latchford and Hill Cliffe ladies. Over the tea tables a missionary con- ference was held, at which the Missionary sug- gested new ways and means of raising mission- ary funds. The evening meeting was presided over by the Rev. 11. Ogden, who delivered a brief and suitable address. This was followed by the Missionary with a talk upon the outcasts of India. The address revealed the new and fruitful sources that were open to Baptist enter- prise. Last night the Missionary addressed a meeting at Lymm, which closed a series of meetings regarded by all as amongst the best in this district.

div.head: Mr. E. Wynne Jones as Pastor.
div.p: Mr. E. Wynne Jones as Pastor.

The recognition of Mr. E. Wynne Jones as pastor of Zarlestown Baptist Church was made the occasion of an interesting service last week- end. The Rev. Dr. J. T. Marshall, ex-President of the Baptist Union, was the special preacher, and amongst others present were the Revs. H. Ogden, Warrington, and E. E. Lovell, Lymm; and Messrs. A. Price and England, Warrington. At the public meeting ,the Rev. H. Ogdert and others paid a high tribute to the capabilities of Mr. E. Wynne Jones for the office the was caned to fill. Mr. E. Wynne Jones, who was received with applause, said he (lid not know how to find words to thank his friends for all the kind things said to him and about him. It had been a trying day to him. As he sat there that after- noon and listened to those thrilling words dir- ected to .himself, he felt that the experience would abide with him for many years to come. Man would be Past redemption who could not find inspiration and encouragement in what had been said. The first and most important duty of the Christian Church and ministry was to sate men. That was the work to which he was called. The Parliament was for legislation, the college for culture, the school for science, the market for business, but the Church was for salvation. He believed that the Church was going to be saved by means which God had placed at their disposal, and these means were going to be wielded by 'human hands.

Births and Deaths.
_ The births in Warrington last week num- bered 35, giving a rate of 24.6. The deaths totalled 28, giving a rate of 19.6.
Tea Tango.

Tea Tango is said to be the latest and best methods of entertainment, and Warringtonians can partake of all its joys at the Parr Hall on Monday afternoon. Tango is to be danced by clever professionals.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY,NOVEMBER 8, 1918.

div.head: To Prevent Cruelty to Children.
div.p: To Prevent Cruelty to Children.

The annual meeting of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children will be held in the Town Hall oin Friday, at 3.30 p.m. Some interesting addresses on the great work the society is performing will be de- livered.

div.head: Electro-Medical Specialist.
div.p: Electro-Medical Specialist.

Prof. Ray, the principal of the Electro- Medical Institute, Kersal, Manchester, is to ad- dress meetings in the Schoolroom, Friars' Green, to-day, to-morrow and Monday. He gives many useful hints how to preserve health and vigour, and his methods are said to bring much relief to sufferers from rheumatic com- plaints.

div.head: Musical Treat.
div.p: A Musical Treat.

The Warrington- Musical Society give their first subscription concert on Wednesday in the Parr Hall. The chief item is Fletcher 's The Deacon's Masterpiece," which in itself. ought to attract a large audience. There is also a first- class miscellaneous programme. The artistes are Miss Eva Vioh, soprano, and Mr. Norman Allin, bass, while Mr. P. 11. Crossley will con- duct a talented chorus and orchestra of 250 vocalists and instrumentalists.

div.head: Faith and Moral Practices.
div.p: Faith and Moral Practices.

"Creed and character" was the subject of an address delivered last evening, under the aus- pices of the Church Society, in the Patten Hall, by the Rev. E: R. Tarbuck, vicar of St. George's, Altrincham,. and formerly of St. Paul's, War- rington. Canon Willis presided. The Rev. E. R. Tarbuck said that creed and character acted and reacted upon each other. Tempt a Church- man to steal and he would rapidly think "I must not. break the eighth commandment, be- cause I believe in God." A growth in faith in- clined one 'to increased efforts in moral practices, and as success attended these efforts one's faith was the stronger 'and better.

Penketh Footpath Dispute. The Penketh right-of-way question was the chief topic discussed at the monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural District Council on Wednesday. Councillor G. Mather presided.— Councillor Garnett said the previous Wednes- day members of the Council went into the matter thoroughly. They had before them four or five' witnesses from 59 to 85 ears of age, who stated that they, their parents, and chil- dren had had uninterrupted use of the foot path. He thought the Council were quite con- vinced that there was a lot in what they said, but as there were so few members of the Council present it was not thought advisable to take any drastic step. They did, however, pass the resolution, which he would propoie to the Coun- cil: "That in view of the evidence placed before the committee, this Council inhtruct the Surveyor to remove the obstacles at Fiddlers' Ferry, and Await developments." Personally, he would have preferred for the parish of Pen- keth to call a parish meeting, and so show that they were or were not prepared for an increase of one penny or twopence on the rates in the event of litigation. —lt was decided, after discussion, that the matter be not pro- ceeded with until the parish had had an oppor- tunity of calling.a parish meeting to discuss the matter.

The Late Mr. William AVright. • We regret to announce the death of Mr. Wil- liam Wright, who passed away at his home, Mayfield-road, on October 30th; at the age el 76. Mr. Wright has lived in comparative re- tirement for some years, but was in earlier life a well-known figure in Warrington. He belonged to an old local family, and until the age of forty served the firm of Messrs. Bolton, at the Orford-lane Glass Works. His special department was that of pattern making for the glass makers, but he served the firm in other and more intimate and important ways. He afterwards entered the grocery bUsinefis in Win- wick-street, and continued there until about twenty years ago, when he took up duties as an agent of the Refuge Insurance Society, retiring when failing strength made retirement impera- tive. He was through life a useful member of the Independent Methodist -Church at Friars' Green, and held, we believe, a life-long connec- tion with it. For more than fifty years he was a minister of the denomination and preached with much acceptance not only in local churches but throughout the- Connexion. Close reading and thinking gave form to his sermons, and made them welcome to thoughtful hearers espe- cially to those who enjoyed doctrinal discus- sion. He also served the Connexion in its business sessions, and at different periods held the posts of Connexional treasurer and secre- tary of the Ministers' Aid Fund. In politics he was an ardent Liberal, and through life gave steady adherence to the Liberal cause.

The funeral took place on Monday, at the Warrington: Cemetery, and was conducted in an impressive manner by Mr. R. Henshall. The relatives who were present were: Messrs. Walter, Alfred, Edward, Thomas, Herbert and Stanley Wright (sons), Mr. Harry Wright, Run- corn (nephew), and Mr. W. Hackett (son-in- law). There were also present Mr. William Mercer, Lymm ; Mr. Silas Cook, Mr. James Evans, Mr. James Shaw, Mr. James Harding, Mr. James Hudson, Mr. A. Jolley, Mr. R. Hazle- dine, Mr. Wm. Mounfield, Mr. Peter Lawton, Mr. John Hudson,' Mr. Rd. Hewitt, Mr. James Birch, Mr. Ben Warburton, Mr. George Leah, Mr. Wm. Harbin, Mr. Thos. Hamblett, Mr. Geo. Blease, and Mr. A. Mounfield, who had charge of the funeral, arrangements.—Many handsome floral tributes Were forwarded. including one from his widow and family, from grandchildren in London and Dover, from members of the Friars' Green and Grappenhall Independent Methodist Churches, and personal friends.

div.head: WYCLIFFE HEADMASTER.
div.p: WYCLIFFE HEADMASTER.
The Reward of Quarter of a Centurg
of Faithful Service.
MR. JEFFERY APPOINTED.

The. School Management Committee of the Education' Committee on Thursday confirmed the unanimous appointment by the managers of Wyeliffe Council Schools, of Mr. Sydney Walter Jeffery, 104, Manchester-road, as head- master, in succession to Mr. Alfred Corney, re- signed. The appointment will give universal satisfac- tion. Mr. Jeffery, who is the son of the late Mr. William Jeffery, manager for many years for Messrs. Rylands Bros., served his appren- ticeship at Wycliffe School under the late Mr. Thomas Gibson and Mr. Corney. He proceeded to the Borough-road College, London, where he studied during 1887 and 1888, and. having. been appointed- assistant to Mr. Corney at Wycliffe, took .0 p the duties at the beginning of 1889. After having held that position for a quarter of a century with all-round satisfaction, he now succeeds to the headship ,of the school in which he has spent the whole of his life, with the ex- ception of the two years he was "going through college."

His appointment comes as a fitting reward for long and sustained service; to become master of his old 'school will doubtless be suffi- cient personal recompense for his having had to wait .so Icing for promotion. We are informed that the survivors, of the old committee from Whom Mr. Jeffery received his first appointment regard the promotion as a just reward to a most deserving and efficient teacher, who, in the days of "the intolerable stram " (vide Mr. Balfour) rendered yeoman service on behplf of the school.

ELIMINATION OF THE HALF-TIMER. "I have seen a great many changes in the school," said Mr. Jeffery to "The Examiner" representative, who was one of the first to con- gratulate him Upon his good fprtune. "We have had as 'many as eighty half-timers in Wycliffe School, and now you can scarcely find a half-timer in the whole town.
"It is not because hall-iimera are not wanted, but it is so difficult for children to become half- timers. Since the Education Authority came

div.head: OFFICIAL PRAISE FOR NIGHT SCHOOL
div.p: OFFICIAL PRAISE FOR NIGHT SCHOOL
WORK.

Mr. Jeffery hao been an evening scliool teacher for 21 years, and has been in caarge of the even- ing commercial classes since the Education Authority came into being in .1902. That year the Commercial Institute contained 180 pupils; it now contains 400. The character of the in- struction has advanced; commercial law and bookkeeping in all its stages are taught, and pupils are prepared for the examinations of the Society of Arts. Last year the Commercial In- stitute had a success in such an out-of-the-way .subject as accounting and banking. Warrington now ranks high for the quality of its Continuation Schools, and Mr. Jeffery has certainly done much to bring about that result. Our evening schools fall into two grades. In the upper come the Technical Schools and the Commercial Institute, Arpley-street, and in the lower five branch schools. At the Arpley-street School, where the commercial classes are con- centrated, Mr. Jeffery has laboured so success- fully as to call forth the somewhat unusual praise of Government Inspectors in an offi.cial report.

In June, 1910, the Board of Education issued a general report by H.M. Inspectors on Tech- nical Schools and Evening Schools in Warring- ton. In that report, referring to Mr. Jeffery, the head teacher Of the Commercial Institute, the docurment states that his "unflagging efforts" deserve "special recognition." "His organisation and administration are both very good," continue the Inspectors, "while his un- failing tact has had a most beneficial influent() on the attendance and work of the school."

The ability to induce evening scholars to at- tend regularly and punctually is the best attri- bute of an evening school teacher. On these points the Inspectors reported : " The best and most regular home work is done by commercial students, the percentage rising as high as 75 at the Commercial Insti- tute, and even higher in certain classes there." "As regards regularity and punctuality of at- tendance, the better qualified and more ad- vanced classes again show marked superiority. Out of six possible hours per week, the best students attend for five hours or more on the average, the best figures being obtained at the Commercial Institute, with an all-round aver- age of five hours."

div.head: WORK FOR HIS PROFESSION.
div.p: WORK FOR HIS PROFESSION.

Mr. Jeffery has accomplished much for the members of the profession to which he.belongs. Tie founded the Warrington Class Teachers' Associatidn, of which he served as hon. secre- tary for five years. On his resigning this post in February, 1908, the Association presented him on March 6th with a mahogany writing bureau, inlaid with satin wood, but the present was not nearly .so valuable as the many nice things that were said uf Mr. Jeffery on the occasion of the presentation. Mr. J. Morgan, who presided, referred to Mr. Jeffery's many good qualities and title to their respect, but said teachers thought most about him for the way in which he had shown his courage in the cause of class teachers. The Council of the Lancashire Federation of Class Teachers, to which the local assocation is affiliated, wrote expressing regret at the loss the resignation would be to the Association, the founding of which and its prosperity had proved his organ- ising ability and his worth. The inscription on the bureau recorded the fact that it was given "in recognition of his services as founder and secretary, 6th March, 1908." The Associa- tion has now nearly 200 members. Mr. Jeffery has been an active member of the N.U.T., and has been continuously on the com- mittee sinee he came out of college. He has been Secretary of the local branch for two (Continued in rext co7umn.)

div.head: ON THE SUNINHT OF THE WETTERHORN.
div.p: ON THE SUNINHT OF THE WETTERHORN.

div.head: Colonel Eales and his son, Monty, and two guides. Eiger and Manch Mountains in
div.p: Colonel Eales and his son, Monty, and two guides. Eiger and Manch Mountains in

Mrs. Eales, . second daughter of the late` Mr. John Cr9slield, sends the iollpwing account of a climb up one of the Oberland giants, done by ' her eleven-year-old son, Monty. The boy, though born in India, belongs to Warrington stock through his mother, whilst his father- is Lieutenant-Colonel Eales, late of the Indian Army. The party consisted of Colonel Eales, Monty, his friend, Alec Bromley-Kemp, aged 13, their tutor, Mr. Mulhollana, and two Swiss guides. They started from Gwidelwald one glorious afternoon last August, made their way up fewest paths through the fragrant pines, and then up steeper tracks over, the shale and rubble at the mountain's base, and slept that night at the Gleckstein Hut, 7,800 feet up on the side of the Wetterhorn. . At one a.m. they were aroused, and dressed . by candlelight, with aching fingers, for the at- , mosphere goes very cold at night, even in summer at such an altitude. Hot coffee and rolls revived them somewhat, however, and at , two a.m. they left the sheltering hut and started forth over the' snow, by the aid of lanterns. Thence it was one long Odd over the hard and steep snow slopes till they reached the summit of the Wetterhorn, 12,150 feet, at 6.15 a.m. The cold was intense, as a sunrise 'wind always blows at that hour off the snow, their enjoyment of the superb view was tempered by the aching of toes and finger-nails. Alec 'had mountain sickness 500 feet from. the summit, and had to remain there, wrapped in
an extra coat, and walking rapidly up and down on a little snow plateau. An Italian lady, who just then arrived with her two 'guides, kindly
the dis Lance,

gave, him medicine from her pocket case, which matte him quite well a.gain, and able to enjoy the romping descent down the vast snow-slopes, when, the others returned. The rising sun soon changed this, however. It quickly softened the snow, which was deeper for. the time of year than it had been for many years, and the guides shook their heads and urged them not to linger, as the softened snow might lead to avalanches. The descent soon became very fatiguing, as the party would sink to the knees in the soft snow and their alpenstocks and the axes often got embedded likewise. The steep snow couloir took two hours to descend, and Mrs. Eales, at the hotel, watched their progress through a tele- scope. They reached the Gleckstein Hut at 11 amt., had lunch and rested, and then began the last descent through the shale and forests, reaching Gwidelwald at four.p.m. in a state of extr9me heat, which was a contrast to the ach- ing cold of a few hours before. The boys looked quite fresh and well, as will be seen in the photograph. The love of snow and ice, and the endurance of such discomforts as frozen hands (in spite of woollen gloves), cold feet, and a parched mouth, when climbing, are good 'things for a boy. But he must have a strong heart., and a strong enough physique not to be overdone by the long strain.

div.head: "MERELY PLAYERS."
div.p: "MERELY PLAYERS."
Lovers of the Bard of Avon Found
Shakespearean Society.
LOCAL COMMEMORATION IN 1914.

"All the world's a stage, and all the men and women merely players." Lovers of Shakespeare in Warrington are to have a stage, and are to become players in the best sense. At a meeting held on Thursday evening, under the chair- manship of Mr. 116 Garnett, it was decided to fOhnd, a Shakespearean Society, and a com- memoration will probably take place. in 1914. Dr. LAW said that up to the present they in Warrington had been unorganised, but the feeling now was that they should form a definite society, properly organised. The 'reason for this was the financial responsibility of the productions. Each year they had spent something like £2OO in their efforts to cora- mehlorate Shakespeare. Fortunately they had got through without a deficit, but it was rather a risky undertaking. If there had been a deficit probably the committee would have had to make the amount up. It was felt that the responsi- bilities should be distributed amongst all those who were interested in the commemoration plays. The following were amongst the sug- gestions 'which Dr. Law then made: "That all those ladies and gentlemen who have been asso- ciated in previous commemoration performances should be invited to attend a meeting, the pur- pose of which is to form a Dramatic Society, to be called 'The Warrington Amateur Shakes- peare Players'; the society to be managed by a committee appointed by the members; each member to pay a subscription of 65., which will carry certain privileges, amongst which will be the obtaining of two reserved seats for the first night of the productions; the society to be man- aged in accordance with the rules of the Green Room Club, Liverpool, and the 'Martin Harvey' Club, Manchester.; that two plays be presented, viz., 'Merry Wives of Windsor' and 'Much Ado About Nothing,' and that each play be presented an equal number of times three' or two, as the committee think advisable; that 200 persons, not members of the society, be secured, each of -whom will guarantee the tak- ing of £1 worth of tickets; guarantors to have the privilege of marking ..£ll worth of reserved seats in any part of the house before the plan was open to the public; no announcement to be made that the performances are, in aid of charity."

div.head: Probable Cost.
div.p: Probable Cost.

The probable available revenue would be £250 if 50 persons joined the society at Cs. each, and 200 £1 guarantors were secured, and if the general public supported the movement to the slight extent of £35. Production expenses would" amount to £165.

r. GARNETT proposed, and Mr. DAINTITR seconded that a society be formed on these lines, and this was agreed to unanimously. The following were elected a Provisional Committee: Dr. Law, Messrs. R. Garnett, 0. Lofthouse, W. Ashton, A. C. Hodgson, H. M. Ashton, H. 0. Wheeler, L. R. Rowson and E. Bradshaw.

div.head: INHERITED LOVE OF CLIMBING.
div.p: INHERITED LOVE OF CLIMBING.

Master Eales appears to have inherited a love of climbing mountains from his grandfather, the late Mr. John Crosileld, which he shares with his Uncles, Mr. Arthur 11. Crosfleld and Captain George Crosfield.

div.head: WELL-KNOWN LADY'S DEATH.
div.p: WELL-KNOWN LADY'S DEATH.
Imposing Interment at Doncaster.

One who was highly esteemed in the town and especially amongst the parishioners of St. Bar- nabas' Church passed away on Saturday morn- ing in the person of Mrs. Jane Elizabeth Hollingworth, mother of the Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth, vicar of St. Barnabas'. Failing health confined Mrs. Hollingworth to her bed for six months, but the end came somewhat suddenly. The Rev. and Mrs. Hollingworth attended the funeral at, Doncaster Cemetery on Wednesday. Prior to departure from Warrington a service was conducted in St. Barnabas' Church by the Revs. Glendenning and Coupe, who also offi- ciated at the graveside. Wreaths were sent by Mr. and Mrs. Fry, Annie and Ethel Fry, Mrs. Connelly,. Mrs. Jones, Misses Whitehouse, "Working Party," Mr. Glendenning, Miss Simp, son, St. Barnabas' Social Club, Church Officers, Mr. and Mrs. Skinner, "Kitty," "The Vigar- age," Misses Pickering, Mrl and Mrs. Iddon, Mr. and Mrs. Booth and family, Mr. and Mrs. Evans and family, Mrs. Greenhalgh, and the grandchildren. The coffin was of oak, with plain brass mounts. On the top was a brass cross, the full length of the coffin, and at the foot was the inscription: "Of your charity, pray for the repose of the soul of Jane Elizabeth Holling- worth. Died Novembei Ist, 1913; 'aged 76
years."
The funeral arrangements were carried out by Mr. W. Stephens, Green-street, Warrington.

div.head: RAPHAEL TUCK'S CHRISTMAS CARDS.
div.p: RAPHAEL TUCK'S CHRISTMAS CARDS.

Messrs. Raphael Tuck and Sons have sent out once again a wonderful selection of Christmas cards, New Year cards, calendars, toy books, and games. Christmas would scarcely be Christ- mas without Raphael Tuck, the firm that has laid itself out specially to advance With the times in its particular line, and to see that the ever-increasing demands of an exacting public are met to the full. Their Christmas cards, from the " Royal " series, made for kings and queens, to the humblest post-card or auto-card, are things of beauty and command our admira- tion, irrespective of cost. The calendars are exceedingly artistic and well calculated to re- tain their attractiveness for the whole of the twelve months they are destined to be in posi- tion. Messrs: Tuck's children's books and games are, like their other produotions, of tho very best—in fact, Father Tuck's Annual is, as it has long been, a prince among toy-books. Its illustrations are such as delight the young heart and the reading matter is selected with the best of judgment. The stationer? shops will soon be showing us how near Christmas is, -and foremost in the demonstration will be the sea- sonable wares of this enterprising and racist suc- cessful of firms.

Messrs. Raphael Tuck and Sons, whose address is Raphael House, Moorfields City, London, will send an illustrated catalogue of their publica- tions, free on application, to any applicant. The catalogue is a valuable and attractive book, containing artistic reproductions from the many artistic works issued.
CROSFIELD'S WORKPEOPLE
Scheme to ROCOglalBo the Added Value
of Long Service.
3/- A WEEK AFTER SIX YEARS.

The directors of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Ltd., have formulated a scheme by which they propose to recognise in is systematic man- ner the added value of a 1111814'& labour, due to long service and experience gained in that t service. Captain Crosfield recently explained :the scheme to the whole of the werkpeople, who, so far as could be seen, were pleased with the proposal. Briefly, the scheme holds that 'a man, however, skilful, reliable, or energetic he may be. is necessarily not so valuable when first engaged as when he has become accustomed to his-. duties and the requirements of the firm. It is calculated that his value grows year by year, until he has been six years in the employ of the firm, and! that by the end of that perid he will be in al position to assert himself and pass- into a higher grade if he has the necessary qmalifi- cations for such promotion. It is these first six years wikb which this scheme is concernedi. The starting point is 21 years of age:. In future, a maw who has been in the continuoua service of the firm for two years from the: age stated is Vol; liave Is. a week long servier pay added to hfiswages; after four years, 2s. a week; and after sizyears 3s. a week.
The scherne,, which is also to apply to Goseage. and Sons, Widnes, will come into operation at the New Year.

div.head: MINIMUM WANTED.
div.p: MINIMUM WANTED.
Messrs. Crosfteld's Employes Not Satisfied,with Firm's Offer.
DEMANDS- TO BE PRESSED.

BY. A. WORKER. As 1 indicated in my notes in the last issue of "The Examiner," there is a considerable danger of trouble at Messrs... Crosfield's Works, which the new scheme of s gitring, advances to the men , with long service is•nat likely to remove. In fact, the proposal.was,u.nder consideration at a meeting of the men on, Sunday, and the views then expressed showed that the men were not at all satisfied with the scheme mooted by the employers. One worker stated that the firm's proposal would be provocative of more unrest than ever. "Some of us," he. explained,. " work alongside men who have beemlonger in the service of the firm than we have been, and these men will be 2s. or 3s. a week. better paid than we will be, while we have the Warder and more responsible work to perform. This will: but lead to jealousy and unrest. What' we want, first of all, is a minimum wage which will allow us to subsist." The applause whichlollowed the remark showed that his explanation had struck- a sympathetic chord amongst his-fellow-workers. To Press the Demand..

The discussion was, a. prolonged one, and finally a resolution was carried unanimously that the union be instructed to press forward the demand for a minimum wage and shorter hours, leaving the other scheme to the firm to deal with as they think fit. The meeting indi- cated clearly that the men were determined to have a minimum wage before any scheme such as has been suggested by the employers. "The Crosfield scheme,:' said a prominent trade unionist, "is based upon that adopted at the works of Messrs.. Brunner, Mond and Co., who now have the contralTing interest in Cros- field's at Northwioh. It has never given satisfaction there, and is never likely to do so here. Since it was introduced at the Northwich works there has been almost con- tinuous unrest. Men, who are experts at their work have found themselires drawing less wages than men who are their.inferiors, but who have had the advantage of being longer on the job. Causes Unrest.

"Naturally when, a worker ends himself in that position he is restive, and the amount of unrest at Northwich to-day is.purely due to the system of granting favours for lbnger service. It is not right that a man should be penalised because he has been a shorter: tiiine in the works, and often he is the better man.

"The employers evidently have adopted this course as a method; to stop the ever-increasing agitation for a living wage and for shorter hours, but it is not likely to have that effect. The resolution on Sunday indicates plainly how the men feel about the nimbler.

"We shall continue to press the demands for a minimum wage and the men are determined to have it. After that is obtained the firm can pension old employes, if they like, but a mini- Ilium living wage must, first of all, be obtained. The palliative suggested does not meet with approval, and instead; of tending to allay the existing unrest it is caculated to increase it:"

div.head: RYLANDS!- MEN'S DEMANDS. Shorter Hours Are Requested.
div.p: RYLANDS!- MEN'S DEMANDS. Shorter Hours Are Requested.

As I indicated in last week's issue, the National Union of Gas Workers and General Labourers, now a minimum wage of 225. per week of 53 hours has been secured at Messrs. Pearson and KRowles and the Monks, Hall Works, are endeavouring to secure similar con- ditions for other iron, works labourers in War- rington.

The union, acting on behalf of the employes, have requested Messrs. Rylands' to put their labourers coa the same terms as the other firms have conceded, namely, a minimum wage of 225. per week, a working-week of 53 hours, and on' Ist May next to bring their employes under the scale of the Manchester and District Engineer- ing Trades Employers' Federation, which pro- vides for the payment of overtime, and which will regulate any future alterations in the wages.

Awaiting the Result. The negotiations have reached a particularly interesting stage as I. write, but it is thought that Messrs. Itylands, who have hitherto acted reasonably in the matter of requests from their employes, will finally come into line with the rest of the employes in the town. _ _

The question- Messrs. Rylande works is riot so much one of wages as of hours of labour. The wages paid average about 21s. to 225. per week. but the hours are 58 per week. The other em- ployers, meAtioned above, have conceded a 53-hour week, and the union are anxious to have that made the standard rate for the whole of the Warrington area. Thus in the application made on behalf of the men special stress is laid on the hours question. _

Anyone. who knows the work undertaken by labourers in iron works will agree that 58 hours per week are unnecessarily long, and 53 hours are quite long enough. Whether the firm view;, it in this light or not, I cannot say, but, at all events, the men are determined to be put on the same footing as other similar workers in War- rington. The reply of the firm is being anxiously awaited.

div.head: GRAPPEN HALL.
div.p: GRAPPEN HALL.

GLEANINGS FROM GItAPPENIIALL. A real, live Mayor is to visit us. He is coming to the opening of the new chapel. To-day will be a memorable day with us. Mrs. John Croslield is to perform the cere- mony. She always does that in .a mot graceful manner.

The New Church.—Mrs. John Crosfield is to open the new Independent Methodist Church and Sunday school at Grappenhall this after- noon, and will: thus forge another link in the history of the congregation. The church origin- ally started in a small room adjoining a shop in 1855, then-in.lBBo a'chapel was erected, but this became too small, hence the new edifice in Knutsford-road. The chapel will seat 250, and the assembly hall 220. The cost is esti- mated at £2,350. The,Mayor of Warrington, the Mayoress, Alderman James Evans, Alder- man rL Bvton and a large company are to attend the opening service at 3.30 p.m. A pub- lic meeting will be held in the evening, Mr. W. i3eesley to take the chair at 7 p.m. Special ser- vices are due to-morrow.

div.head: RIX TON.
div.p: RIX TON.

Whist Drive.—With a view to assisting the Endowment Fund in connection with St. Helen's Church, Hollinfare, a whist drive and dance was promoted at the Rixton .Mission Room on Saturday, and resulted in a very successful gathering. Dancing was enjoyed until late in the evening in the large Mission Room, the good floor lending itself admirably to this form of amusement. There were several close finishes in the whist drive, andeventually the following were returned as the winners :—Ladies: 1, Mrs. FlYe; 2, Mrs. J. Astall. Gentlemen 1, Mr. Hugh 131undell ; .2, Mr. J. Gibson. Mr. George Eaves acted as M.C: and Mr. I'ye was in charge of the whist. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 8, 1913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 8, 1913.

STOCKTON HEATH
TOWNSHIP TITTLE-TATTLZ.

"Bang-rip-rip-rap--bang!" Nothing else was needed on 'Wednesday To tell us that it was sth of November. . The youngsters sail/ carefully to it. Guy Fawkes was burnt in effigy. • Fireworks and bonfires were numerous:Ah, well! 'Lis good to be young. It was the teachers' rest this week. "And it was also the mothers' torture." At least one "Heathen" put it so.' - The nippers cared not;. they had the holiday. The Parochial Committee Meet on Tuesday. . Will the deputation be present to, ask That the meetings should be Opened with prayer? 'A doctor has complained about the Stag Swing Bridge being closed 19 niinutes. Of course, ships are more important than Are hurrying, busy human beings. Still the coniPlaint is justified. "Heathens" are said to be proper heathens So far as the Swing Bridges are concerned.' The language df held-up, pedestrians and vaninen • Is said to be very pronounced at times. There is always, something to upset us " Heathens." Sunday gambling has been rampant. It has proved .a pest to respectable folk. .The, gamblers, however, kept out of The way of the Stockton Heath police

And played " banker " on the Warrington side of The bank 'of the Ship Canal near the Bridge. Still their presence has been an annoyance. Warrington police have been constrained to take action. Their raid tin a Sunday produced a bag of seven.
Well-merited fines have since been imposed on six. More of that sort should put an end to the gambling pest.
Teachers' Rest.—The schools in Stockton Heath were closed this week for the .mid-term holiday, better known as the "teachers' rest."
The Vicar.—The Vicar. the Rev. J. Collins, has this week been spending a brief holiday in Yorkshire. and returned during the latter part of the week.

The £2,520 Loan Allowed.—At the fortnightly meeting of the District Council on Tugsday the Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board, sanctioning the borrowing of £2,520 for private street works in Stockton Heath.

An Invitation.—Councillor J. Whitley, as chairman of the Stockton Heath Parish Coun- cil, was invited to witness the official test of the new motor fire engine recently secured by the Warrington Corporation on Wednesday, but on account of another engagement was unable to be present.

Sunday Gambling N u iiance.—Respectable members of the community of Stockton Heath have, during past weeks, been much annoyed by the presence of "schools" of gamblers.. These kept to the Warrington side of the canal, but all they did could be seen from the Heath side, and 'their unsavoury language, was too plainly heard. Complaints have made to the Warring- ton Police, and they have taken prompt action. Plain-clothes officers were told ofl to break up the "schools" and their raid produced seven. The sequel .was heard at the iWarrington Borough Court on Thursday, when Harry Henton, 2, Shrewsbury-street; Edward Hard- man, 15, Oldham-street; William Brown, Barry- street; Thomas Barnes, ,19, Hewitt-street; Cyril Brooks, 1, Leonard-street, Stockton Heath; George Hughes, • • Wilderspool-causeway ; and James Whittaker, Church-street, were charged with gaming. All pleaded guilty, with the ex- ception of Barnes. The case against Barnes Was dismissed, as he was not playing, and the other defendants were • fined is 6d., including costs. DELAYED AT THE SWING BRIDGE. A Doctor's Protest to the Council. The delay occasioned by the Swing Bridge wa's the subject discussed at the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council at Dutton on Tuesday. A letter was read from Dr. Binns, of Stockton Heath, complaining of the unnecessary long waits at the Swing Bridge over the Ship Canal. He thought the matter should be taken up by the local authorities. On Friday he arrivted at the Stag Bridge at 4.58 p.m. and found the gate had been closed some minutes. It remained closed to traffic until 5.17 p.m. The Clerk: •That is 19 minutes. Councillor Mclntyre: It is beyond their limits. I think it is 13 minutes. The Clerk: I don't think the limit of time is stated.
Councillor Mclntyre: I understood there was a limit.

The Clerk: "IteaSonable-time," I think.. Councillor Hallows: We., in Stockton Heath, would be very glad if the District Council could do something for us. We have tried, but we cannot do anything. I propose that the Clerk be instructed to write to the Ship Canal Com- pany. calling their attention to .the delays occurring at the bridges. Councillor Pilling seconded. The resolution was carried. "THE CRY OF BURMA." Pageant Is Much Improved.

A repetition of the Missionary Pageant, "The Cry of Burma," was given in the Church Room, Stockton Heath, on Thursday evening, before a large audience, and the production bore traces of great improvement. - Prior to the commence- ment the Vicar, the Rev. J. Collins, made a few remarks with regard to the different tribes and customs of the people living in -Burma: Great credit -is clue -to tliki Vicar, Mrs. Wood, head of the pageant, Mrs. Worrall and Miss Fawcett, for the pains they have taken in the careful training of those who took part, and also to' the performers themselves, for their attendance week after week at the tedious part, of preparation. _ _ .

It may be mentioned that the parts of first and second English girls, two of the principal parts, taken by Miss L. Howes and Miss C. Hay- ward, were performed by their understudies, Miss P. Downes and Miss E. Shaw; and great credit was'due to them for the admirable way in which they performed the parts. The following is the cast for the pageant as it will be presented at the MissionarY Exhibition in Patten Hall on Ntmember 20th and 27th : Burmese: Mrs. Worrall, Misses Hallows, L. Barlow; A. Astall and M. Shepherd, and Messrs. E. S. Taylor, H. Battersby and J. H. Caldwell. Monk, Rev. E. W. Clarke; attendant boys, Eric Rose and Frank Caldwell; Karens, Misses Bag,uley, Astall, A. Thompson and G. Thatcher, and Messrs. A. Moores (Sgau), A. Thompson (Paku) and F. Caldwell (Bway); Tamils, Misses 0. Gleave, Thatcher and E. Gleave, and Messrs. B. Isherwood and T. Twiss, P. Downs, •E. Hughes, C. Coppock, I. Bailey, I. Smith, L. Rathbone, G. Williams, D. Taylor, B. Owen, D. Probyn, M. Barrington and E. Baguley • cross-bearer, D. Hallows; choir boys, F. Williams, J. -Hughes, E. Haslam and E. Rose; and pianist, Miss ,Fawcett.
No Swear Words!
"Old Journalist" writes :

The proximity of the bit of Stockton Heath tittle-tattle about the notice against swearing to the High Lgh rei)ort of the missionary address on Japan suggests another observation that seems to me to be worth repetition. Miss Legh, who had so much to say about the Japan- ese as a "smiling and agreeable people," would no doubt be ready to testify to any who ques- tioned her upon the point that their language is positively devoid of oaths' or expletives. Well may they sing in the musical • comedy "Happy Japan !" We in thts cohhtry are too ready to burst into Langauge (wittk a capital L), and the youths in our streets seem to think it manly. to follow' the example of their elders in this respect—and to .03 one better, if possible. Once, while. going round the wards of the Manchester Eye Hospital, I happened• upon a

group of patients thus interlarding their con- versation. Said one as I passed, "I wonder .wltat colour, the ,air .is in . this place?""" NAirejl," ventarM mildti...toliterpOse, "1 should think At's blue." I ,have often been, and there are generally some terrible 'swearers among the men 'under treatment there.

div.head: LATE MR. ROBERT AVYLLIE.
div.p: THE LATE MR. ROBERT AVYLLIE.
Wycliffe Preacher's Tribute to the Memory of a Worthy Man.

A touching tribute was paid to the memory of the late Mr. Robert Wyllie, who, as an- nOunced last week, passed away. suddenly at the Central. Station, 'Warrington, and was interred from his residence at Fillesmere-road, Stockton Heath, by the Rev. T. T. James, in the course of his sermon on "A prophet's climax," at Wycliffe Congregational Church on Sunday. The Rev. Mr. James said: To Robert Wylie the love of Christ :was no passion flaming for the moment, and dying into ashes in,the passing days; it was soniething that sustained him through the life-long tramp of this earth's com- mon tasks. In the unwearying service of the days of his physical strength, in the gifts of friendship and sympathy devoted to the highest service, in the constant endeavour to lead young men and women into the highest inheritance, he displayed that indomitable loyalty to Christ which: overcomes the enervating influence of the 1 sameness and routine of life. And th It)rYhic of him which is with us to- day, a memory which will be cherished .a ieem mor3 em v xeil and will abide through many days to cope, is that of one .who in daily contact with the common pursuits and. ordinary occupations of men, shed abroad' the sweetness and light of true Christian discipleship. To him was entrusted, and by the simplicity of his faith he was enabled to be true to die trust, the privilege of presenting to us a life of service and effort which the years did not ex- haust. "They shall walk and not faint !"

He worked 'tivo.or, three hours extra every nigbt "harvest- He worked from six o'clock in the morn- ing until eight, nine,-and ten o'clock at night. When he was discharged, after three 'weeks, he asked for his harvest money, but defendant told him he had not been there long enough.—His Honour: Fifteen,hours‘a day, fOr six weeks for Li a week seems miserably low pay, but I am not concerned with that in this Court.
