The Vicar's Tribute.
In the November number of the Lymm.Parish Magazine, the Rectoripeaks of Alr. W. S. Hodg- son in the following terms: "I find it difficult

to write in a short space here of such a man as William Stanley Hodgson. His life and career wore almost unique. The son of a dis- tinguished family, without any derogation to his personal character or true dignity, it was remarkable, both for himself and for the credit of I ymm, that in ten short years, as a crafts- man among us, he and his brother should have won the warm affection and high respect of all classes, which undoubtedly they have done. "We. shall. all -remember him „with, gratitude, not only as a very true son of the Church to which he ministered so faithfully, as a regular member of the choir and as honorary secretary of the Men's Society, but as a friend and com- panion in the wider circle of our village life, identifying himself with all its good yiorks and helping them forward to the utmost of his ability. We shall miss .his presence among us for a long time to come."

div.head: IRELAND MUST HAVE HOME RULE.
div.p: IRELAND MUST HAVE HOME RULE.
mm Steady In Support Of It For Forty Years.
CHAIRMAN'S REMINISCENCES.

The case for Ireland was put in a plain and concise manner to a Lymm audience on Tuesday night.which assembled in the Methodist School- room, Eagle Brow. The. principal speaker was Mr. M. Joyce, M.P.-for Limerick City, who dealt extensively with the question of Home Rule, and proved conclusively that the granting of such a measure was justified in many ways. Mr. G. L. Welford presided and. he was sup- ported by Mr. Joyce, 'Mr. J. S. Devine (Liver- pool), Mr. F. Milne (Bowdon), Mr. J. D. B. Smith and Mr, R. Barker (Lymm Liberal Association).
MR. WELFORD AND THE ENDING STRUGGLE.

The Chairman said he was not surprised that there was not a larger gathering, because most of them were convinced HOme Rulers and had quite made up their minds that the struggle Was nearing its end. .That being so, they did pot feel there was the' same urgency for attendance .at public meetings as 'there used to be. He re- membered the time in Lymin when to announce a public meeting on Home Rule meant a very large and enthusiastic meeting, but in that day they were fighting the question. They were try- ing to convince those who were open to be con- vinced; to persuade those who were not per- suaded that the granting of Home Rule to Ire- land was a wise and just step for Englishmen to take. (Hear, hear.) -

div.head: Convinced Home Rulers.
div.p: Convinced Home Rulers.

They accomplished a great deal in those days, in the way of instruction, persuasion and con- version, and, it was a long time since working men- in: Lymm and elsewhere became convinced Home Rulers. They were not there that night to try to persuade people to be Home Rulers, but to congratulate each other on the fact that the long struggle was nearing its conclusion—(ap- plause)—and that before twelve months had passed the Home Rule Bill would be on the Statute Book. (Hear, hear.) He 'hoped that this time next year they might be able to con- gratulate themselves on the first- meeting of the Parliament in Ireland having taken place. (Applause.) He remembered quite well taking part in a meeting on the Home Rule question before the year 1885. They had gathered together to dis- cuss the question befere Mr. Gladstone took up the matter. He recalled some very enthusiastic meetings they held in the little room in Eagle Brow which was now Mr. Priestner's chip shop. They held many meetings of an educational character, and discussed all kinds of political questions. Amongst the topics discussed in 18834-5 was the great question of Home Rule for Ireland. He remembered one important meet- ing, when the room was crowded to suffocation, and amongst those present was Mr. William Long, of Thelwill: He remembered M. Long's speech very well, and from it. he thought Mr. Long Would be a Home Ruler Of a most extreme character. They all remembered that after- wards he was a personal friend of Mr. Joseph Chamberlain; he was swayed and influenced by him, and was one of those who separated from the Liberal party in consequence of the mea- sure introduced by Mr. Gladstone. Many years afterwards it was their pleasure to welcome him back to the Liberal party, and he was sure he was with them. in spirit—although, through age and infirmity, he was no longer able to attend those meetings. (Applause.)

Many Battles Fought. The Home Rule question had been before the country for a long time and a great many battles had been fought in connection with it. Little by little, and step by -step, the whole country had been brought to see the wisdom and justice of granting to Ireland a Parliament in which she might conduct her own affairs. He sincerely hoped that the Government would not surrender one single jot of anything of importance to the rebel party—Sir Edward Carson and those asso- ciated with him in Ulster. Personally, he (the speaker) was afraid he would be disposed to show them short shrift if he had the 'dealing with them, • although he agreed that it would be a great advantage, in the interests of quiet and orderly government, if a measure acceptable to their Irish Home Rule friends could be assented to by all parties, and any danger of conflict or disorder removed altogether. He hoped; how- ever that the Government would go forward. with unflinching step and undaunted courage, not allowing any threat of rebellion to stay them for a moment, that at the very earliest opportunity the Home Rule Bill in all its essential features would be placed upon the Statute Book, and that next year they would witness the establishment of a Parliament in Ireland. (Applause.)

div.head: "WHEN MEN WERE SLAVES."
div.p: "WHEN MEN WERE SLAVES."

' Mr. Joyce said he remembered living at home in those old and bad days some 40 years ago, when men were slaves and nothing seemed to stand between them and their oppressors except the power and might of a great national organ- isation., Now, the working classes met man to Man, the best and bravest in, the land on a footing of 'perfect equality. (Applause.) The old ideas of slavery and slavishness had passed away.' After giving many historical details in regard to the struggles for Home Rule and the consistent demand of the Irish people, Mr. Joyce said that in spite of rebuffs they plodded on and were determined to do so until England saw the justice of their claim._
They would never give up the question until

England recognised the right of the Irish people to govern themselves in their own way, in their own land. They wanted a Parliament to deal witla their own race in their own land; a Par- lament that would sympathise with the people in their struggles for a higher state of social existence, and be able to pledge the credit of the country to help those who required helping to live a better, cleaner and nobler life. That was what they had asked for and what the great demo- .cratic, forces of. the 4 c,ountry ,had said -,lreland must get. (Applause.) If .the Liberal Govern- ment were beaten to-morrow, a Tory Govern- ment would be face to face with the Irish ques- tion, and would have to take it up—and the Tories themselves knew it. (Applause.) The Irish question was going to be settled in the very near future. He piesumed to know some- thing of what was going on in political circles in London, and he had it on the best authority from many members who were high in the coun- sels of the Tory party that Home Rule for Ire- land must become an accomplished fact. (Applause.)

div.head: No Persecution in Ireland.
div.p: No Persecution in Ireland.

Speaking in regard to the North, of Ireland, he said he never met a reasonable man or woman in Ireland, North or South, who thought for one moment that there would be anything in the nature of persecution of any people in Ire- land. He did not honestly think that Sir Ed- ward Carson believed, in his heart of hearts, that any' persecution of a religious sect in Ire- land by the Roman Catholic majority could take place. But those men, for reasons of their own, did it, *find the reasons were...as plain as a pike- staff. Those who had hitherto held the ascend: ancy were opposing Home Rule not because they dreaded legislation or administration at the hands of an Irish Government, but because they dreaded the time when the people in the North of Ireland, who had been led blindfold so long, would have their eyes opened; and would take their share in the work of the regeneration of Ireland. On the day that Home Rule became the -law of the land all the mistrust—he would not Say hatred, because they had never hated the English—they had with regard to England would vanish like a fog before the rays of the sun, and if ever the time came. that England was pinched and wanted friends She would have 500,000 of the finest fighting men in the world to carry the banner through blood and fire the world over. , (Applause.)

div.head: NO IRISH HATRED.
div.p: NO IRISH HATRED.

Mr. J. S. Devine, in a spirited address; refuted the allegations made by members of the Opposi- tion party that the Irish hated the British Empire. Did they fight as they had done for the Empire because they hated it? Surely no •man in his right Senses would say that they lost so many men in South Africa for an Empire which they hated. The Irish were. indeed a loyal race, and their representatives in the House of Com- mons had supported a number of 'measures for the social advancement of the working classes. The Irish had been most consistent in their demand for Home Rule; they had never once given the question up, and never ceased in their energies. Some people said they wanted separa- tion.,. They were not fools; 'they- were bound to England .by ties that could never be 'broken. There might be seine people who were asking for separation,. but if a person owed a man £5, and that man asked for £2O, was that any legi- timate reason why the person should not pay the £6? (Applause.) After jocularly referring to Carson's Provi- sional Army, Mr. Devine touched upon Conscrip- tion; and said it was looming upon them at the present time. In Germany every week there was one schoolboy of ICi to 17 years of age who committed suicide rather than face. the terrors of One year's military service. They did not want such a state of things in England, he was sure.

Dealing with the religious side of the Home Rule question, which had been introduced by the Opposition, he said ,that he was a Protes- tant, and had lived a most happy and contented life amongst Roman Catholics in Ireland. They would%be making the people of Ireland happier, brighter and more contented by giving them the Parliament at College Green. (Applause.)

div.head: RESOLUTION.
div.p: THE RESOLUTION.

Mr. F. Milne „ proposed the following resolu- tion: " That this meeting welcomes the Home Rule Bill now; , before the country as a just, sagacious, and . adequate solution of the Irish question, which meets the wishes of an over- whelming majority of the Irish people, who have long desired and pressed for Home Rule, and which will also safeguard permanently and effectually the rights of the minority in Ulster. Further, the meeting records its conviction that. the Government should use every effort speedily to place on the Statute Book this measure which will heal the long breach between the peoples of Great Britain and Ireland, and unite them for all purposes in a common loyalty to the Crown and Constitution." lie was strongly in favour of the Home Rule Bill and thought it was long overdue. (Applause) 31. r. J. D. B. Smith, in seconding the resolution, said that if in the future they wanted to amuse an audience they would read to the mem- bers, of the audience what had been talked of by Mr. Harold Smith and other gentlemen, who spoke of the wonderful things the women of Warrington were about to do if they got tho chance. Tell the audience of the wonderful army in Ulster, and also tell them that that was told to the people of to-day as fact, not as mere 1-vaporous fiction; and that. this and .that would happen if justice and 'right • were :granted land. (Laughter.) Less than 20 'years hence such statements made by .Harold Smith and his friends would be received with much merri- ment by any audience that had the slightest sense of humour. (Laughter and applause.) Mr. Baker proposed a. vote of thanks to the 3peakers and chairmarr, which was heartily accorded.

div.head: ORFORD.
div.p: ORFORD.

Dedication Anniversary.—The anniversary services for the dedication of the Church of St. Margaret and All Hallows Were held on Sunday. Special music was rendered by the choir, includ- ing the anthems "I will arise" and "The -radiant morn.". The preacher in the morning was the Vicar, • the lessons being read by- Mr. Sutton,. of Liverpool. A children's service was held in the afternoon, when Mr. Sutton deliv- ered an address. The Preacher in the evening was the Rev. Horace Gray, headmaster of the Warrington Grammar School.

div.head: RISLEY.
div.p: RISLEY.

Independent Methodist Church, Fearnhead.— The bazaar realised the handsome sum of £l3O ss. 4d. Mr. William Hughes, of Padgate, oq Friday occupied the chair, and spoke of the good work done. He had great pleasure in asking Miss A. Houghton, Miss Gertie Hughes and Miss Edith Monks to open- the bazaar. Miss Alice Houghton responded with an apt speech, wishing the bazaar every success, and was fol- lowed by Miss Gertie Hughes, who said, though young in years, she realised some of the crush- ing responsibilities of debt, and she hoped the stalls would be cleared. he invited her audi- ence to gather up the fragmens, so that nothing might he left. Miss E. Monks eirpressedsher plea- sure at being able to perform. such a ceremony as to assist in opening a bazaar, and ,hoped that all would be sold so that they might get rid of some of the debt. Votes of thanks were moved by Mr. Joshua Hughes, seconded by Mr. T. Harrison.

div.head: MOOR.
div.p: MOOR.

Wes I e yan Church.—The foreign missionary. services were held on Sunday, and were con- ducted, morning and evening, by the Rev. E. Morgan. Both services were well attendekand in the evening the anthem "Oh, worship the Lord," was rendered by the choir.

Wesley Guild.—At the devotional meeting on Wednesday evening an excellent address was given by the Rev. Morgan entitled "Tile Beauty of the Bible." About 37 tuild members were present. Mr. J. Lawton presided.

Missionary Meeting.—ln the schoolroom' on Thursday evening the missionary meeting was held. The speakers were the Rev. 11. William- son and Mr. J. Upson, while Mr. Murphy, of Penketh, proved hiniself an excellent chairman. It was gratifying to hear, in the course of Mr. Williamson's report, that last year's total was £3 9s. 10d. more than the previous year. The collections for Sunday and this meeting were an advance of £1 ss. on last year.

div.head: PADGAT E.
div.p: PADGAT E.

The collections for Sunday amounted to, ..t4 195. Bd., and on the following night to £8 175., a total of .#ll3 16s. Bd., which is in advance of ,last year. The Rev. T. F. Nich- olson, who has had 15 years' practical mission- ary experience in the neighbourhood of 'Madras, India, was the special preacher at both th 2 morning and evening services, whilst he further addressed a gtv:hering of children in the after- noon, over which Alderman A. Whittle was fesponSible for the humorous ele- ment, and his items. were "Country Curate," "I do love my Wife." "A Day Trip to Douglas," and "Appetite." div.head: GREAT MISSIONARY GATHERING.
div.p: GREAT MISSIONARY GATHERING.
What Patigate is Doing for the Cause
Abroad.
INSPIRING ADDRESSES.

Taking the attendances at the foreign mis- sionary meetings at the Padgate Wesleyan Church last Sunday and -Monday as a criterion, it would appear that there were many well- wishers of the missionaries' cause there, and this was borne out by the enthusiasm displayed. The assembly on Monday evening was a large one, and excellent addresses were delivered by the Rev. T. F. Nicholson, and Mr. Isaac ,H. Holden, of Southport. Mr. William Bennett was the chairman.
Calling for Help.

Mr. Bennett said that Ile was very pleased to be privileged and, spared once more to take part in their annual missionary 'meeting. He had been attending them for over 50 years, and he did not think he had missed one, and he added that this year his interest was greater than ever. He spoke of the great Centenary Fund, by which the Wesleyan Church intended to raise £250,000. Touching upon the mission work proper, he said that .he could not forget that the doors were open on every side in China, India and West Africa. The people in those countries were calling for help, and they knew that there were millions who had never heard the Gospel, and when they heard those things it behoved them all to do their very best for the People who could not help themselves.

div.head: Faith in the Future.
div.p: Faith in the Future.

Mr. Isaac Holden, Southport, who was greeted with a hearty cheer, said he was very pleased and encouraged to hear what they in Padgate had done for the Centenary Fund, and. his ex- perience, going about the country, was that folk who were making things go in Methodism were those who always had a lot to do. They had been spending a great deal of time in consider- ing what had been done in the last century, .and what God had allowed them to accomplish, but now they must speak with zeal, enthusiasm and faith of the work that God would do in the next century. Many of them would say, "What can God do?" The speaker thought they had got past that stage. They were taught when children that God could do everything, and as they faced the coming century they must remind them- selves of the earliest things they were taught, and must apply them in all their Church life by saying, `f What will God do in the next cen- tury?" He thought the answer was on every- body's tongue—" God will do just as much as we ask Him to do, as much- as we allow Him to do." This they must bear in mind in the century that was coming.

div.head: Laymen's Movement.
div.p: The Laymen's Movement.

Ile was vell aware of the fact that they asked him to come to that meeting because of the men he was associated with, and perhaps with the intention of hearing something he would have to say about the; laymen's movement, and what was going on there. The movement worked through meetings generally not as big as that one, and for the last .twelve months they had been going about their business in small meet- ings: They had held their meetings under all kinds" of circumstances and places, in hotels, cafes, Schoolrooms, but not yet in a chapel. They had had some in private houses, and such a system of meetings he did not think should be limited to the laymen's movement. They had gone back to the old Methodist principle of meeting-places, and to the old Methodist system .of fellowship. He had; not returned from any of their meetings yet without going back more enthusiastic than he went, and Ile had never yet been discouraged, and he was certain they had a good time ahead of them.

div.head: Five Thousand Years A9o.
div.p: Five Thousand Years A9o.
TOLD FOR YOUNS PEOPLE.

Last week. I tried to describe the writing and writing materials that were in use in the days of Abraham. Many young people have been much interested in the article, and I propose to 'tell them a little more about this remote period of the world's history.
As inbst people know the Bible story of Abra- ham, it will perhaps be interesting if I tell of the discovery of his early home in Chaldea.

the sun supplied heat in abundance, and then, as now, the oven for baking the bread was like a huge stationary pot built of mud in the street. AN ANCIENT CEMETERY, Equally interesting with; the houses of the living were the graves of the dead. Protected by the ruins above them, many of the graves have remained in a state .of perfect preserva- tion. They might be likened 'to a modern vault, though not of hewn stone, but of unbaked bricks of mud, which, if protected from the influence of weather, endure for ever. They were minia- ture houses, about seven feet long and four feet in width and height. - The Babylonian of Ur carefully prepared the ground- for a. cemetery, surrounded it with a wall, and underlaid it. with tiles to drain away all moisture. The body was laid upon the level ground thus prepared; the arms and feet were placed in the required position, and the brick mason, who.then played an important part in the 'ceremony, began 'to build the tiny houses about the dead. At his side was a pile of sun- dried bricks, and .some damp mud for mortar. Quickly building the Walls about the body -to a few inches in height,- he placed within .some

beyond the marshes the Arabs are the fiercest of the desert tribes, over whom the Turkish Government has little or no control. About the temple, which still rears its lofty tower above the surrounding. marshy plain, lie the ruins of Ur of the Chaldees, the birthplace of Abraham and of the Hebrew race.

div.head: ER OF THE CHALDEES.
div.p: ER OF THE CHALDEES.

In. the year 1853 the English Consul at Busreh, while exploring the various mounds of Southern Babylonia, happened upon some extensive ruins a few miles west of Nasarieh. Among the Arabs the mounds, are known as Mubeir, or Pitch, because the great square bricks of the temple tower are laid in bitumen the 'native pitch of the country. . . Whilst searching among the ruins Mr. Tay- lor found numerous 'bricks stamped with in- scriptions in the wedge-shaped characters of ancient Babylonia, bearing the name of Urgur, who called himself the King a Ur. Still other bricks and inscriptions were found, containing the same name of Ur. 'Later it was learned that the country in which the ruins stand was the well-known Babylonkm province of Chaldea. Mr. Taylor had iJiscovered Ur of the Chaldees, the birthplace of Abraham,. a city as important as any in history, for it gave to tht world the Hebrew nation.

The most important of the inscriptions found at Ur, and one of the Most valuable ever dis- covered in Babylonia,, is a cylind,r of baked clay covered with minute Babylonian writing. Its inscription related how Nabonidus, the King of Babylon, restored the ancient temple of Ur. At the very moment when Mr. Taylor found it in the wallS of the temple at Ur, some Ger- man critics were advancing the theory that Belshazzar, who, so the story in the Book of Daniel says, saw the fingers of a hand writing his doom upon the wall, was but ,a 'mythical character, and that he never existed except in legend. When the long inscription upon the cylinder from Ur was read it was found to bnd with a prayer, of which the closing words were these: "May reverence for Thy great divinity, dwell in the heart of Belshazzar, my first born son. May he commit no sin, and with the fulness of life may he be satisfied." The supposed mythical Belshazzar was at once restored to history, and since then numerous inscriptions, among others a lease for the house which he rented, have come to light. The ruins of Ur are now a circular group of mounds, a little , more than half a mile in diameter; ahout the outer edge a ridge, some- what higher than any of the inner mounds, con- ceals the•reinaing: of the ancient city. wall. • Towards, the northern end of the space within the walls rises a lower of massive brickwork, which, though washed by the , rains of four thousand seven hundred winters since the reign of Urgur, the King who built it, is still in a fair state of preservaticin. The upper of its three storeys has disappeared, but the two lower, 'ris- ing seventy feet above the plain, remain. Mr. Taylor, dealing the summit of the tower, found the stairway which led to the upper storey, and he dug about the base among the chambers, which were filled with the rubbish of long past ages.
The other mounds of the group, like most. Babylonian. ruins of great antiquity, are covered with- fragments of ancient. .pottery, so thickly scattered that in places the ground beneath is invisiNe. •

div.head: BABYLONIAN HOUSE.
div.p: A BABYLONIAN HOUSE.

Here and there Mr. Taylor dug below the sur- face. In one. mound 'near the temple he_un- covered a small square building of which the ancient roof was still in place. The sand and dirt hadi filtered in through the doorway, filling the one room of the house completely; above it the dirt had accumulated, and, thus Pro- tected, the house has remained intact. Its roof is the. only roof of a Babylonian house which time Iths not destroyed. In such a house in this very town, Abraham lived when a child. -- There were no windows in it, and the only light entered by the doorway. There was no floor save the well-trodden dirt' of the ground.; no chairs or tables, for then, as now, the Oriental sat upon the ground, and only kings employed \chairs to raise them above the people. The furnishings were simple; a reed Mat for the bed was spread at night upon the 'floor, or in summer. time upon, the roof; during the day it was rolled up and' stored away. A .stone mortar, for grinding the grain, an earthen pot. for bringing the water from the river, a stone knife, and a clay whorMor spinning, comprised the greiter part of the household furnishings. 'Mere was no fireplace in the house, for there

clay vessels of various shapes and sizes, con- taining food and drink for the spirit of the dead. Then the laying of the bricks was continued to the customary height. .To form the roof, each of the 'side courses of bricks was set in, gradyally nearing each other, and covering the grave, until finally the one-top course shut out the light, the rain, and,even the air. Thus buried, even the fragile pottery in the little house-like graves has remained uninjured during all of the thousands of years since Abraham left Ur. In one such grave was found the skeleton lying upon a reed mat, with a reed basket at the feet, fourteen clay vessels, a copper bowl, and.an inscribed cylinder, a band of pure gold about an, inch broad, four statuettes, a cat's-eye stone,, and a white stone *seal. Thus the people of Abraham in Ur were interred,

div.head: EASTERN LIFE FOUR THOUSAND 1-I,,Aits
div.p: EASTERN LIFE FOUR THOUSAND 1-I,,Aits
AGO.
It is from these early houses and graves that we learn how the people of Abraham lived and dressed.

Imagine a tall, broad 'man, with head bare, save for ,the long black hair, with a full black beard, barefooted (for sandals were then not commonly used in Babylonia), with a, great square cloth of goat's hair, perhaps embroid- ered along the edge, thrown about the body, concealing the left 'arm, but leaving the right arm free and we have a picture of Abraham, as the ruins of his city present him. His herds, for he was a shepherd, were in the care of keepers who grazed thein in the valley of the Euphrates, or, as the winter rains Per- mitted, further in the interior. We may see him going from flock .to flock counting the animals, and taking from the shepheras little receipts recorded in wedge-shaped letters upon clay; such receipts are now found among the ruins.
The picture which We have of his wife, his mother, and his sisters is not less vivid.

Even in those days, it was not proper for a woman in the Orient to reveal her fate to the stranger in public, therefore she is seldom represented upon sculpture. Her outer garment resembled that of her husband, though more richly embroidered. Her heavy black hair way knotted upon the head, and held in place by moans of a single long bronze pin. She • was proud and sought to increase her natural charms by tattoo marks upon her face and body, and she even coloured her cheeks and darkened her .eyebrows. A marble cos- metic case with two cells, one containing henna, the, rouge of The Orient, and .the other the black kohl, was found in one grave. She was exceedingly fond of jewellery. Her most striking adornment was a wide ,band of gold about her forehead. Her nose and rs, which were pierced, were decorated with rings of bronze or silver, sometimes set with stones or shells. Her fingers and thumbs bore ings of bronze, silver, or gold.

Bracelets or anklets and large neckbands were among her jewels, but the meg common adornment of all was the beads about her rick. Some were of brightly coloured stone cut ir to every imaginable shape and highly polished; others were of gold spread over a filling of bitumen. She was not. the slave- that the woman rf a later date in the Orient became. Generally, the only wife, of her husbhnd, she ground the barley meal in the stone mortar; she brought the water from the canal, and sothetimes she wandered, over the desert, gathering the roots of the shrubs for fuel.

div.head: ABRAHAM AS A BOY.
div.p: ABRAHAM AS A BOY.

Of the early child of Ur the ruins have given us a picture. There was a rattle of clay for the infant days, and the clay dolls ond animals of fantastic shapes when the rattle was out- grown. At 4ismoya was found a game board of clay, 'showing that the boy of Abraham's tune knew a game similar .to 'chess. • Ile was fond of the chase, and then game was more plentiful than now about Ur. Mounted' upon the horse which he had learned to ride when a wee child, he hunted the elephant and the lion and the ostrich, but now they have .0 dis- appeared from • the valley. ' With the grey- hounds he chased the gazelles the jackals and wolves of the desert, and the wild boar of the marshes he despised.

, Though the Biblical 'picture of the life of Abraham and of the home of his boyhood days is faint, the ruins of his native .city have at last made it distinct. One may rim walk in the streets where Abraham used to play, and may climb the steps of the great temple, which, when boy, he mounted to gaze far out upon the horizon, beyond which he, at a later day, led out his family when he made his Memorable journey to the land of Canaan. A.M.

QUAINT AND AMUSING.

The gasoline slot. machine,- now being intro- duced, requires no attendant. - The car is drawn up to the machine, a hose connecting with. the car tank is inserted, a half-dollar is dropped into the slot, arid the crank is turned. This sets a pump in action which delivers the gaso- line into the tank of the car. A graduated gauge at the front of the machine shows the buyer just how much gasolipe he is getting, while, if the -supply happens to be exhausted, the money- is automatically returned. The mechanism is adjustable to deliver the fluid at current prices.

div.head: Low German Birth-rate.
div.p: Low German Birth-rate.

Genuine concern has been awakened among patriotic Germans by the disclosure that the birth-rate throughout the empire is sinking far more rapidly than had been supposed. An authority on the subject has now published 'some figures - which reveal the extraordinary 'fact that the decline in the birth-rate of Germany is greater than that "of ally other European country, with • the possible exception of Bel- gium. Altogether the annual increase of popu- lation is between 60,000 'and 70,000. less than it would be if 'the birth-rate of fifteen years ago were maintained. The revelations have. be- come the subject of anxious discussion, espe- cially in military and official circles.
Millions of Stamps Destroyed.

_ . Perhaps the most colossal error that has ever occurred in the history of stamps happened in the United States. To commemorate the .ipen- ing of the _Panama Canal a new series cf :011r values was prepared. The one cent., five cent., and :ten cent. appeared, and it was. found that the picture on the two cent. stamp was a view of the San Pedro Miguel Locks instead of the Gatun Locks, although the stamp was inscribed with the latter name. The Government imme- diately withdrew the whole printing, consisting. of over twenty million stamps, and destroyed them. The new printing shows the view of San Pedro Miguel, but is inscribed "Panama Canal."
The Origin of Bridge.

One of the most extraordinary facts about bridge is that, despite its popularity, its history should be so Obscure. -Discussing the subject\in his book, "Pastimes in Times Past," Mr. 0. Paul Monckton says that it cannotobe much more than fifty years old—" an age vllll which few players will be inclined ,to credit it, but which is quite small when compared with such hoary veterans as chess, bowls, or even playing cards themselves." Although he has made researches in many countries as to the origin of the game, Mr. Monckton has foimd the quest, in the main, fruitless. The idea that the game originated in Russia is probably due to a pamphlet, " Biriteh or Russian Whist," which was received in the University Library at Cam- bridge in 1886.
Ancient Customs of the Sea.

In the "Marine Magazine" numerous phases of sea life are dealt with in a series of entertain- ing articles, not the least notable contribution being the graphic description of certain ancient ping, were. regularly kept up by seamen. Of sea customs which, man earlier period of ship- these customs two will still be remembered by a good number of present-day seafarers. They are the "casting overboard of the 'dead horse,'" and the visiting of 'the ship by. Father Neptune, as the vessel crosses the Line. The dead horse" performance had to do with the end of the first month of the voyage, and was carried out by the sailors to mark their satisfaction at by their Month's advance of ' having finished working off the period covered wages:.

Skeletons from the Deep. On the night Of April 12, 1904, the 110ssian battleship. Petropavlovsk, while manoeuvring against the blockading fleet of the Japanese off Port Arthur, struck a floating., mine, and was so seriously injured by its explosion that she sank almost immediately, carrying down Ad- miral Makaroff, Rear-Admiral Molas, the lids- sian artist Verestchagin, and nearly 600 officers and men. Last spring a Japanese contractor hamed Sakurai succeeded in locating the sunken wreck by means of divers, and lately his ex- perts, Working at a depth of nearly 800 feet, entered what was believed to be the council- room of i.he battleship, and found there the remains 'of Admiral Makaroff, Rear-Admiral Molt's, and four other officers whose skeletons cohld not be identified.
Fish Drowns Man.

A remarkable drowning tragedy took place in the Grande Ronde River, 'Oregon. :Orville Sannar (20), son of Postmaster Sannar, of 'Promise, was jerked under water by an 18-inch fish he had hooked, and lost his life. The stream was deep and swift. The young man, after fishing on the bank ..for a time, started to swim across, holding his light rod in his mouth and letting the baited hook float. The current carried him down the stream, but he was advancing safely when suddenly those on shore saw his head go under. lieirose to the surface, and then his head went down suddenly again, as if jerked. A third time he rose, and then disappeared. After two hours' search his body was found at the bottom of the stream. The rod, with the fish still on the hook, was re- gained. The fish was heavy, and still vigorous when drawn from the water.

div.head: Camphor as a Vitalising Agent.
div.p: Camphor as a Vitalising Agent.

Abroad, where great pride--and just pride— is taken in the mileage per gallon of fuel that can be obtained, a small band of motorists re- cently has been experimenting with gum camphor as a " dope "for gasolin6. Usually, about one ounce of camphor is placed in five gallons of gasoline, and it is stated by those who use the mixture that the operation of their motors is much superior with the camphor in the gasoline than without it. One motorist even goes so far as to claim that he has been ,able to increase his mileage per gallon as much as 20 per cent., though it would seem that the increase cannot be due to the use of camphor alone. The idea is not new, of course, for Curtiss, at 're- sent of' aeroplane fame, used it a number of years ago in hiS racing motor cycles, and it is said he sometimes uses it now in his aeroplane engines.
A German Explosive.

, In German`y, where disappointment has attended the employment of acetylene for illum- inating purposes, use has been 'found for the g9s in the form of an explosive for blasting. Carbide of calcium in small particles is inclosed in a tin cartridge, the upper part of which con- tains water separated from the carbide ny, a partition. At the top of the cartridge is an electric percussion device'. An iron pin, worked from outside of •the cartridge, perforates the partition and allows the water to come in eon- .tact with the carbide. This is effected by a blow five minutes before it is desired to cause an explosion. At the end of that time, sufficient gas having been developed in the cartridge, the electric spark is fired and the explosion occurs. The effect in blasting is said to be the rending of the rock with innumerable cracks, so that the fragments are easily removed.

In the Days of Lionheart. By NVallace Gandy. Yondon: G. G. Harrop. 3s. 6d.

This old-time romance is written by 4 War- ringtonian, who is to be congratulated on pro- diting such a stirring story-. The book Is beautifully illustrated, and tells the tale of peasant life in Yorkshire during the times when Richard the First, our Lion-hearted King, was fighting in the Crusades. The hero, George-a- Green, simply • chains our attention with • his exploits from the time when he settles the bully and coward, Snodge, about the game of marbles, to the .end, when he claims the beau- tiful daughter . of Justice Grymes lor his wife. The .conversations are quite breezy. . Whilst . reading them we are no longer in the 20th cen- tury, but living in the times when. rushes were strewn on the floor, and every housewife brewed her own ale, without any hops. The mystery play arranged for present-day education is very beautiful and certainly interesting for any an- tiquarian. In fact, any old-time lover,, would revel in its pages, for there we find, among other things, a vivid description of .an old- fashioned betrothal and wedding among the peasantry. The fight where George gains his pinder.s position is bound .to interest- boy 'readers, for every boy loves a good fight. We see where the -jealousy of the ever-famous Maid Marion leads her bold Robin •HOod, and how, after the trial of strength between Robin and George, Marion makes a firm friend, of Beatrice, The Tart that -Richard the King plays is interesting, he does not. escape a few blows, much -to everybody's consternation, when .they find out who he really is, for he had travelled. incognito to Yorkshire to see for himself if the pinder was as redoubtable as he had heard! The book -breathes the spirit of old times, and is destined to be 4 favourite among young and old. NOt the least calculated to claim our at- tention is the preface which deals with the life and customs of Old England. The book is beautifully produced, and "In the Days of Lionheart keeps up the repute of the publishers in public opinion. .
The Future of Tropical America. Published by the Tropical Exploitation .Syn- dicate, Ltd., 28, Mincing-lane, London, E.C. is. and 2s. Gd.

The book is written in a Very clear, concise and common-sense manner. - The, facts are plainly and lucidly expressed and cannot fail to .give, iatisfaction to anyone who has the in- tention of settling in One of these American countries. There are ample opportunities for capitalists, farmers, mechanics, architects, en- gineers, builders, gardeners and miners. F,spe- daily interesting are the notices of the British possessions. Here, with the enormous possi- bilities and the natural wealth, thousands of energetic young men who find no outlet. for their increasing ambitions and earnest -desires .to make headway in the already over-stocked market at home, Can - turn westwards and satisfy their longings in a ' new country. For indeed these lands have a great commercial future before them. In Guatemalce the teach- ing of English and French in the schools is com- pulsory and in most of the countries English is spoken, though, of course, Spanish is the recognised intermediary. In Biltish Guiana, Honduras and Trinadad, one would have the benefit of living under British jurisdiction: The climate of these countries is quite favourable to the. people accuStomed to live in the temperate zones. Of British. Guiana, Mr. George Bayley writes: "The climate compares favourably with that of most other tropical countries. The ordinary clothes and straw_ hats. vorri, during the English sunimer are generally all that Is 1-equired 'for people accustomed. to ~the climate, The mid-day siesta, rendered necessary in parts of India, is rarely indulged .in. . . . • The nights are sufficiently cool. to be pleasant and conducive to sleep." "Yellow fever," Mr. Rod- way testifies, "has not appeared for 31) years.: The problem of• how to live healthily in the tropics has been studied for many years With patience; the mOsquito swamps are ,gradually being 'drained, and in many parts of the tropics Englishmen are living quite as safely as • they ever did'. at home. The discomforts have dis- appeared with a -change in the methods of &illy life, and now, with the opening of the Panama Canal, the countries will have 'a rapid develop- ment, so that there will be ample -scope for young, energetic and ambitious men of almost 'every trade or profession. The book' gives a very good and interesting dissertation On the cultivation of different fruits, which would be of special interest to planters or manufacturers of fruit jellies. That there are ample possibilities ahead for these countries is irrefutable, and the 1560 k is a splendid invest- ment.

div.head: HUMAN OSTRICH.
div.p: A HUMAN OSTRICH.

An extraordinary story.was told at an inquest held at York on Saturday on the body -of an inmate of the North Riding Asylum named Mary Elizabeth Jeremiah, wife of Raymond Jeremiah, of Great Ayton, near Middlesbrough. Nurse Watson missed her keys from her belt just after she had been attending to the deceased on October 10th. Shortly afterwards she found deceased with the keys in her hand, but.two of them—a large and a small one-were missing, and the patient said that she had swallowed them. The nurse did not believe her, and did not therefore report the matter till next day.

On October 14th it was found. necessary to per- form an operation, and the surgeon extracted the large key, several wooden matches and 'a piece of rag five inches long by two and a half inches wide, which had been rolled ;nth a ball before being swallowed. After the woman's death on Friday a further examination was made, when the smaller key was found, also two metal buttons and three small pieces of wood. These had caused ulcera- tion and /kW contributed to her death. •

div.head: Literary Gleanings.
div.p: Literary Gleanings.
THE SELF-MADE MAN.

If there be one man before me who honestly' and cOntentedly believes that, on the Whole, he is doing that work to which Ws powers are best adapted, I wish to congratulate him. My friend, I care not whether your hand be hard or soft. I care not whether you are from the office or the shop; I care not whether you preach the everlasting Gospel from the pulpit, or swing the hamtner over the blacksmith's anvil; I care not whether you have seen the inside of a college or the outside—whether your work be that of the •head or the hand—whether the world accounts you noble or ignoble; if you have round your place, you are a happy man. Let no ambition ever tempt you away from it by so much as a questioning thought. I say, if you have found your place—no mat- ter what or where it is—you are a happy man. I give you joy of your good fortune; for if you do the work of that place well, and draw from it all that it can give you oil merriment and discipline and development., you are, or yoli will become, .a man filled up, made after God's pattern, the noblest' product of. the world—a self-made man.—Dr. Holland, in "Great Thoughts."

div.head: PREHISTORIC ARTISTS.
div.p: PREHISTORIC ARTISTS.

Among the remains of prehistoric man, found in some European caves, there are pictures which make it certain that the.men'of the stone age could paint and draw as well as the aver- age man of to-day.- . • A Spanish nobleman, Marcellino de Sautuola, was. industriously digging in a cave on his estate in search of prehistoric stone implements and bones, while the little daughter, who accom- panied him, occupied herself in play, says a writer in the "New York Sun." ,

She happened to look up at the vaulted ceil- ing- overhead; and began to shout " Toros ! Toros !" in such excitement that her father paused to -investigate. Immediately he forgot his search for stone implements. The little girl had discovered some very remarkable prehis- toric paintings. . The paintings *were of the now extinct bison, which the little girl mistook for bulls, or " toros." The colours were red, black and grey. The technique of the drp.wings and the propor. Lions of the figures were really good, and the positions were very lifelike. • In the cavern' of Font de Gaume, France, paintings of mammoths, bison, and other animals haye been found, and most .of them show a considerable degree of skill. In the great caverns of Niaux, near Tarascon, France, half a mile from the entrance, the smooth, pOl- - walls are covered with outline drawings of game animals, drawn in oxid of manganese mingled with grease, which gives permanent lithographic effect' on the smooth limestone. Some of the cave paintings from a cave at Alt amira, especially a bison, and a mare With her foal, are reproduced in a mural series now in the American museum of Natural' History.

A PET PROVIDED WITH A SILVER JOINT. With an elbow joint of silver and chilled steel, a little pet monkey in San Francisco is proving by his agility that the artificial union is a success. He ,is demonstrating what is likely to prove a tremendous discovery in surgery— that ankylosed joints (hardened and stiffened by disease) can be replaced` by an operation that is not necessarily costly or dangerous. The same sort of operation has been performed with equal success upon a pet dog and in this case the hind leg of the animal was provided with a joint of metal, which appears to be as satisfac- tory for the possessor as the one 'provided by Nature. In the near future it is planned to pro- vide .a human being with this style of steel-and- silver joint, and the perfecting of this device will restore to usefulness many people who have become absolutely helpless by reason of acci- dent or disease. There are various causes for this complete or partial rigidity of the joints, such as rheumatism, gout and tuberculosis; and in extreme cases it has been necessary to break a joint about which osseous material had deposited. Of course, it is only in extreme cases, and after all other methods fail, that it should be necessary to perform.this operation of removing the natural joint and replacing it with metal. In the operations upon -animals'it was found that when the tendons were extended properly the muscles did their work as perfectly as in a normal limb, and the joints responded with the readiness of natural ones. In the case of the monkey in question the bones are capped with sockets, which are of silver, and. these are joined to a joint of steel. The inventor of this remarkable joint is a leading San Francisco surgeon, Dr. Milton Francis' Clark, whose ex- perience among crippled wOrkmen in .a rail- road hospital led him to search for this method of relief.—From the November Strand Maga- zine."

div.head: GERMAN EMPEROR..
div.p: THE GERMAN EMPEROR..

If Dr. Stanley . Shaw, in a recent issued volume, has not been able to throw any fresh illumination on the character of the German Emperor, he has, at any rate, produced a book of substantial worth. It has been the aim of the author to show how the Wide powers of government possessed by the monarch and his own belief that he has been divinely appointed to rule, influence the Imperial utterances and actions. "The German Emperor believes, and assumes his people to believe that the zollern monarch is specially chosen by Heaven to guide and goyern a folk entrusted to him as the talent was entrusted to the steward in the Scripture." The views "of the Sovereign and of his subjects concerning the God-given 'mis- ton of the Hohenzollerns do not in all respects\ ' agree; but the Emperor's faith gives a consist- ency to his character seemingly wholly at vari- ance with his manifest impulsiveness. "He is to-day the same Hohenzollern he va the day he mounted .the throne,, observing ex- actly the same attitude to the world abroad and to his folk at home, tenacious of exactly the same views in politics,„ religion, morals and art ,—in everything which concerns the foundations of social life. He still believes himself, as his speeches and conduct show', the selected instru- ment of Heaven, and acts towards his people and addresses them accordingly." The Emperor is at once medimfal in nature 'and modern in character, and such, in the view of Dr. Shaw, he will remain to the end of his life. Tried by the standard of conduct—the only one as yet available—the Emperor ,shows us a high type of humanity. "First of all, he is a good man; good as a Christian, good as a husband, good as a father, good as a patriot. He has high ideals, and is not ashamed of them. He is neither indolent nor fussy; neither a cynic nor-an intriguer nor a fool; he is neither wrong-headed nor stub- born; lie is honest and sincere to a degree, that does him, honour as a man,' if it has sometimes proved perilous and blameworthy to him as a monarch. -He is no physical or intellectual giant; but he is a man of more than average , all-round intelligence and capacity." Dr. Shaw does not omit to make mention of the Emperor's human failings. In his earlier years he showed some lack of judgment and the power of balancing considerations, and he has still less tact than character.

The Telltale Face. Like a garden where the flowers Are killed by ugly weeds, Your face tells if you give hours To unkindly thoughts an deeds. • • But think a generous -thought,' Act with a kindly grace, Do the thing you know you ought, And you'll carrY a shining face. The years will leave their lines, And when you're old, 'Us truth, Your face will bear unfailing signs Of the thoughts and deeds of youth.

Autumn Sadness. Strolling through a large wood one autumn day, I saw the sere and yellow leaves fall from the trees in brilliant showers, Covering the ground with a glowing carpet. They had lived . their brief 'life, they had done their humble but useful work. It seemed only yesterday that I had seen the trees clothed in a garment of lovely green, and now .most of them were stripped of their glory Those that were not bare of their f.aliage presented a sight pleasing to the eye. Their leaves were of a yellow tint., most restful to look upon, and as the gentle wind softly swept by them, they gave a murmuring Eigh like the ripple of a brook.

Loohing up among the fOliage, I saw a young finch unfolding in the sun its.silvery wings. and-.: a- robin darted out. from the leafy bower. W4l nests were to be seen in the clefts df trees, but they were desolate, as the birds had flown off to rind other homes.

• Through the vista of the trees I could set the farmer and his helpers busily ploughing, some ploughing down stubble, and others ploughing up potatoes. On coming nearer to the field, I found this was being done in two ways, first by means of a common plough, and, second, by 'a potato lifter, the last way being the metre inter- esting to watch. In the distance stood a white-washed farm- house gleaming in the sun. The cereal crop was thatched carefully to preserve it from tilt storms of winter.

All this I saw one autumn day, .and as I stood taking a farewell look at the wood, I thought how closely the autumn of Nature represents the autumn of our life, when we too areigetting into the sere and yellow. When the_ winter of Pour life comes, We will, be ready to obey the .call of the Ileaper, whom none can escape.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEIVIBEF 8, 1913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEIVIBEF 8, 1913.
NO" ELECTION SURPRISE.
The Conservatives Fail to Capture

div.head: Attacked Seats,
div.p: Attacked Seats,
OLD MEMBERS RE-ELECTED.

There was no election surprise in connection with the polling which took place on Saturday. The Conservatives failed badly in their attack on Whitecross and Latchford Wards, but they retained St. Austin's Ward against an Inde- pendent. The position of parties up to Monday next, when Aldermen have to be elected, remains as before, namely, 16 Liberals, 15 Conservatives,. and 5 Independents. The election results were declared on Saturday evening as follow :
WIIITECROSS WARD.
I. hawthorn (L.) T. G. Brookes (C.)
Liberal majority
LATCHFORD WARD.
R. Ilenshall (I.) A. Ashton (C.) .
Independent majority... 202
ST. AUSTIN'S WARD.
J. Broadhurst (C.) A. Browne (1.)
Conservative majority... 316

In Whitecross Ward 1,277 voters polled, out of die total of 1,631 on the list; in Latchford 1,536 polled, out of 1,939; and in St. Austin's 966 polled, out of 1,159. The elections were marked by an absence of excitement, but in each ward the Conservatives,seemed to poll to their last voter, several being brought from considerable distances outside the borough to vote.

Votes of thanks were passed to Aldermen Pierpoint, Bolton and Bennett for presiding in the different Wards. Councillor Henshall, thanking the Latchford Ward officials, said that he had had record elections with the Brothers Ashtoti, and he was on the most friendly terms with them. If he had to fight again he could not wish for a better opponent than Mr. Ashton. Alderman Bennett expressed the thanks of the officials for the vote.

div.head: AGED PAUPERISM V.,A.NISFI/NG.
div.p: AGED PAUPERISM V.,A.NISFI/NG.

In the meantime, returns for England and Wales show that old-age pauperism is vanish- ing as the result .of the operation of the Old-age pension scheme. On March 31, 1906, the paupers over 70 years of age receiving outdoor relief numbered 168,096; on the Ist January this year they numbered 8,563, a decrease of 94.9. per cent. The figures for indoor relief for the same period showed a decrease of 19.8. In Cumberland and Rutland the outdoor decrease was 99 per cent. In 90 unions, mainly rural, there were no per- sons over seventy in receipt of outdoor relief on January 1 this year.

div.head: PRICE OF A DOUBLE MURDER.
div.p: PRICE OF A DOUBLE MURDER.

Hatred of his mother-in-laF has led a master -in a well-known college at Paris into a very disagreeable plight. He accosted two young lads, who were apparently out of work, and pro- posed that they should murder his mother-in- law, but in order that the crime might be looked upon as the outcome tof a burglary they. were also to murder an old lady nearly 80 years of age, an intimate friend. For this double crime he agreed to pay the sum .of

The two boys appeared to accept the bargain. but they confided in a friend and were per- suaded to report the matter to the police. The master confessed that he had really made the offer,. but nothing can be done to him because his propdsals were not carried into effect.

div.head: ART GALLERY NEEDS.
div.p: ART GALLERY NEEDS.
More Pictures Wanted and More
Space Required.

div.head: MR. J. UPSON'S IDEAL.
div.p: MR. J. UPSON'S IDEAL.

The question of additions to the Art Gallery 1 for Warrington was raised at a lecture given under the auspices of the Museum Committee in the Co-operative Hall on Saturday evening. The lecture was on " Venice ; its history and its art," and it was the first of three to be delivered by Mr. J. E. Phythian, an authority on the subject. Mt. J. UPSOII, who presided, mentioned the need of an extended Art Gallery. They had such a place, he said, but it was scarcely worthy of the name of an Art Gallery. It. was crowded into the Museum and Library. They felt proud of the Museum, and the Library was as goOd an institution as they could expect in a town of the size of Warrington, but they 'felt they 1 were lamentably short in regard_ to the Art Gallery. They wanted more accommodation for the display of the pictures they had and might receive in the future. Perhaps the lectures arranged by the Museum Committee would encourage local .patriots of wealth to add to the. 'collection they possessed, especially the works of local artists. If local patriotism did not, result in .that the people might say that the town should provide the pictures themselves and see that the Town Council should provide a gallery with an ade- quate display of the works of local artists, so that these might prove a pleasure to the people of the town and district. - (Applause.) He was told there were some very. fine pic- tures in the possession of people in Warrington and the district, but, so Mr, unfOrtunately, these had. not got so far as the Art Gallery. Some of the pictures he was told would find their Way to the Gallery on the death' of the Owners. They did not wish .for the death of anyone, but they would like to see some of the pictures, now reserved for the pleasure of the few, displayed on the walls of the Art Gallery, so that, all might be able to take pleasure in studying them. (Applause.) Mr. J. E. PHYTHIAN hoped that his lectures ‘N.1111(1 stir up the people of Warrington to' take deeper interest in the Art Gallery and also 1 influence some to provide a better collection of the pictures in the town. lie then described the history of Venice, and many scenes from the historic city were shown on the screen.

div.head: OAKUM PICKING.
div.p: OAKUM PICKING.
Not Suitable Work for Old Men Say
Runcorn Guardians.
FIREWOOD CHOPPING INSTEAD.

Tho fortnightly meeting- of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at Dutton on Tuesday, Mr. J. L. Jones (vice-chairman) pre- siding. In view of the fact that there is a shortage of accommodatiOn at the Homes, it was decided that application be made for two children to be admitted into the Newton Homes. It was stated that there were now 59 children in the Children's Home in connection with the Run- corn Union, and that the Inspector, on his last visit, had stated that no more children should be admitted. The Rating System.

The •Easington 'Board a Guardians asked the Board to support the following resolution: •"rhat the time has now arrived when the whole rating, system of the country should be over- hauled, and also when a larger contribution should be paid from the Imperial Exchequer towards the increased burden imposed upon Local Authorities, notably Education Author- ities." Mr. Morris moved that the resolution be sup- ported. He thought it was a matter they ought to support, as the burden of education increased year by year, and that they should receive more help from the Imperial Government. Air. Hallows seconded, and said: "It presses very heavy on the local rates." It was decided to support the resolution. The County Asylum Authorities wrote stating that the rate of maintenance of pauper lunatics in the Asylum for the ensuing quarter had been fixed at 9s. Old. per head .per week. The Clerk explained that the amount was the same as that for last quarter.

div.head: Mental Deficients.
div.p: Mental Deficients.

A letter was read from the Clerk to the con- ference of representatives of all the Unions in Cheshire recently held that the following reso- lntion was passed unanimously: "That in view of the Mental Deficiency Act it is desirable that the Cheshire Poor Law Unions should combine together for the purpose of providing or arrang- ing for the provision of suitable accommodation for chargeable defectives and epileptics, and that an Executive Committee should be ap- pointed to work out details and arrange terms for combination, and report and recommend to a future meeting of the Conference." Mr. Pillink said he had been present at the meeting. The final meeting would be held on the 14th inst., and after that he would have something to say on the matter.

div.head: Association of Unions.
div.p: Association of Unions.

The Clerk said that the annual meeting of Poor Law Associations Would be held on Nov- ember 21st. An important matter would be raised in connection with the report of the Commission appointed to consider the question of the management of Workhouses and Work- house Infirmaries. It was decided that the Clerk and Chairman attend the meeting. The Clerk • read the recommendations of the sub.committee appointed by the Conference for the more successful method of dealing with the question of vagrancy. , The Board decided to empower their delegates to support the recommendations of the sub-com- mittee at the joint conference to be held shortly.

div.head: Oakum Picking by Old Men.
div.p: Oakum Picking by Old Men.

In moving the adoption of the minutes of the 'Visiting Committee, Mr. Morris said that the Local Government Board Inspector, Mr, Duff, had taken serious objection to the way in which old men were employed in picking oakum, and he recommended that Some other, form of em- ployment be tried. As a trial the Committee recommended that tke men be employed in chopping sticks. There would be no large outlay at first, and the com- mittee would report further to the Guardians on the result. In regard to the conversion of lavatories and the matter of the floors, they recommended that fresh tenders should be in- v'itet'excludilig the provision of the verandah, as they thought the scheme was a rather lavish one. Mr. P. Booth seconded. • The minutes of the Visiting Committee were passed. ' Contract for Drugs.

Considerable discussion took place on the Health Committee minutes in regard to the con- tract for drugs. Mr. Hallows proposed that Mr. J. Rymer Young, War4ngton, be included in the list of chemists to tender. _ .

Mr. Gibbs said that if they passed that they would.be going back on their resolution. ,They had, at the beginning of the season, deciiled to appoint Mr. Weston to supply the drugs, and it, wOuld not be fair to him.
Mr. Hallows' proposition was defeated.

div.head: POISONED BY YEW TREE BARK.
div.p: POISONED BY YEW TREE BARK.

Mrs. Winter, of Meaburn Hall, Westmorland, has just lost a valuable colt, worth about' 100 guineas, by yew poisoning. The animal was found dead, and a veterinary surgeon, on mak- ing a post-mortem, found that the animal had died, from eating yew tree bark, a quantity of which was found in the stomach.

The annual prize -distribution in connection with the Works Bowling Association took placc. in the dining hall at Messrs. Greening's W orb on Saturday evening. The association has had an excellent season, and the popularity of J. Spencer's win was manifested by the large attendance to witness the distribution of prizes by the Mayor. Mr. Spencer, who was a Pearson and Knowles rCpresNitative, won the "Greenall" Cup and Lady Greenall's J:5 ss. prize, whilst W. Farrington, the runner-up, also of Pearson and Knowles, wae awarded the President's (Captain George Crosfield) prize, value £3 38. In the temporary ,abseme 4if Captain Croslield,

W. FARRINGTON, RUNNER-CP.

might be very fine, but it was discipline obtained at the expense of the human heart, and there- he it not sound discipline. Cultivation of human feelings, which raised a man to a higher state, was crushed by the blood and iron a the German system. It was very different in the French Army, where a feeling of good com- radeship existed between non-commissioned officers and men. It was also very different in the Austrian and Swiss Armies. There was none of that turning an officer into a tin-god or set- ting him upon a pedestal where the men might look at him. Such a state of things was pro- historic, and when he talked about National Service he did not want to introduce anything of that kind. He believed that it was perfectly possible to have a Citizen Army in which per- fect good feeling existed between officers and men, and it was for that end he was working. (Applause.)

div.head: WINNER
div.p: WINNER

Things were moving rapidly, and those people who would be unjust had not the same power to be so as they had in the past. The working men could now trust to their own efforts for the redress of anything they looked upon as a grievance. The spirit of good sportsmanship helped them in that direction. (Applause.) lie had great pleasure in presenting the prizes and congratulated the winners.

div.head: NOT TO BE TIED TO PUBLIC-HOUSES.
div.p: NOT TO BE TIED TO PUBLIC-HOUSES.

- Mr. W. WEBSTER • proposed the toast of "The President." He said they all knew the Presi- dent fjr his sterling worth and upright charac- ter—(hear, hear)—and appreciated the efforts he had made for the cultivation of howling in the town. Indeed, he was interested in everything appertaining to the welfare of the working people, and they would be. exceedingly sorry if .he were to resign his position as president— (hear, hear)-,--because he helped them in so ina,,y ways. There was some big selteme com- ing forward, to which the President gave his hearty .support. Ire (the speaker) hoped the scheme would fructify, and that they would get the means whereby the Works .A.ssociation 'would have greens and a club-house of their own. Bowling. used to he •looked upon as a middle- aged man's game, but to-day the majority of the trundlers in Warrington were quite young men. It was not right that those young men should have to go to a-public-house or a club to play bowls--,(hear, 'hear)—and the association's scheme would solve that difficulty. (Applause) The toast was accorded with musical honours.

div.head: CAPTAIN CROSFIELD AND THE VALUE
div.p: CAPTAIN CROSFIELD AND THE VALUE
OF RECREATION.

Captain CROSFIRLD, who had a hearty recep- tion, said that if it were their Wish that he should continue as President he would be glad to do so. (Applause.) He had been greatly interested in the remarks made by the Mayor, especially *here he had referred to the necessity of a little play and healthy recreation in these days of stress and strife, and how necessary it was—lith all the new complicated conditions of existence—to enjoy tivqnselves in their leisure hours. If they did not do that they might get to take things too seriously. (Hear, hear.)
Relations of Master and Man.

In the difficult problem of labour unrest they had extremists both amongst the employers and the employes, who did not help the situation aL all. (Hear, hear.) They had, on the employes' side, a ccrtain type of man who looked upon a capitalist as a fellow who wore a fur overcoat, even if the thermometer were at 90, smoked two

div.head: Succmsful Season.
div.p: A Succmsful Season.

He congratulated them on having had a most successful season. He understood the entries had been 663, as against 602 last year. In re- gard to the scheme to which 'llr. Webster had referred he Would like to say that when Mr. Patrick mentioned the matter to him he said " It is a capital idea if the members of the association take it up, but if they will not take it up and back the committee, then don't touch it." It was .to be a democratic undertaking in which all the members should join. So far, he understood, the response had not been very encouraging. Everyone said: "I will join if the green is next to my front door." He (the speaker) suggested that the committee should look round for ground as central as possible, and then call a meeting. He wished them every success in their undertakings. (Applause.)

div.head: "THE ASSOC/ATION."
div.p: "THE ASSOC/ATION."

Mr. STRAW proposed the toast of "The Asso- ,ciation." ,He had, he said, watched the progress of the association, from year to year, and had been delighted with the results which accrued from the committee's efforts. (Applause.) -
MR. PATRICK AND THE NEW SCHEME

Mr. PATRICK (the honorary secretary), in reply, said the association was creating a better feeling amongst the working men of the town. Their thanks were 'due to the President for the time and energy he had devoted; to the committee and officials; and to Mr. Rushworth, who kept the green in such a splendid condition. He hoped they would soon have a -clubroom of their Own. The Scheme which had been mentioned was one which was entirely in, the hands of the mem- bers. They Wanted to devise some scheme where- by they could have their games on their own green. He, for one, did not believe in fastening round his neck a millstone which would drag him down. If the members were prepared to go on with the scheme and to take up a number of the shares,, then the scheme would go on. (Ap- plause.) But he did not think they would have much or 9ny difficulty in promoting the new association. (Hear, hear.) He wanted it to be. for the benefit of the workers. There would be a town's meeting in the winter months to decide on the matter. They 'had been mitered for ex- cellently at the King and Queen, Bank Quay, and the Horse and Jockey, but the difficulty .they had to contend with was that the competi- tors were not given a fair. chance, as they had to play the games in one afternoon. If they had three or four greens of their own they would solve the .difficulty. '(Applause.)

div.head: SUMMER CAMP AND NURSING ASSOCIA-
div.p: SUMMER CAMP AND NURSING ASSOCIA-
TION BENEFIT.

Captain CROSFIELD then handed Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins £64s. on behalf of the Children's Sum- mer Camp, and said that ;,t6 would be handed over to Mr. Henry Hope for the Warrington and District. Nursing Association. That did not represent the amount received at the charity match, as there were more subscriptions to come in. (Applause.)

S.7WILLETT proposed, and Mr. PATRICK seconded, a hearty vote of thanks to the donors of prizes; and, on the proposition of Mr. HORRA- BIN, seconded by Mr. WEBSTER, the artistes were also heartily thanked.
Mr. JENKINS thanked the association for their generosity. _
- An excellent Programme was contributed to 1)3- Messrs., T. Triumphiies, J. Willett, and W. Farringtbn (humorist). Mr. Trow was an able accompanist.

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.
Warrington Workingmen's
Association.
N.A. CENTRE.
CHESTER AT ITS WORST.

Angling at Chester, both in the Dee ai Canal, was almost a blank. Members who we there two days last week-end returned witho .a scale. Two contests arranged ended in a far( One lot of competitors started their match the Dee, but there was nothing "doing, and th' finished their contest in the Canal. After hours' angling in each water all the prizes ire not won.

Another competition that was held on the D resulted in the competitors drawing their entri back. We are now at the worst time of C season for finding suitable bait. The feeder al maggot are practically done with and the sto baits are not yet reatly.

div.head: GOWY
div.p: THE GOWY

The stream here was in splendid conditie both for water and colour, but anglers could n get get them going. Several had ones, twos, al threes, yet none were good enough to upset Cl culations. We heard of one angler losing alt dace about 13in. long (lint after last wee) salmon story these things are best left unsai4 On the whole, more members returned witho fish than with them.

The only good catch we heard of was Mr. Jolley's, who visited Northwich and return, with a general catch of about 101 b. Those w. visited Norton returned home:disappointed aft a rough time in the canal.- Other places roil; Chester way were tried without .success, the or fish on feed being gudgeon. L`p to the time writing not a specimen fish had been record this week.
TOM DIXON'S WONDERFUL RECORD

Mr. Thomas Dixon, who is a well-k no% angler amongst all Northern Anglers, gained more honours than many who have be at the sport7three times the length of time has been at it. He has only been club angli .a little over four years, but he has enou prizes to supply a Northern Annual Match, a: those who pay him a visit at his home will ha a hearty welcome, for he is only too pleased meet any anglers to talk matters over wi them. He is open at any time to give advice .novices, and many now that are members ha followed his advice - in contests with succe He is 26 years old, and although only tab seriously to angling after he had seen his 21 birthday, it is questionable if anyone can poi to such an array of prizes (with the except' of our old champion, F. Jolley). At the Finl where he is employed, he has carried off fo first prizes, first at the Howley Hotel, first .the Royal Oak Branch, first at Northwich V, unteer (open), first at Gladstone Arms, and flu in Warrington N.A. Official Match. He pref( to have his prizes in goods rather than coin, a: he points to his splendid clocks with pleasul three of them all ticking together., and keep' time to the second. To describe all his pri2 would take up more space than I am all Owe suffice it to say he has won 45 prizes in a liti over four years' fishing. His whole study is cc test fishing, providing his o*n baits, making I own rods, fishing as light as possible, al

- - - taking note of some of our older anglers. T 1 is the secret of his success. His one ambiti is to win the Challengp Cup and Medal, alo with the Northern Anglers' Championship. I favourite stream is the Weaver, and, in 1 opinion, Warrington possesses the finest anglt in the country in this water. When asked for his idea of a team, "Wl' about these?" said. Tom : "F. Jolley, H. Moor J. Barry, A. Bradley, B. Bradbury, J. Pr ton, J. Sanson, E. Hill, W. Bailey, J. Green, Griffiths and T. Dixon." These, he says, vron give -any other twelve men a good run, even they selected them from all England. Va asked for the best individual out of this tes] he said, "F. Jolley an easy first, and, tall all waters in, H. Moores a good secontl." fie remarked on not being able to get 59. plied with all the material anglers who bill their own rods require in Warrington, ai considering the Jiumber of anglers in town, 1 the many who make their own rods, or get 01';' anglers to make them; it is a wonder we calth' be supplied. This is his first year of being,' official of the N.A., and, if possible, he to continue in office, as angling is the only 'o.?_" he follows, and his opinion of Virarringu Northern Anglers is, "They mutif be one of finest societies in the country; look at the you: anglers who are joining, and it is the number novices that go to ninke a society strong." Tom Dixon is one of our young anglers th the older ones are taking an interest in, al remarks are numerous that he will be one Warrington's greatest contest anglers. He li the best wishes of all the old champions for t great effort he- has made for chimpionsh honours in so- short a time.
NOTICE. Club night at headquarters on Monday nel November 10th, at 8 p.m. A.S;

div.head: HEROISM AT SEA.
div.p: HEROISM AT SEA.
ON BOARD THE BRIGANTINE HARVESTEI

A tragedy -which may well lar compai son, in a minor way, with the burning of t: "Kent," or of "Bombay," is that the brigantine "harvester," ' which eaug fire in the South Pacific, having on board, the time, besides her crew, seven passenge including three women, and the captait wife. The fire broke out aft, and in two' minutes, such way had it made, the mains was flarin. As it chanced, land lay sor sir uult fg lwa,r nd Master -Marin Ilackson had the yards on the ioremast ra idly squared in. and the vessel's head was lowed to pay off in the direction of the shoT Even as they belayed the braces the mai mast,eame crashing down, killing two 01 t crew and smashing their one bin' boat atoms. The captain was knocked down minute later, by a fallinz block; on wlii' Jumbo a big negro who had the wheel,eall out to them to re-secure the braces of the ii per yaids, which had been loosed by the fo of the main, and after that he shouted, them to make a raft; but already the li, was too near and fierce for them to make ti attempt; whereupon he sung out to them get out upon the jib-boom, and this all vvl ,i'ere able did, the men helping the war( out, and lashing them to trie guys. All Ui time Jumbo was at the wheel and his blai face had risen up in great blisters, with ti heat of the fire. Yet he stayed there, dii•ee ing the brigantine towards a smooth san spit. The minutes passed, and some of men shouted aft to Jumbo to know how was with him. He called out something in strange voice; but what it was, no one ev! knew. They were near the shore now; oil' a few hundred yards, and again they call( to Jumbo to know how it was with him. 13' there came no coherent reply, only a brokel moaning sort of shout. They saw him dinli through a curtaift of fire and smoke. Th( the vessel took the sand smoothly and easii. running up clean and almost free, so far her bows went, of the water. In the sarr moment, through a gap in the fire curt'i they saw big Jumbo disappear into a chaos flame, as the after-decks caved in. All • ' those on the jib-boom were saved. So di black Jumbo, one of the crew of the "113, vester," even as, later, died another man somewhat similar circumstances, but war( to our own coast. Yet few know the gcs3 fame of the big negro. Let it spread. ti Most of us remember the tragedy of "Eurydice," in which over three -hundre boys were drowned—the vessel having c'al sized suddenly in a squall. It is probalb that no naval tragedy excepting, Passib that of the "Victoria" or that of the ear turret-ship "Captain," ever excited atle overwhelming and universal sympathy. yet, the Merchant Service can show th gedies just as complete and terrible. In hi middle, of the last century, an emigrant a_ with over two hundred passengers, includ_ro a large number of women and children, 7,1, caught in just such another squall. heeled right over on to her starboard beak and the sea burst in down the hatchwaP• 0, less than three minutes she was gone, a_a_i every person aboard was drowned. The WILL tragedy occupied nu more than 9ne and eighty seconds.
